meta/disclaimer/1: This tool helps you compare. It shows which party's ideas are closest to yours. It does not tell you how to vote. You decide.
meta/disclaimer/3: This tool is independent of all parties. It compares your answers with parties' promises and records. It is a starting point, not a recommendation. Parties were still announcing promises as of October 13, so check for updates. Party names and logos belong to the parties.
meta/disclaimer/5: Independent voter-information tool. Scores reflect published 2026 commitments as of October 13, 2026, weighted against the 2016-2026 governing and legislative record where the two conflict. CentreBC released a full platform on October 10 with its own costing, not independently checked; the Greens' full platform was still pending; the other parties campaign on rolling announcements without a complete costed platform. Low-confidence positions rest on prior-leader statements, 2024 platforms or silence. Party names and logos are trademarks of their owners, shown for identification only. Not an endorsement.
meta/method_summary/1: You pick answers. Each answer is close to some groups and far from others. We add it up and show the closest group.
meta/method_summary/3: Each option scores 0 (opposite) to 4 (match) for every party. Your match is the percentage of the maximum you could score. Important questions count more; skips and 'not sure' do not count. Questions where a party has no published position are left out of its score. Partly agreeing with everyone tends to favour centrist parties. Near ties show as close. Where record and words conflict, the record decides.
meta/method_summary/5: Alignment(P) = sum(w_q x s_q(P)) / sum(w_q x 4) over answered questions, where s_q(P) is the chosen option's 0-4 score for P and w_q the importance weight (low 0.5, medium 1, high 2). Skipped questions (including 'not sure') leave both sums. Questions where P has no published position leave both sums for P only. Inferred positions use an adjacent stated policy. Close: top two whole-number percentages within 3 points. Family score: mean of members' percentages per party, plus an adults-only mean (levels 3 to 5). For candidates, local questions count double on top of importance; no candidate-specific adjustment. Scores were set from the cited sources with an AI assistant (Claude) and checked by separate review passes; every score, rationale and source is public at github.com/vinistoisr/bc-vote-helper. Reading level changes wording only.
levels/0/hint: Short sentences and everyday words. No names of laws, no numbers.
levels/1/hint: Plain words with a few real examples. Terms explained as they come up.
levels/2/hint: The real issues in everyday words. Some policy names, few numbers.
levels/3/hint: Specific promises, key figures and the main trade-offs.
levels/4/hint: Bill numbers, rates, dollar figures, court rulings and vote counts.
parties/ndp/leader_note: Premier since November 2022; former Attorney General and housing minister.
parties/ndp/one_liner/1: The party that has run the government since 2017. It wants government to run more programs and set rules to help people.
parties/ndp/one_liner/3: In government since 2017. Uses provincial power actively (housing taxes, zoning rules, big projects) and asks higher earners to pay more, but has reversed several policies under pressure.
parties/ndp/one_liner/5: Governing since 2017. Record: speculation and vacancy tax (2018), Bills 44 and 47 density mandates (2023), Bill 36 Surrey police transition (2023), consumer carbon tax repeal (2025), decriminalization ended (2026), Budget 2026 deficit $13.3B (revised $13.8B). 2026: +2 points on brackets above $190,405, 24.5% above $1M, 10 c/L fuel tax cut, grocery margin caps, ICBC freeze to 2030, 20 clinics.
parties/ndp/record_summary/3: The NDP has governed for nine years. It is building the Surrey-Langley SkyTrain and a new Surrey hospital, and it brought in $10-a-day child care, then froze new spaces. It taxed empty homes, ordered Surrey's switch to a city police force and passed the law on Indigenous rights (DRIPA). It later ended the drug decriminalization trial, scrapped the carbon tax on fuel and paused a promised $1,000 rebate. The deficit reached its highest dollar amount ever, and credit agencies lowered BC's rating in 2026.
parties/ndp/record_summary/5: Party-line votes: Bill 45 (43-39, 2018), Bill 36 (56-27, 2023), Bills 44 (housing density) and 46 (development financing) (2023), Bill 7 (48-44), Bills 14 and 15 (46-46, Speaker's vote, 2025), Bill 3 budget measures (46-42). Reversals: Bill 7 Part 4 withdrawn, $1,000 rebate paused, carbon tax to $0, decriminalization not renewed, witnessed-only safer supply, EV mandate dropped, DRIPA suspension bill withdrawn, vehicle levy ruled out. Budget 2026: lowest bracket 5.06% to 5.60%, indexation frozen 2027-2030. Four downgrades in 2026.
parties/conservative/leader_note: Interim leader since September 20, 2026, after Kerry-Lynne Findlay resigned; party rules bar an interim leader from seeking the permanent job.
parties/conservative/one_liner/1: The main party trying to replace the government. It wants lower taxes, fewer rules for business and more gas and mining jobs.
parties/conservative/one_liner/3: Opposition since 2024. Promises a $1,000 income tax cut and no new taxes; would repeal DRIPA and SOGI 123, end safe supply, expand mandatory treatment and double gas production. Four leaders in a year; no costed plan.
parties/conservative/one_liner/5: Opposition since 2024 (44 seats). 2026: basic personal amount to $32,000 (about $1,050 each; uncosted; outside estimate $2.5B a year), no new taxes, repeal DRIPA and SOGI 123, end safe supply, mandatory treatment, 250 police, 500 RCMP, 50 prosecutors, double gas output by 2032, 120 Day Permitting Act, ICBC hybrid tort, portable LTC funding. No deficit target or balance date.
parties/conservative/record_summary/3: Its 2024 calls to end the carbon tax and for mandatory treatment and bail reform preceded NDP action. Opposed nearly all NDP bills. Most MLAs backed first reading of gender identity and Human Rights Code repeal bills, citing courtesy. Many backed DRIPA as BC Liberals, then voted for first reading of two bills to repeal it in 2025 and 2026; both were defeated. Three leaders since Rustad resigned in December 2025.
parties/conservative/record_summary/5: Nay on Bills 7, 14, 15, 32 (Mental Health Amendment), the Supply Act 2025 and Bill 3 (2026); non-confidence amendment lost 44-48. Yea at first reading on independents' property rights (40-48), gender identity (38-49) and Human Rights Code repeal (37-50) bills. BC Liberals, including Rustad, backed DRIPA (82-0 in committee, 2019); as Conservatives, every Conservative MLA present, including Rustad, Halford and Doerkson, voted yea at first reading on independent Jordan Kealy's DRIPA Statute Repeal Act (lost 43-48, November 19, 2025) and on Halford's DRIPA Repeal Act (lost 44-47, April 22, 2026). Rustad resigned December 4, 2025 after the caucus moved against him, then Halford (interim), Findlay (113 days), Doerkson (interim). 2024 pledges (rent rebate, Bill 44 repeal, balance in two terms) dropped.
parties/green/leader_note: Leader since September 2025; does not hold a seat. Two MLAs at dissolution.
parties/green/one_liner/1: A smaller party. It wants to protect nature, tax the richest people more, and spend more on child care, transit and homes.
parties/green/one_liner/3: Two seats. A wealth tax on fortunes over $50 million would fund free child care, free youth and senior transit, and non-market housing. Would strengthen DRIPA and SOGI 123, restore decriminalization, stop new fossil fuel projects. Revenue estimate method unpublished.
parties/green/one_liner/5: Two MLAs; 8.2% in 2024. Fair Share Act: one-time 5-20% levy on net wealth above $50M, then 2-5% yearly (party estimate $22.2B, then $5.4B; uncosted). 26,000 non-market homes yearly, vacancy control, free child care by 2031, free transit under 25 and over 65, health centre per riding, PR bill within 100 days, decriminalization, no new fossil fuel development. Platform pending.
parties/green/record_summary/3: Backed NDP confidence votes under written deals (2017-2020, 2024-2026), gaining the corporate and union donation ban and the 2018 voting referendum. Opposed the fast-track laws and the carbon tax repeal. Voted for the 2026 budget at second reading, against at third. Left the deal in February 2026, citing stalled promises.
parties/green/record_summary/5: CASA 2017-2020: Bill 3 donation ban and 2018 PR referendum (lost 61.3 to 38.7). Yea on Bill 45 spec tax (2018) after amendments; nay on Bills 44 and 46 (2023); yea on Supply Act 2025; nay on Bills 14 and 15 (2025), the carbon tax repeal and Bill 3 at third reading (2026); nay on Armstrong's gender identity, Human Rights Code repeal and drug recovery bills. NDP accord (December 2024) not renewed February 9, 2026.
parties/centrebc/leader_note: Named leader September 22, 2026; the party's only incumbent MLA (Surrey-Cloverdale, running in Surrey South). Fourth leader since the party formed in March 2025.
parties/centrebc/one_liner/1: A new party in the political centre. It wants a cost on every promise, a slow return to a balanced budget, and to replace the law on Indigenous rights with treaty deals.
parties/centrebc/one_liner/3: New centre-right party, 35 candidates. Its October 10 platform, costed by the party, cuts the bottom tax rate, balances the budget by 2034-35 with 10,000 fewer public jobs by attrition, keeps ICBC and health care public, adds 650 treatment beds and 500 RCMP, and would repeal DRIPA for a treaty-based law. Seven of its eight MLAs rejoined the Conservatives at the election call.
parties/centrebc/one_liner/5: Registered March 2025; leaders Kirkpatrick, Bernier, Milobar, Sturko (September 2026). Platform October 10 ($13.7B over four years, party costing): first bracket 5.06%, renter's credit $600, balance 2034/35 in law, Independent Budget Officer, 10,000 positions by attrition; repeal DRIPA and s. 8.1 for a treaty law (reverses its August stance); industrial carbon pricing kept, 2030 target reset to 20%; 650 treatment beds, involuntary assessments; 500 RCMP, 60 Crown; ICBC public, rate cap; 20,000 child care spaces, 25,000 seats; Surrey Memorial tower. Silent on SOGI 123, zoning law, safer supply, electoral reform.
parties/centrebc/record_summary/3: No governing record. At the election call, then-leader Milobar and seven of eight MLAs rejoined the Conservatives. Sturko was elected in 2024 as a Conservative on a platform to repeal DRIPA and remove SOGI 123, left that caucus in 2025, and voted against first reading of gender identity and Human Rights Code repeal bills but for first reading of two bills to repeal DRIPA.
parties/centrebc/record_summary/5: Sturko (elected 2022 as BC Liberal; Conservative 2024; removed from caucus September 22, 2025) voted nay at first reading on the Gender Ideology and Child Protection Act and the Human Rights Code Repeal Act (February 2026) and yea at first reading on the DRIPA repeal bills (43-48, November 19, 2025; 44-47, April 22, 2026); chaired the police complaints committee. As MLA she introduced Mental Health Act amendments on family contact before involuntary admission and opposed non-medical safer supply. The October 10 platform supersedes statements by prior leaders Kirkpatrick and Bernier; on DRIPA it reverses Bernier's August 2026 'no repeal' position.
parties/onebc/leader_note: Co-founded the party in June 2025 after being removed from the Conservative caucus in March 2025 over posts about residential school burial claims; removed and reinstated as leader by the party board in December 2025.
parties/onebc/one_liner/1: A small new party. It wants much lower taxes, fewer rules, and to end some laws it sees as unfair.
parties/onebc/one_liner/3: New right-wing party, 34 candidates. Would cut every tax rate by 25%, balance in four years, repeal DRIPA and SOGI 123, end safe supply and consumption sites, allow private care alongside public, open car insurance to competition. All uncosted.
parties/onebc/one_liner/5: Founded 2025 (Brodie, Armstrong). Repeal DRIPA, void UNDRIP, end voluntary land transfers, seek Indian Act repeal; 25% cut to every bracket including corporate; PST down 2 points; balance in four years; end safe supply, consumption sites; involuntary rehab; private care, HPOA repeal; end ICBC monopoly, no-fault; repeal SOGI 123; Parental Bill of Rights; end mail-in and early voting. All uncosted.
parties/onebc/record_summary/3: No governing record. Its MLAs' bills to restrict youth gender transition, ban land acknowledgements and protect property rights were all defeated. Its board removed and reinstated leader Brodie in December 2025. It is standing aside for eight Conservatives who share its SOGI views.
parties/onebc/record_summary/5: Private members' bills by its MLAs: Protecting Minors from Gender Transition Act (Armstrong) defeated 48-40 at first reading (October 8, 2025); Land Acknowledgement Prohibition Act (Brodie) defeated 85-5 at first reading (October 23, 2025); Property Rights Protection Act (Brodie) 40-48 (October 29, 2025). Brodie voted yea on the DRIPA repeal bills moved by independent Jordan Kealy (lost 43-48, November 2025) and Conservative Trevor Halford (lost 44-47, April 2026). The board removed Brodie as leader in December 2025 and she was reinstated December 21. Brodie was its only MLA when the election was called; Brent Chapman announced a move to OneBC on September 22, 2026, but did not file it before dissolution, so party standings did not change (Canadian Press); he is not running. Not running against eight named Conservatives.
other_parties_note/3: Not scored, because they have not published platforms to compare: BC Libertarian (4 candidates), Communist (4), Christian Heritage (3), CanWest (2), Freedom (1), and 14 independent or unaffiliated candidates. They are listed with your riding's candidates when they are on your ballot. BC United is not running.
other_parties_note/5: Not scored, because no platforms were found: BC Libertarian (4 candidates), Communist Party of BC (4), Christian Heritage Party of BC (3), CanWest Party (2), Freedom Party of BC (1), plus 7 independent and 7 unaffiliated candidates, per the Elections BC candidate list (October 12, 2026; 355 candidates in all). They appear in the riding section when they are on the voter's ballot. BC United ran no candidates.

questions/q_cost_of_living/prompt/1: Food, gas and rent cost more now. How should the government help people with costs?
questions/q_cost_of_living/prompt/2: Groceries, gas and rent cost more than they used to. How should the province help families pay for them?
questions/q_cost_of_living/prompt/3: Cost of living is the top issue for BC voters. Which approach should the province take to make life more affordable?
questions/q_cost_of_living/prompt/4: Which cost-of-living approach should come first: tax cuts, price rules, more help for low incomes, or targeted credits and rate caps?
questions/q_cost_of_living/prompt/5: Which mix of cost-of-living measures should the province put first: broad tax cuts, price controls, income support, or targeted credits and rate caps?
questions/q_cost_of_living/context/1: Prices for food, gas and rent have gone up. Every party says it wants to make life cost less. Some want to cut taxes. Some want rules that keep prices down. Some want more help for people with low incomes.
questions/q_cost_of_living/context/2: Prices were 2.9% higher in July 2026 than a year before. Every party promises to make life more affordable, but they disagree on how. The province could cut taxes for everyone, limit some prices, give more money to people with the lowest incomes, or lower costs for businesses so they can charge less.
questions/q_cost_of_living/context/3: Cost of living is the top issue for BC voters. In 2025 the NDP government ended the consumer carbon tax, but it paused a $1,000 rebate, and in 2026 it raised the lowest tax rate. Every party promises relief in a different way. Some would cut income taxes for everyone. One would cap markups on gas and some groceries. Another would raise support for the poorest people. Others mix smaller tax cuts with limits on power and car insurance increases.
questions/q_cost_of_living/context/4: Cost of living ranks first for 56% of BC voters, according to an Ipsos poll. The minimum wage is $18.25 an hour and rises with inflation each year. In 2025 the NDP government paused a $1,000 grocery rebate, and in 2026 it raised the lowest income tax rate. The parties' price tags are hard to compare. The Conservative and OneBC tax cuts have no published cost. The Greens have not published how they estimated their wealth tax revenue, and CentreBC's cost figures are its own, not checked by anyone else.
questions/q_cost_of_living/context/5: Consumer prices rose 2.9% in the year to July 2026. The NDP government ended the consumer carbon tax in April 2025, and Budget 2026 raised the lowest income tax rate from 5.06% to 5.60%. The NDP proposes a 10-cent-a-litre fuel tax cut with a BC Utilities Commission cap on gas margins, caps on grocery margins, and a freeze on Insurance Corporation of British Columbia (ICBC) rates. The Conservatives would raise the basic personal amount, the income you earn tax-free, to $32,000. The Greens would raise income assistance to the poverty line and make transit free for people under 25 and over 65. CentreBC would return the lowest rate to 5.06%, raise the renter's credit to $600 and cap BC Hydro and ICBC increases. OneBC would cut every income tax rate by 25% and the provincial sales tax (PST) by two points.
questions/q_cost_of_living/options/a/tex: Cut income tax by a quarter for everyone, businesses too, and cut sales tax.
Cut every income tax rate by a quarter, for people and companies, and lower the sales tax.
Cut every income tax rate by 25%, including the rate companies pay, and lower the provincial sales tax.
Cut every personal and corporate income tax rate by 25%, and cut the provincial sales tax (PST) by two points.
Cut every personal and corporate income tax bracket by 25%, and lower the provincial sales tax (PST) by two percentage points.
questions/q_cost_of_living/options/b/tex: Raise the amount people can earn before paying income tax. Add no new taxes.
Raise the amount you can earn tax-free, so most workers save about $1,000 a year. Add no new taxes.
Raise the tax-free amount to $32,000, worth about $1,000 a year for most workers, and add no new taxes.
Raise the basic personal amount (income you earn tax-free) to $32,000, about $1,000 per taxpayer, pledge no new taxes, and temporarily remove PST from Canadian alcohol.

Raise the basic personal amount from $13,216 to $32,000 (about $1,000 a year per filer, the same for everyone earning over about $40,000), add no new taxes, and temporarily remove PST from Canadian alcohol.
questions/q_cost_of_living/options/c/tex: Cut the gas tax, limit milk and egg prices, and freeze car insurance rates.
Cut the gas tax, limit store markups on milk, eggs and poultry, and freeze car insurance rates.
Cut the gas tax by 10 cents a litre, cap store markups on milk, eggs and poultry, and freeze car insurance rates.
Suspend 10 cents a litre of fuel tax and cap gas station margins, cap margins on dairy, eggs and poultry, and freeze ICBC rates.
Suspend 10 cents a litre of fuel tax with a BC Utilities Commission cap on gas margins, cap dairy, egg and poultry margins, and freeze ICBC rates until 2030.
questions/q_cost_of_living/options/d/tex: Give more help to people with the lowest incomes, paid for by the richest.
Raise government support for the poorest people to the poverty line, paid for by a tax on the very rich.
Raise income assistance to the poverty line and make transit free for young people and seniors, paid for by a tax on large fortunes.
Raise income assistance to the poverty line, move toward a living wage, and make transit free for people under 25 and over 65, paid for by a wealth tax.
Index income assistance to the Market Basket Measure poverty line, move the minimum wage toward a living wage, make transit free under 25 and over 65, and tax net worth over $50 million.
questions/q_cost_of_living/options/e/tex: Undo this year's tax rise and give renters a bigger tax break.
Undo this year's rise in the lowest tax rate, raise the renter's credit, and cap Hydro and car insurance increases.
Reverse the 2026 rise in the lowest tax rate, raise the renter's credit, add a transit-pass credit, cap Hydro and car insurance increases.
Return the lowest tax rate to 5.06%, raise the renter's credit to $600, add a 15% transit and ferry pass credit, cap Hydro and ICBC increases at inflation, and widen PST relief on machinery.

Cut the first tax bracket from 5.60% to 5.06% in January 2027, raise the renter's credit to $600 (indexed, full up to $80,000 income), add a 15% refundable commuter credit, and hold Hydro and ICBC increases at or below inflation.
questions/q_cost_of_living/party_positio: This party wants to cut the gas tax, limit some grocery prices and freeze car insurance rates.

The NDP promises a 10-cent gas tax cut, caps on grocery markups and a freeze on car insurance rates until 2030. In government it ended Medical Services Plan premiums and the consumer carbon tax, but it also paused a $1,000 rebate and raised the lowest income tax rate.

The NDP would suspend 10 cents a litre of fuel tax, with a BC Utilities Commission cap on gas margins; the Canadian Press reports it would cost about $250 million, and the party's release gives no cost. It would cap dairy, egg and poultry margins and freeze ICBC rates to spring 2030. In government it ended Medical Services Plan premiums in 2020 and the consumer carbon tax in 2025, and paused the $1,000 grocery rebate in 2025. In 2026 it raised the lowest tax rate from 5.06% to 5.60% and froze bracket indexing for 2027 to 2030.
This party would let people earn more before paying income tax, and it promises no new taxes.

The Conservatives promise to raise the tax-free amount to $32,000 (about $1,000 a year), add no new taxes while in government, and remove provincial sales tax from Canadian alcohol until the trade conflict ends. The plan has no published cost and gives nothing to people who pay no provincial income tax. They would also undo the 2026 rise in interest on property taxes that homeowners 55 and older put off paying.

The Conservatives would raise the basic personal amount from $13,216 to $32,000, which the party says is worth about $1,000 a year; the saving is the same for everyone earning over about $40,000. It is a non-refundable credit, so people who owe no tax get nothing. The party has not costed it; an NDP candidate calls it a $2.5 billion hole and economist Ross Hickey estimates about $2 billion a year. It promises no new or higher taxes while in government, no PST on Canadian beer, wine and spirits until the trade conflict ends, and a three-year PST exemption on business machinery, tools and software. It would reverse the 2026 change to the Property Tax Deferment Program, which moved taxes deferred from 2026 on from simple interest at prime minus 2% to prime plus 2% compounded monthly. It voted against the 2026 bill (Bill 2) that raised the lowest rate.
This party wants more help for people with low incomes, and free public transit for young people and seniors.

The Greens would raise income assistance to the poverty line, move toward a living wage, and make transit free for people under 25 and over 65. A tax on fortunes over $50 million would pay for it. The party has not published how it estimated that tax's revenue.

The Greens would raise income assistance to the Market Basket Measure poverty line and index it, move the minimum wage toward a living wage, make transit free under 25 and over 65, and make large essential-goods companies disclose their margins, with limits where prices or margins are excessive. A wealth tax would pay for it; the party estimates $22.2 billion in year one and $5.4 billion a year after, but has not shown how it modelled those figures. The party has two MLAs. In 2018 it secured a change to the speculation tax.
This party would undo this year's tax rise, give renters a bigger tax break, and cap power and car insurance increases.

CentreBC's platform would return the lowest tax rate to 5.06%, raise the renter's credit to $600, add a 15% transit-pass credit, cap Hydro and car insurance increases at inflation, and add 20,000 $10-a-day child care spaces. It has no price caps on groceries or gas and nothing on minimum wage or income assistance.

The platform cuts the first bracket from 5.60% to 5.06% from January 2027, about $540 a year for a two-income family. It raises the renter's credit from $400 to $600 and adds a 15% refundable commuter credit. Hydro increases are capped at inflation and 3%, and ICBC rates are frozen to spring 2027, then held at or below inflation. The party costs its tax relief at $4.5 billion over four years. It has no position on the basic personal amount, price caps, minimum wage or assistance rates.
This party wants everyone to pay much less tax. It does not propose limits on prices.

OneBC would cut every income tax rate by 25%, including the rate companies pay, cut the provincial sales tax by two points, and phase out the public insurer's monopoly on car insurance. It has published no costing and no plans on prices or income assistance.

OneBC would cut every personal and corporate income tax bracket by 25%, lower the PST by two points, phase out ICBC's monopoly and end its no-fault system, and scrap the BC Energy Step Code. It has published no costing and no policy on prices, assistance or wages, yet promises a balanced budget within four years alongside these cuts.
questions/q_taxes_deficit/prompt/1: The province spends more money than it takes in. What should it do?
questions/q_taxes_deficit/prompt/2: BC spends more than it takes in. How should it close the gap, and who should pay?
questions/q_taxes_deficit/prompt/3: BC is spending far more than it takes in. How should it handle that, and who should pay more or less tax?
questions/q_taxes_deficit/prompt/4: Which path should BC take on its deficit: tax cuts, taxing high incomes or wealth, spending restraint, or borrowing to protect services?
questions/q_taxes_deficit/prompt/5: Which fiscal and tax path do you support for dealing with BC's $13.8 billion deficit?
questions/q_taxes_deficit/context/1: The province spends more money than it takes in, so it borrows the rest. Borrowing costs extra because of interest. The province could spend less, raise some taxes, or keep borrowing to protect services.
questions/q_taxes_deficit/context/2: BC expects a deficit of about $13.8 billion this year, which means it spends that much more than it takes in. It borrows to cover the gap, and that adds interest costs. It can spend less, tax some people more, keep borrowing until the economy grows, or mix these.
questions/q_taxes_deficit/context/3: BC's deficit, the gap between what it spends and what it takes in, is about $13.8 billion. That is a record in dollars. All four credit rating agencies lowered BC's rating in 2026. No party has a fully costed plan, so the parties' promises and price tags are hard to compare.
questions/q_taxes_deficit/context/4: BC now forecasts a $13.8 billion deficit this year, up from $13.3 billion in Budget 2026, and debt rising to 37% of gross domestic product (GDP), the size of BC's economy, by 2028-29. The parties' plans differ in size. The NDP's higher tax on high incomes would raise about $1 billion a year. The Conservatives have not costed their tax cut; an economist puts it at about $2 billion a year. The Greens estimate their wealth tax would raise $22.2 billion in its first year. CentreBC says its promises cost $13.7 billion over four years and would balance the budget in 2034-35. OneBC has not costed its cuts.
questions/q_taxes_deficit/context/5: Budget 2026 projected a $13.3 billion deficit for 2026-27, and the September quarterly update raised the forecast to $13.8 billion. Taxpayer-supported debt is projected to reach 37.4% of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2028-29, and all four credit rating agencies downgraded BC this year. The NDP would add two points to the top two income tax brackets and charge 24.5% above $1 million (about $1 billion a year), and plans 15,000 fewer full-time-equivalent public positions. The Conservatives would raise the basic personal amount to $32,000 (not costed by the party; an economist puts it at about $2 billion a year and an NDP candidate at $2.5 billion) and set no deficit target. The Greens would tax wealth above $50 million ($22.2 billion in year one, party estimate). CentreBC would write a 2034-35 balanced budget into law, cut 10,000 positions as people leave and return the lowest rate to 5.06% (its tax relief costs $4.5 billion over four years, party costing). OneBC would cut taxes 25% and balance in four years.
questions/q_taxes_deficit/options/a/text: Cut taxes a lot and spend much less, to stop borrowing within four years.
Cut everyone's taxes deeply and cut spending, so the budget balances within four years.
Cut every income tax rate by 25% and cut spending enough to balance the budget within four years.
Cut every income tax bracket by 25% and the PST by two points, with a firm target to balance the budget within four years.
Cut every personal and corporate bracket by 25% and the PST by two points, balance the budget within four years, and put part of any surplus toward debt.
questions/q_taxes_deficit/options/b/text: Cut taxes a little and let a growing economy close the gap over time.
Cut taxes by about $1,000 per worker, add no new taxes, and let job growth close the gap over time.
Give a $1,000 income tax cut, add no new taxes, protect health funding, and rely on growth instead of a date to balance.
A $1,000-per-taxpayer income tax cut, a no-new-taxes pledge and a promise to protect current health funding, with resource growth to close the gap and no deficit target.

Raise the basic personal amount to $32,000 (not costed; estimates run from about $2 billion to $2.5 billion a year), add no new or higher taxes, protect current health funding, and rely on resource-led growth, with no balance date.
questions/q_taxes_deficit/options/c/text: By law, stop borrowing in about eight years. Undo this year's tax rise.
Balance the budget by law in about eight years, undo this year's tax rise, and cut government jobs without layoffs.
Write a 2034-35 balanced budget into law, undo the 2026 rise in the lowest tax rate, and shrink the public service as people leave.
Legislate a balanced budget by 2034-35, checked by an Independent Budget Officer, return the lowest tax rate to 5.06%, cut 10,000 public positions through attrition, and review all spending.

A Balanced Budget and Spending Control Act (balance in 2034-35, an Independent Budget Officer, ministers' pay at risk), the first bracket back to 5.06%, 10,000 positions cut by attrition, and zero-based spending reviews.
questions/q_taxes_deficit/options/d/text: Keep borrowing so schools and hospitals are not cut. Top earners pay more tax.
Keep borrowing to protect services, keep this year's tax changes, and raise taxes on top earners.
Keep borrowing to protect services, keep the 2026 rise in the lowest tax rate, and tax top earners more.
Run deficits above $11 billion a year instead of cutting services, shrink the public service through attrition, keep the Budget 2026 tax measures, and raise rates on income above $190,405.

Run deficits of $13.3 billion, $12.2 billion and $11.4 billion (Budget 2026 figures; the first is now forecast at $13.8 billion), cut 15,000 full-time-equivalent positions, keep the Budget 2026 tax measures, and raise the top two brackets by two points, with 24.5% above $1 million.
questions/q_taxes_deficit/options/e/text: A new tax on the richest pays for child care, transit, housing and debt.
Tax people worth over $50 million and spend the money on child care, transit, housing and paying down debt.
Tax fortunes over $50 million and use the money for child care, transit, housing and debt.
A one-time, then yearly, wealth tax above $50 million, plus a windfall tax and higher resource royalties, with revenue split between programs and debt.
Tax net worth above $50 million (one-time 5%, 10% or 20% by tier, then 2%, 3% or 5% a year), add a windfall tax and 50% net-profit royalties, and fund programs and debt.
questions/q_taxes_deficit/party_position: This party would keep borrowing to protect hospitals and schools, and raise taxes on top earners.

The NDP plans deficits above $11 billion a year until 2028-29 and 15,000 fewer public sector jobs. It proposes higher tax on income above $190,405, raising about $1 billion a year. In February 2026 it raised the lowest tax rate and stopped tax brackets from rising with inflation.

Budget 2026 plans deficits of $13.3 billion, $12.2 billion and $11.4 billion, with debt rising from 30.6% to 37.4% of GDP, 15,000 fewer full-time-equivalent positions, a 5.60% lowest rate and paused bracket indexing. On October 4 the NDP proposed top rates of 18.8%, 22.5% and 24.5% from 2027, raising $1 billion by 2028-29. All four credit rating agencies downgraded BC in 2026. Eby said he chose not to cut 'to meet a credit rating'.
This party would cut taxes, add no new ones, and count on more jobs to close the gap.

The Conservatives promise a $1,000 tax cut, no new taxes and no health cuts, relying on resource growth. They have published no costing or date to balance the budget. They voted against the last two budgets and did not repeat their 2024 promise to balance within two terms.

The Conservatives would raise the basic personal amount to $32,000 (no party costing; economist Ross Hickey puts it at about $2 billion a year and an NDP candidate at $2.5 billion), add no new or higher taxes and protect current health funding. Their other pledges are not costed. Interim leader Lorne Doerkson says the plan is to 'supercharge the economy ... that is our revenue'. There is no deficit target. They voted against the 2025-26 Supply Act and the 2026 budget bill (Bill 2) and have not repeated the 2024 pledge to balance within two terms.
This party would tax the richest people more to pay for child care, transit and housing.

The Greens propose a tax on fortunes over $50 million, plus a windfall tax and higher resource royalties. They project $22 billion in the first year for child care, transit, housing and debt, but have not published how they estimated it. They voted against the 2026 budget.

The Greens' Fair Share Act would charge a one-time 5%, 10% or 20% on wealth above $50 million, $100 million and $1 billion, then 2%, 3% or 5% a year. The party estimates $22.2 billion in year one and $5.4 billion a year after; its October 11 FAQ says a new provincial bureau would value net worth and payment could be deferred up to five years. Separately, it plans a windfall tax, a minimum corporate tax and royalties aimed at 50% of net profits. Both Green MLAs voted against the 2026 budget bill (Bill 2) at second and third reading, and backed the 2025-26 Supply Act under their accord with the NDP.
This party would put a price on every promise, balance the budget slowly without layoffs, and lower the lowest tax rate.

CentreBC's platform cuts the deficit every year and writes a 2034-35 balanced budget into law, checked by an Independent Budget Officer. It would cut 10,000 public positions as people leave, and return the lowest tax rate to 5.06%. It costs its whole platform at $13.7 billion over four years, plus $7.8 billion borrowed for capital projects.

The platform cuts the deficit to about $9.0 billion by 2030-31 and balances in 2034-35. A Balanced Budget and Spending Control Act would create an Independent Budget Officer and cut ministers' pay if the target is missed. Spending would grow 1.5 points a year less than Budget 2026 plans, with 10,000 positions cut by attrition. Savings total $5.6 billion and tax relief $4.5 billion over four years, by the party's own costing. Its fallback list sets a manufacturing fund at $30 million, below its $60 million pledge.
This party wants everyone to pay much less tax and to stop borrowing within a few years.

OneBC promises to cut every income tax rate by 25% and the provincial sales tax by two points, and still balance the budget within four years. It has not shown how the numbers add up or what it would cut.

OneBC would cut every bracket by 25%, including corporate, lower the PST by two points, balance within four years with part of any surplus going to debt, and audit 176,000 regulations. It has published no costing and no list of spending cuts. It has the shortest balance target of any party, and also the largest tax cuts.
questions/q_housing/prompt/1: Homes cost a lot to buy or rent. How should the government help?
questions/q_housing/prompt/2: Buying or renting a home in BC is expensive. How should the province help people afford housing?
questions/q_housing/prompt/3: What should the province do about the cost of housing?
questions/q_housing/prompt/4: Which housing approach should the province take: lower builder costs, taxes on empty homes, public building, faster approvals, or fewer rules?
questions/q_housing/prompt/5: Which mix of housing taxes, zoning rules, approval reforms and public building should the province pursue?
questions/q_housing/context/1: Homes cost a lot in BC. The government already charges extra tax on some empty homes. Some parties want fewer rules and fees so builders build more. Others want higher taxes on empty homes, or more homes built by government.
questions/q_housing/context/2: Since 2018 the province has taxed some homes left empty, and since 2023 it has made cities allow more homes on each lot. Rents in the Vancouver area are falling, but prices are still high and homelessness is up. Parties disagree on whether to cut builder costs, raise taxes on empty homes, or build more non-profit homes.
questions/q_housing/context/3: Housing ranks third among BC voters' concerns. The NDP government added a tax on homes left empty (the speculation and vacancy tax) in 2018 and a tax on homes resold quickly (the flipping tax) in 2025. A 2023 law makes cities allow up to four homes on most lots. Rents in the Vancouver area are easing, but homelessness is up. The parties disagree on whether to add more taxes and rules or remove them.
questions/q_housing/context/4: Metro Vancouver rents are falling and the rental vacancy rate is at a 30-year high, but prices are about 20% above 2016 levels and homelessness is up. The NDP government brought in the speculation and vacancy tax (SVT) on empty homes in 2018 and a flipping tax on quick resales in 2025. A 2023 law requires cities to allow up to four homes on most lots. In 2026 the NDP proposed doubling the SVT and taxing condos left unsold for over a year.
questions/q_housing/context/5: In Metro Vancouver, 3.7% of purpose-built rentals were vacant in 2025, and the benchmark home price was about $1.08 million in September 2026, down 5.5% from a year earlier. Metro Vancouver started 27,185 homes in 2025, and Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) forecasts fewer starts each year to 2028. The 2025 count found 5,232 homeless people, up 9%. The 2018 law creating the speculation and vacancy tax (Bill 45) passed 43 to 39, with the Greens for it and the BC Liberals against. The 2023 law letting up to four homes be built on most city lots (Bill 44) passed 45 to 29; BC United and the Greens voted against it. The 2023 law requiring more homes near transit (Bill 47) passed unanimously.
questions/q_housing/options/a/text/1: Cut fees, taxes and rules on building, and add no new housing taxes.
questions/q_housing/options/a/text/2: Cut taxes, fees and rules on building so builders build more, and add no new housing taxes.
questions/q_housing/options/a/text/3: Cut taxes, fees and red tape on building, and add no new housing taxes.
questions/q_housing/options/a/text/4: Cut fees and approval delays, drop new housing taxes, and return Metro Vancouver's housing role to the province and cities.
questions/q_housing/options/a/text/5: Reject the Unsold Condo Tax and a higher speculation tax, cut permit times and development charges, and remove Metro Vancouver's housing role.
questions/q_housing/options/b/text/1: Tax empty homes more, and make cities allow more homes on each lot.
questions/q_housing/options/b/text/2: Raise taxes on empty and unsold homes, and make cities allow more homes on each lot.
questions/q_housing/options/b/text/3: Raise taxes on empty homes and unsold condos, keep the tax on quick resales, and keep rules that make cities allow more homes.
questions/q_housing/options/b/text/4: Raise the speculation tax, add a tax on unsold condos, and keep the flipping tax and provincial rules for four homes per lot and density near transit.
questions/q_housing/options/b/text/5: Raise the speculation and vacancy tax to 2% (5% for foreign owners), add an Unsold Condo Tax from 2%, keep the flipping tax, Bills 44 and 47 and municipal targets, and continue BC Builds.
questions/q_housing/options/c/text/1: Build many more non-profit homes. Limit rent increases when a new renter moves in.
questions/q_housing/options/c/text/2: Build thousands of non-profit homes a year, and keep rent limits when a new renter moves in.
questions/q_housing/options/c/text/3: Build or protect about 26,000 non-profit and public homes a year, and keep rent limits when a new renter moves in.
questions/q_housing/options/c/text/4: Public and non-profit building of about 26,000 affordable homes a year, a restarted Community Housing Fund, and vacancy control so rent limits stay between tenants.
questions/q_housing/options/c/text/5: Build 26,000 non-market homes a year, reinstate the Community and Indigenous Housing Funds, bring in vacancy control, and pay for it with a wealth levy and land tax.
questions/q_housing/options/d/text/1: Give cities deadlines to approve homes, cut fees on rentals, build homes in factories.
questions/q_housing/options/d/text/2: Set deadlines for city permits, halve fees on new rentals, build factory-made homes, and build more below-market homes.
questions/q_housing/options/d/text/3: Set provincial deadlines for city approvals, halve development fees on rentals, build factory-made homes, and double below-market building.
questions/q_housing/options/d/text/4: Set six-month rezoning and eight-week permit deadlines, halve development charges on rentals, build 5,000 factory-built homes a year, double the below-market program, and add no new housing taxes.
questions/q_housing/options/d/text/5: Set a 2028 standard of six-month rezonings and eight-week permits with fee refunds if missed, halve development charges on rental and below-market homes, build 5,000 prefab homes a year, and grow BC Builds to 20,000 by 2031.
questions/q_housing/options/e/text/1: Drop energy-saving building rules that add cost, and stop cities from limiting rent.
questions/q_housing/options/e/text/2: Remove energy-efficiency rules for new buildings that raise costs, and stop cities from limiting rent.
questions/q_housing/options/e/text/3: Scrap the Step Code, BC's energy rules for new buildings, and block cities from bringing in rent control.
questions/q_housing/options/e/text/4: Eliminate the BC Energy Step Code, pass a law against municipal rent control, and rely on the market to add supply.
questions/q_housing/options/e/text/5: Eliminate the BC Energy Step Code, prohibit municipal rent control, and rely on market supply with no demand-side taxes or zoning mandates.
questions/q_housing/party_positions/ndp/: This party taxes empty homes and makes cities allow more homes. It wants higher taxes on empty and unsold homes.

The NDP created the speculation tax on empty homes, a flipping tax on quick resales and the four-home zoning law. It would double the speculation tax to 2% (5% for foreign owners) and tax condos unsold for over a year. Rents have fallen, but home building slowed and homelessness rose.

In government the NDP brought in the speculation and vacancy tax (2018), the 2023 housing laws (Bills 44, 46 and 47), the flipping tax (2025) and BC Builds, and paused Community Housing Fund intake in 2026. It now pledges a 2% speculation tax (5% foreign) and an Unsold Condo Tax starting at 2% and rising one point a year, with no revenue estimate. Vacancy is 3.7%, two-bedroom rent for new tenants fell from $2,883 to $2,696, starts are forecast to fall to 2028, and homelessness rose 9%.
questions/q_housing/party_positions/cons: This party says taxes and rules make homes cost too much, and wants building to be cheaper.

The Conservatives promise lower building and buying costs, no new housing taxes, and taking housing away from Metro Vancouver's regional government. They have taken no 2026 position on the speculation tax or the density law and have not repeated their 2024 rebate and repeal ideas.

In 2026 the Conservatives reject the NDP's housing tax plan (the Unsold Condo Tax and a higher speculation tax), saying 'every new tax on housing ends up in the price a family pays', pledge no new taxes, and would return Metro Vancouver's housing and climate roles to the province and cities. They have not said whether they would repeal the speculation tax, change Bills 44 or 47, touch rent control or revive the 2024 rebate. MLAs of the parties before them voted against the speculation tax in 2018 and Bills 44 and 46, and for Bill 47.
questions/q_housing/party_positions/gree: This party wants government to build homes rented at cost, and limits on rent increases when a new renter moves in.

The Greens would build or protect 26,000 non-market homes a year, restart the paused Community Housing Fund and bring in vacancy control, which keeps rent limits in place between tenants. They voted against the 2023 density laws, citing local control. Their 2025 vacancy-control bill was defeated.

The Greens would build 26,000 non-market homes a year, reinstate the Community and Indigenous Housing Funds, protect 2,000 rental units a year through a Rental Protection Fund, bring in vacancy control and pilot a land value tax. They voted for the 2018 speculation tax after securing a 0.5% rate for domestic owners, voted against Bills 44 and 46 over local control, and saw their 2025 vacancy-control bill defeated.
questions/q_housing/party_positions/cent: This party wants cities to approve homes faster, lower fees on rentals, and more factory-built homes.

CentreBC's platform sets provincial approval deadlines for cities, halves development charges on rentals, and plans 5,000 factory-built homes a year, a doubled BC Builds program and 1,000 supportive homes. It adds no new housing taxes. It proposes no change to the speculation tax beyond stronger audits, is silent on the four-home zoning law and rent control, and keeps the rules for homes near transit.

By 2028 the platform requires six-month rezonings and eight-week permits, with refunds if missed, backed by a $125 million a year performance fund. It halves development charges on rental and below-market homes and adds a $240 million a year growth fund. It plans 5,000 prefab and mass-timber homes a year by 2030, BC Builds at 20,000 homes by 2031, a 2027-2032 PST rebate on rental building materials and 1,000 supportive homes. It does not mention the Unsold Condo Tax, flipping tax, foreign buyer tax or rent control, and mentions the speculation tax only to add audit teams to collect it.
questions/q_housing/party_positions/oneb: This party wants to remove building rules that add cost and stop cities from limiting rent.
OneBC would scrap the Step Code, BC's energy rules for new buildings, and stop cities from bringing in rent control, saying both discourage building. It has no supply target or housing spending plan.

OneBC would eliminate the BC Energy Step Code and block municipal rent control, which it says would 'disincentivize development'. It proposes no demand-side taxes and no supply program. It has no record in government; its MLAs were elected as Conservatives in 2024.
questions/q_health/prompt/1: Many people cannot find a family doctor, and waiting rooms are full. What should change?
questions/q_health/prompt/2: How should the province help people get a family doctor, emergency care and surgery sooner?
questions/q_health/prompt/3: How should the province improve access to family doctors, emergency rooms and surgeries?
questions/q_health/prompt/4: Which way of running and paying for health care should BC choose to cut waits and connect people to a doctor?
questions/q_health/prompt/5: Which health care delivery and funding model do you support?
questions/q_health/context/1: About one in four people in BC has no family doctor. Every party says health care should stay free. They disagree on who should run clinics and care homes, and on how to pay for more care.
questions/q_health/context/2: About one in four people in BC has no regular family doctor or nurse practitioner, up from fewer than one in five in 2017. Every party says care should stay free for patients. They disagree on whether companies should run more care, and on how to pay for it.
questions/q_health/context/3: Health care ranks second for BC voters. About one in four people has no regular family doctor or nurse practitioner, even after the NDP government changed how family doctors are paid in 2023. All parties say care should stay publicly funded. They differ on building more public clinics, paying non-government providers, allowing people to pay for faster care, and how to fund it all.
questions/q_health/context/4: About 1.26 million people in BC (23%) have no regular family doctor or nurse practitioner, up from 18% in 2017, even though the NDP government brought in a new pay model for family doctors in 2023. The median wait from a doctor's referral to treatment is 32 weeks. A provincial law, the Medicare Protection Act, bars private clinics from charging patients for services the public plan covers.
questions/q_health/context/5: In April 2026, 1,259,425 people (23%) had no regular primary care provider, compared with 897,000 (18.2%) in 2017. The Health Connect Registry links more than 4,000 people a week to a provider, and a new family doctor payment model (LFP) has been in place since 2023. The Fraser Institute puts the median wait from referral to treatment at 32.2 weeks. The first phase of minimum nurse-to-patient ratios was 81% in place by March 2026, according to the BC Nurses' Union, and the health budget is about $36 billion. The Medicare Protection Act bars extra-billing for services the public plan insures.
questions/q_health/options/a/text/1: Open more public clinics and train more doctors, paid for by top earners.
questions/q_health/options/a/text/2: Open more public clinics, train more doctors, buy more scanners, and raise taxes on top earners.
questions/q_health/options/a/text/3: Expand the public system with more clinics, training seats and scanners, paid for by higher taxes on top earners.
questions/q_health/options/a/text/4: Scale up public care and testing with 20 clinics, 1,000 training seats and more MRI and CT scanners, paid for by a higher top tax rate.
questions/q_health/options/a/text/5: Expand the public system with 20 clinics, a bridge for foreign-trained doctors, 1,000 training seats, 8 MRIs, 10 CT scanners and regional waitlists, keep the LFP pay model, and raise top tax brackets.
questions/q_health/options/b/text/1: Care stays free. Families can pick approved care homes, run by government or not.
questions/q_health/options/b/text/2: Care stays free, public money follows patients to approved providers, even company-run ones, and emergency rooms stay open.
questions/q_health/options/b/text/3: Public funding follows patients to approved non-government providers, and an emergency fund keeps emergency rooms open.
questions/q_health/options/b/text/4: Public funding with mixed delivery: protect current spending, a $50 million emergency fund, a 100-day wait-time commission, and long-term and home-care funding that follows the patient.
questions/q_health/options/b/text/5: Universal public funding with mixed delivery: current funding protected, a $50 million health care emergency fund, a 100-day wait-time commission, and long-term and home-care funding patients can take to any qualified provider.
questions/q_health/options/c/text/1: People can pay to get care faster. Free care stays for everyone else.
questions/q_health/options/c/text/2: Let private clinics charge people who want to be seen sooner, alongside the free public system.
questions/q_health/options/c/text/3: Allow private-pay care alongside the public system so people can pay for faster treatment.
questions/q_health/options/c/text/4: Add a private-pay option for services the public plan covers, alongside the public system, and loosen rules on health professions to add capacity.
questions/q_health/options/c/text/5: Allow a parallel private tier for services the Medical Services Plan insures and repeal the Health Professions and Occupations Act, which needs the Medicare Protection Act amended or left unenforced.
questions/q_health/options/d/text/1: A public health centre in every community, and no private nursing companies.
questions/q_health/options/d/text/2: A public health centre in every area, and no more hiring nurses through private agencies.
questions/q_health/options/d/text/3: Public care only: a community health centre in every riding, no private agency nurses, and public mental health care.
questions/q_health/options/d/text/4: Public delivery only: a community health centre in every riding, full nurse-to-patient ratios, no agency nurses, and public coverage for counselling.
questions/q_health/options/d/text/5: A community health centre in every riding, nurse-to-patient ratios completed, agency nursing phased out, mental health care in the public plan, and single-entry surgical referral.
questions/q_health/options/e/text/1: Give everyone a regular doctor or nurse, paid for by cutting health office costs.
questions/q_health/options/e/text/2: A doctor or nurse practitioner for everyone, more surgeries and care homes, paid for by cutting health office costs.
questions/q_health/options/e/text/3: A doctor or nurse practitioner for everyone by 2031, a law on emergency room closures, more surgeries and care beds, and fewer health executives.
questions/q_health/options/e/text/4: A primary-care team for everyone by 2031, an ER Accountability Act, 15,000 more surgeries a year and 2,500 care beds started, paid for by merging health-authority back offices, with no private pay.
questions/q_health/options/e/text/5: Team-based care for everyone by 2031 with automatic registration, 600 nurse practitioners, an ER Accountability Act, 15,000 more surgeries, 2,500 long-term care beds under construction and one health-authority back office, with no private pay.
questions/q_health/party_positions/ndp/t: This party wants more clinics, nurses and doctors, paid for by higher taxes on top earners.

The NDP promises 20 clinics, 1,000 training seats, 18 scanners and 500 home-care workers, paid for by a higher top tax rate, and would phase out agency nurses. In government it brought in a new pay model for family doctors and nurse-to-patient ratios, but the share of people without a regular provider rose from 18% to 23%.

The NDP's 2026 plan adds 20 clinics, a bridge for foreign-trained doctors, 1,000 training seats, 8 MRI and 10 CT scanners, regional waitlists and 500 home-care workers, scraps home-care fees and restarts seven paused long-term care projects. On October 12 it pledged to phase out agency nurses over three years and close loopholes that let clinics charge user fees. Higher top brackets would raise about $1 billion a year. In government it introduced the LFP pay model in 2023 and has put 81% of the first phase of nurse ratios in place, while the share of people without a provider rose from 18.2% in 2017 to 23% in 2026.
questions/q_health/party_positions/conse: This party wants care to stay free, emergency rooms kept open, and more choice of care homes for families.

The Conservatives promise open emergency rooms, a $50 million emergency fund, a 100-day wait-time commission and no cut to current health funding. They would let long-term and home-care funding follow patients to non-government providers. They have not repeated their 2024 private-clinic plan.

On October 5 the Conservatives promised open ERs, a $50 million emergency fund, support for rural practices, a 100-day commission drawing on 'other public systems' and protection of current health funding, calling care 'universal and publicly funded' with 'nothing more than their health card' needed. On October 9 they promised long-term care funding that seniors can take to a qualified public or non-government provider. On October 12 the party repeated its health card pledge. They have not repeated 2024 pledges on private-clinic partnerships or out-of-province care guarantees. They voted against the NDP's 2025 mental health bill (Bill 32).
questions/q_health/party_positions/green: This party wants a public health centre in every community and no private nursing companies.

The Greens would put a community health centre in every riding, finish nurse-to-patient ratios, phase out private agency nurses, cover mental health care publicly and keep public health money in public care.

The Greens would put a community health centre in every riding, complete nurse ratios, phase out agency nurses, add public mental health coverage and single-entry surgical referral, review loan forgiveness and paid practicums for health students, and assess the health effects of liquefied natural gas (LNG) and fracking. Their 2024 accord with the NDP included health centres and psychologist coverage; the Greens say commitments of $15 million and $50 million were not delivered.
questions/q_health/party_positions/centr: This party wants a doctor or nurse for everyone, open emergency rooms and more care homes, with no paying for faster care.

CentreBC's platform promises a family doctor or nurse practitioner team for everyone by 2031, a law on emergency room closures, 15,000 more surgeries a year, 2,500 long-term care beds started and free counselling. It rejects private pay and phases out agency nurses. It pays mainly by merging health-authority back offices, at about $4 billion over four years (party costing).

The platform promises a provider for everyone by 2031 with automatic registration, 600 nurse practitioners, 100 residencies, more foreign-trained doctor assessments and 30-day licensing for out-of-province staff. It adds an ER Accountability Act with a $25 million a year rural fund, 15,000 surgeries, 5 MRIs, 2,500 long-term care beds under construction by March 2031 and a $400 a month caregiver benefit. It rules out private pay, phases out agency nurses and keeps the LFP model. The party puts the cost at $4.0 billion plus $3.2 billion capital over four years.
questions/q_health/party_positions/onebc: This party would let people pay for faster care, while free care stays for everyone else.
OneBC would allow private health care alongside the public system and repeal the Health Professions and Occupations Act. It has no plan for clinics, training or long-term care.

OneBC would allow private health care alongside the public system and repeal the Health Professions and Occupations Act, and shift administration and HR spending to frontline staff. It makes no commitments on primary care, diagnostics, nurse ratios or long-term care. A parallel private tier would conflict with the Medicare Protection Act as it stands.
questions/q_dripa/prompt/1: A BC law says provincial laws must respect Indigenous rights. What should happen to it?
questions/q_dripa/prompt/2: A 2019 law says BC's laws should match Indigenous peoples' rights. What should happen to it now?
questions/q_dripa/prompt/3: After a 2025 court ruling, what should BC do with the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act?
questions/q_dripa/prompt/4: Should BC repeal, amend, replace, keep or strengthen the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (DRIPA)?
questions/q_dripa/prompt/5: Which legislative response to the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (DRIPA) do you support after the Gitxaala ruling?
questions/q_dripa/context/1: In 2019, BC lawmakers passed a law, with no one voting against, saying BC's laws should respect Indigenous peoples' rights. In 2025, a court said judges can check BC's laws against it. Parties disagree on what to do. First Nations keep their rights either way.
questions/q_dripa/context/2: In 2019, BC passed a law promising to bring its laws in line with the United Nations declaration on Indigenous peoples' rights. In 2025, a court ruled that judges can check BC's laws against it. Supporters say the law builds fairness and trust. Critics say it leads to court cases and uncertainty. First Nations keep their rights either way.
questions/q_dripa/context/3: The Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act passed in 2019 with no votes against. It commits BC to bring its laws in line with the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. In 2025 the BC Court of Appeal ruled that this promise can be enforced in court. Repealing the law would not end the province's duty to consult First Nations or their land title cases, because those rest on section 35 of Canada's Constitution.
questions/q_dripa/context/4: The Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (DRIPA) passed unanimously in 2019. In December 2025, in a case brought by the Gitxaala Nation, the BC Court of Appeal held that courts can assess whether provincial laws are consistent with it. The Premier then proposed suspending parts of the law for up to three years, but dropped the plan in April 2026 before introducing a bill. In an Angus Reid poll in May 2026, 47% supported repeal and 33% opposed it. Repeal would not end the duty to consult, which rests on section 35 of the Constitution.
questions/q_dripa/context/5: DRIPA (Bill 41) passed 82 to 0 in 2019. Under section 7 of the act, BC has signed consent agreements with First Nations, including a 2022 agreement with the Tahltan under which the Eskay Creek mine was approved in January 2026. In Gitxaala v. British Columbia (2025 BCCA 430), the Court of Appeal ruled 2 to 1 that DRIPA duties can be enforced in court, and the Supreme Court of Canada agreed in May 2026 to hear an appeal. In Cowichan Tribes (2025 BCSC 1490), the BC Supreme Court found Aboriginal title under section 35 that includes privately owned land; that ruling is under appeal. The government dropped its plan to suspend parts of DRIPA on April 19, 2026, before any bill was introduced. Bills to repeal DRIPA failed at first reading in November 2025 (43 to 48) and April 2026 (44 to 47). A petition to repeal DRIPA can be signed from October 26, 2026 to January 25, 2027.
questions/q_dripa/options/a/text/1: End the law, and stop new deals that give First Nations land or money.
questions/q_dripa/options/a/text/2: Cancel the law, declare that the United Nations declaration does not apply in BC, and stop land and money transfers.
questions/q_dripa/options/a/text/3: Repeal the law, declare the United Nations Declaration of no effect in BC, and stop voluntary land and money transfers.
questions/q_dripa/options/a/text/4: Repeal DRIPA, declare the UN Declaration (UNDRIP) of no force in BC, end voluntary cash, land and resource transfers, and seek repeal of the Indian Act.
questions/q_dripa/options/a/text/5: Repeal DRIPA and section 8.1 of the Interpretation Act, declare UNDRIP of no force in BC, freeze voluntary transfers, and repeal the Indian Act.
questions/q_dripa/options/b/text/1: End the law, but keep partnering with First Nations on projects and jobs.
questions/q_dripa/options/b/text/2: Cancel the law, but keep making project deals with First Nations that create jobs.
questions/q_dripa/options/b/text/3: Repeal the law and rely instead on project partnerships with First Nations, with no new law to replace it.
questions/q_dripa/options/b/text/4: Repeal DRIPA, pursue economic reconciliation through project partnerships with First Nations, and pass no replacement law.
questions/q_dripa/options/b/text/5: Repeal DRIPA and pursue economic reconciliation by building projects with First Nations, with no replacement law, while section 35 duties continue.
questions/q_dripa/options/c/text/1: Keep the law, but stop judges from using it to strike down other laws.
questions/q_dripa/options/c/text/2: Keep the law, but change it, working with First Nations, so courts cannot strike down other laws.
questions/q_dripa/options/c/text/3: Amend the law, in talks with First Nations, so courts cannot use it to strike down other laws.
questions/q_dripa/options/c/text/4: Amend DRIPA so courts cannot enforce the duty to align laws, keep consent agreements, and negotiate the change with First Nations leaders.
questions/q_dripa/options/c/text/5: Amend the DRIPA alignment duty and the Interpretation Act provision so courts cannot enforce them, keep section 7 agreements, and negotiate with the First Nations Leadership Council.
questions/q_dripa/options/d/text/1: Replace the law with a new one based on treaties, and protect people's homes.
questions/q_dripa/options/d/text/2: Replace the law with one focused on reaching treaties, and promise no family loses their home over a land ruling.
questions/q_dripa/options/d/text/3: Repeal the law and replace it with a treaty-based law, protect private land and homeowners, and let the legislature, not courts, decide.
questions/q_dripa/options/d/text/4: Repeal DRIPA and replace it with a treaty-based law: $30 million a year for treaty talks, homeowner compensation after title rulings, no private land transferred without a willing owner, and deals published before signing.
questions/q_dripa/options/d/text/5: Repeal DRIPA and section 8.1 of the Interpretation Act, pass a treaty-based law funded at $30 million a year, treat UNDRIP 'as a guide', compensate homeowners up to assessed value, and publish agreements 60 days before signing.
questions/q_dripa/options/e/text/1: Make the law stronger, with a clear plan and public education about it.
questions/q_dripa/options/e/text/2: Make the law stronger, with a clear plan to carry it out, public education and expert advisers.
questions/q_dripa/options/e/text/3: Strengthen the law with a new law setting out how to carry it out, public education, and an expert advisory committee.
questions/q_dripa/options/e/text/4: Pass a law to carry out DRIPA, fund public education, create an expert advisory committee, and oppose any suspension or weakening.
questions/q_dripa/options/e/text/5: Pass a DRIPA Implementation Act that sets out alignment and reporting, fund public education, create an expert advisory committee, oppose suspension, and follow the First Nations Leadership Council proposal.
questions/q_dripa/party_positions/ndp/te: This party passed the law. It now wants to change it, working with First Nations, so courts cannot strike down other laws.

The NDP passed the law in 2019. After a 2025 court ruling, it proposed suspending parts of the law for up to three years, then dropped the idea when one of its own members of the legislature and First Nations leaders objected. It says it must amend the law so courts cannot strike down other laws, but has published no wording.

The NDP passed Bill 41 in 2019 (82 to 0) and has signed section 7 consent agreements, including a 2022 Tahltan agreement under which the Eskay Creek mine was approved in January 2026. After the Gitxaala ruling Eby cited 'serious legal liabilities'. On April 2 it announced a bill to suspend parts of DRIPA for up to three years, framed as a confidence vote; on April 19 it said no DRIPA bill would be introduced that session. On April 20 it and the First Nations Leadership Council promised a solution 'before the fall legislative session'. In October Eby said it had worked with First Nations over the summer 'to see if we can find a path forward that we all agree on'. Its Bills 14 and 15 (2025) passed over First Nations objections.
questions/q_dripa/party_positions/conser: This party wants to end the law and work with First Nations on business projects instead.

Interim leader Lorne Doerkson says, 'I will repeal DRIPA.' The party says it wants to build projects with First Nations instead and names no replacement law. Its members voted in 2025 and 2026 to introduce bills repealing the law; both failed. Many of them were BC Liberals who voted for the law in 2019.

The Conservative plan page 'Repeal DRIPA, Promote Economic Reconciliation' (October 7) promises repeal, and Doerkson says he wants to build projects 'together with First Nations'. It names no replacement law and takes no position on section 7 agreements or private property. Its MLAs, including Rustad, Doerkson and Halford, voted for first reading of independent MLA Jordan Kealy's DRIPA repeal bill (lost 43 to 48, November 2025) and Halford's own repeal bill (lost 44 to 47, April 2026). In 2019 Rustad and other BC Liberals voted for Bill 41, which passed 82 to 0; Rustad says he had 'no choice'. He also pledged repeal in 2024.
questions/q_dripa/party_positions/green/: This party wants to make the law stronger and teach the public about it.

The Greens would pass a law setting out how to carry out the Declaration Act, fund public education and create an expert advisory committee. They oppose weakening the law; in February 2026 leader Emily Lowan said a government weakening Indigenous rights 'cannot expect our support'.

On September 30 the Greens pledged to implement the Declaration Act through legislation, fund public education on it and create an expert advisory committee on Indigenous rights, DRIPA and constitutional law. Green MLAs voted for Bill 41 in 2019, against Bills 14 and 15 in 2025 and against both DRIPA repeal bills. Ending the NDP accord in February 2026, Lowan said a government 'willing to weaken Indigenous rights for political expediency cannot expect our support'.
questions/q_dripa/party_positions/centre: This party now wants to replace the law with one based on treaties, and to protect people's homes.

CentreBC's platform would repeal the law and replace it with one built on negotiated treaties, with $30 million a year for treaty talks, compensation for homeowners hit by title rulings and no private land transferred without a willing owner. The legislature, not courts, would decide how laws reflect the United Nations Declaration. In August 2026 it called repeal 'political messaging'.

A first-session bill would repeal DRIPA and section 8.1 of the Interpretation Act and pass a treaty-based law with $30 million a year for treaty and overlap talks and a yearly treaty report. UNDRIP would be 'a guide', and section 35 and the duty to consult stay. Homeowners get compensation up to assessed value after title rulings, with no private-land agreements until the Cowichan appeals end. Agreements are published 60 days before signing. On August 13 the party had rejected repeal as 'political messaging', though Sturko voted for first reading of the DRIPA repeal bills in November 2025 and April 2026.
questions/q_dripa/party_positions/onebc/: This party would end the law and stop new land and money deals with First Nations.

OneBC would repeal the law, declare the United Nations Declaration of no effect in BC, stop voluntary transfers of cash, land and resource control, end mandatory land acknowledgements, and seek to repeal the Indian Act.

OneBC would repeal DRIPA, declare UNDRIP of no force in BC, halt voluntary transfers, and seek constitutional reform to repeal the Indian Act and turn reserves into townships; at its 2025 launch Brodie said it would 'defund the reconciliation industry'. In October 2025 her bill to ban land acknowledgements failed 5 to 85 and her Property Rights Protection Act failed 40 to 48. She voted for first reading of the DRIPA repeal bills from independent MLA Jordan Kealy (November 2025) and Conservative MLA Trevor Halford (April 2026). Rustad removed her from the Conservative caucus in March 2025, saying she mocked residential school survivors' testimony.
questions/q_sogi/prompt/1: What should schools teach about gender and different kinds of families?
questions/q_sogi/prompt/2: Some BC schools use SOGI 123, teaching materials about sexual orientation, gender identity and families. What should the province do?
questions/q_sogi/prompt/3: Should the province repeal, step back from, keep or expand SOGI 123, optional school materials on sexual orientation and gender identity?
questions/q_sogi/prompt/4: SOGI 123 (sexual orientation and gender identity) is optional and chosen by each school district, and provincial funding for its creator ends in 2026-27. What should BC do?
questions/q_sogi/prompt/5: SOGI 123 is an optional, district-selected sexual orientation and gender identity (SOGI) resource from the ARC Foundation (2016). Choose the provincial stance you support.
questions/q_sogi/context/1: Some schools use lessons about gender and different kinds of families. Each school district decides whether to use them. The government is ending its funding for the group that made them. Everyone wants kids safe at school. People disagree on who should choose these lessons.
questions/q_sogi/context/2: SOGI 123 is a set of optional teaching materials about sexual orientation and gender identity. Each school district chooses whether to use it. Supporters say it reduces bullying. Critics say families should decide what children learn about gender. The province is ending its funding for the group that created it.
questions/q_sogi/context/3: SOGI 123 is an optional set of school materials on sexual orientation and gender identity, first released in 2016. The Conservatives and OneBC would repeal it. The NDP government is ending funding for the group that created it but keeps anti-bullying work. The Greens support it 'unequivocally'. CentreBC opposes repealing anti-discrimination protections but has not committed to SOGI 123.
questions/q_sogi/context/4: SOGI 123 is optional, and each district chooses whether to use it. The Conservatives would repeal it but have not said how they would end a resource that is not required. OneBC would also pass a Parental Bill of Rights. Premier Eby says 'it's up to the teachers'. The Greens would expand it. CentreBC opposes repealing rights protections. Pronoun rules and parental notification are not scored, because the parties have no 2026 positions on them.
questions/q_sogi/context/5: The Conservative plan says it would repeal SOGI but names no mechanism. Its 2024 platform promised to remove SOGI-derived lesson plans, a zero-tolerance anti-bullying policy and parental notification of suicidal intent. The NDP government cut ARC Foundation funding from $350,000 to $0 by 2026-27, and the ministry says the resources stay online. OneBC's bill on pronouns and puberty blockers was defeated 48 to 40. The Greens would expand SOGI 123 and fund one counsellor per 250 students. CentreBC would not repeal anti-discrimination law. The Human Rights Code has covered gender identity since 2016.
questions/q_sogi/options/a/text/1: Remove all lessons on gender identity from schools, and pass a parents' rights law.
questions/q_sogi/options/a/text/2: Remove SOGI 123 and all lessons on gender identity, and pass a law on parents' rights.
questions/q_sogi/options/a/text/3: Repeal SOGI 123, remove all gender-identity content from schools, and pass a parental rights law.
questions/q_sogi/options/a/text/4: Repeal SOGI 123, remove all gender-identity content from curriculum and resources, and pass a Parental Bill of Rights.
questions/q_sogi/options/a/text/5: Repeal SOGI 123, remove all gender-identity content from kindergarten to Grade 12, and pass a Parental Bill of Rights.
questions/q_sogi/options/b/text/1: End these lessons, focus on reading and math, and keep every student safe.
questions/q_sogi/options/b/text/2: End SOGI 123, focus on reading, writing and math, and keep every student safe from bullying.
questions/q_sogi/options/b/text/3: Repeal SOGI 123, refocus schools on reading, writing and math, and keep schools safe for all students.
questions/q_sogi/options/b/text/4: Repeal SOGI 123, replace it with general anti-bullying rules, and refocus on reading, writing and math.
questions/q_sogi/options/b/text/5: Repeal SOGI 123, remove derived lesson plans and policy guides, adopt zero-tolerance anti-bullying rules, and refocus on reading, writing and arithmetic.
questions/q_sogi/options/c/text/1: Keep laws against discrimination, and let each school district choose its own lessons.
questions/q_sogi/options/c/text/2: Keep laws against discrimination, let districts and teachers choose materials, and have the province fund no specific program.
questions/q_sogi/options/c/text/3: Keep anti-discrimination protections, let districts and teachers choose resources, and fund no specific program.
questions/q_sogi/options/c/text/4: Keep the Human Rights Code and anti-bullying policies, leave SOGI 123 as an optional district resource without provincial funding, and let teachers lead.
questions/q_sogi/options/c/text/5: Leave the Human Rights Code unchanged, keep SOGI 123 available for districts to choose, give its creator no provincial funding, and add no new gender-identity policy.
questions/q_sogi/options/d/text/1: Keep these lessons, use them in more schools, and hire more school counsellors.
questions/q_sogi/options/d/text/2: Keep SOGI 123, use it in more schools, and hire more school counsellors.
questions/q_sogi/options/d/text/3: Fully support and expand SOGI 123, and hire more school counsellors.
questions/q_sogi/options/d/text/4: Fully support and expand SOGI 123, and fund one school counsellor per 250 students.
questions/q_sogi/options/d/text/5: Continue and expand SOGI 123, fund one counsellor per 250 students, and close the inclusive education funding gap.
questions/q_sogi/party_positions/ndp/tex: This party keeps the laws against discrimination but is ending funding for the group that made the lessons. Teachers choose.

The NDP government is ending funding for the ARC Foundation, which created SOGI 123. It says the materials stay online, districts choose, and anti-bullying work continues. In 2024 it passed a law creating zones around schools where disruptive protest is an offence. It has no 2026 platform item on SOGI.

The NDP cut ARC Foundation funding from $350,000 (2024-25) to $200,000 (2025-26) to $0 (2026-27), citing 'expenditure management'; the ministry says SOGI 123 is 'not defunded' and stays online. Its Safe Access to Schools Act (2024) created access zones within 20 metres of schools where disrupting or intimidating students and staff is an offence. Eby says it is 'up to the teachers'. It voted against the gender-identity and Human Rights Code repeal bills and has no position on pronouns, parental notification or athletes.
questions/q_sogi/party_positions/conserv: This party would end these lessons, focus on reading and math, and keep students safe.

The Conservatives would repeal SOGI 123 and refocus on 'arithmetic and reading', but have not said how they would end an optional resource. In 2026 most of their members voted to let bills on gender identity and on repealing the Human Rights Code be introduced, calling that a procedural step.
