The Safe Schools plan would repeal SOGI but names no mechanism. The 2024 platform promised to remove SOGI-derived lesson plans and policy guides, adopt zero-tolerance anti-bullying rules and notify parents of suicidal intent. Most Conservative MLAs voted to give first reading to a gender-identity bill (defeated 38 to 49) and the Human Rights Code Repeal Act (37 to 50), saying all bills should get first reading without opposition. SOGI 123 began under the BC Liberal government while Rustad was a minister.
questions/q_sogi/party_positions/green/t: This party wants to keep these lessons, use them in more schools, and hire more school counsellors.

The Greens support SOGI 123 'unequivocally' and would expand it and fund one counsellor per 250 students. Their members voted against every bill on gender identity and on repealing the Human Rights Code.

The Greens 'unequivocally support SOGI 123' and would continue and expand it, fund one counsellor per 250 students and close the inclusive education funding gap. They voted against the Gender Ideology and Child Protection Act, the Human Rights Code Repeal Act and the October 2025 transition bill.
questions/q_sogi/party_positions/centreb: This party supports laws against discrimination for every student but has not promised to fund these lessons.

CentreBC's Elenore Sturko said on September 28 that she opposes repealing any anti-discrimination law. The October 10 platform does not mention SOGI 123, gender identity or parental rights, so that statement stands. The platform adds one counsellor per 400 students and a Children's Well-Being Act, with no commitment to fund or expand SOGI 123.

Sturko told CBC on September 28, 2026 that she opposes repealing anti-discrimination law, and CentreBC voted against the Gender Ideology and Child Protection Act and the Human Rights Code Repeal Act. The platform (pages 20-24) says nothing on SOGI 123, gender identity, parental notification or pronouns. It promises one counsellor per 400 students by 2030, 1,500 education assistants and a Children's Well-Being Act. The party is scored on the September statement and the platform's silence.
questions/q_sogi/party_positions/onebc/t: This party wants all lessons on gender identity out of schools, with parents deciding at home.

OneBC would repeal SOGI 123, 'remove all gender ideology content' from classrooms, and pass a Parental Bill of Rights. Its bill to stop puberty blockers for minors and to bar use of the 'wrong pronoun' in schools was defeated.

OneBC would repeal SOGI 123, remove gender ideology content and pass a Parental Bill of Rights. Its October 2025 bill, Tara Armstrong's Protecting Minors from Gender Transition Act, to stop puberty blockers for minors, bar wrong-pronoun use and ban public funds for transition was defeated 48 to 40. Armstrong left OneBC in December 2025; her February 2026 Gender Ideology and Child Protection Act, which Brodie voted for, was defeated 38 to 49. It is not running candidates against eight Conservatives who share its views on SOGI.
questions/q_drugs/prompt/1: Many people in BC die from toxic street drugs. How should the province respond?
questions/q_drugs/prompt/2: Should BC focus on keeping people who use drugs alive, on required treatment, or a mix?
questions/q_drugs/prompt/3: BC's toxic drug emergency is ten years old. What approach should the province take now?
questions/q_drugs/prompt/4: After the decriminalization pilot ended and involuntary care expanded, which direction should BC's toxic drug policy take?
questions/q_drugs/prompt/5: Decriminalization expired in January 2026, all prescribed alternatives now require witnessed dosing, and involuntary care is expanding. Choose the policy mix.
questions/q_drugs/context/1: Toxic street drugs kill many people in BC. Some parties want places where people can use drugs with staff nearby, and doctor-prescribed drugs to replace street drugs. Others want people with the worst addictions to be required to get treatment. Some want both.
questions/q_drugs/context/2: BC runs sites where people use drugs with staff on hand. Doctors can prescribe drugs to replace street drugs, and some people are required to get treatment. From 2023 to early 2026, carrying small amounts was not a crime, but that has ended. Deaths have fallen since 2023, but the coroner has not linked the drop to any one cause.
questions/q_drugs/context/3: The NDP government let its decriminalization pilot, under which people were not charged for carrying small amounts, end in 2026. It now requires most people on prescribed safer supply to take their doses in front of a health worker, and it is expanding involuntary care. The Conservatives would end safer supply and expand required treatment. OneBC would also close supervised sites. The Greens would bring decriminalization back. CentreBC puts treatment first, with 650 more beds.
questions/q_drugs/context/4: Drug deaths fell from 2,511 in 2023 to 1,826 in 2025, but the coroner has not linked the drop to any one cause. Supporters say supervised consumption sites prevent overdose deaths, while police chiefs point to public disorder and prescribed drugs being passed on to others. In July 2026 the BC Supreme Court struck down the parts of the Mental Health Act used for involuntary treatment and gave the government six months to amend the law.
questions/q_drugs/context/5: Drug deaths were 2,511 in 2023 and 1,826 in 2025 (preliminary), and the coroner does not attribute the decline to any one cause. The prescribed alternatives program fell from about 5,200 people at its March 2023 peak to about 3,900 in early 2025, when the province began requiring witnessed dosing. The province has announced 132 involuntary care beds in Prince George and Surrey. In July 2026 the BC Supreme Court ruled the Mental Health Act's treatment provisions unconstitutional and gave the government six months to amend them.
questions/q_drugs/options/a/text/1: Close drug-use sites and turn them into recovery centres. Require treatment for severe addiction.
questions/q_drugs/options/a/text/2: Turn drug-use sites into recovery centres, stop prescribing replacement drugs, and require treatment for severe addiction.
questions/q_drugs/options/a/text/3: End safer supply (prescribed replacement drugs), turn supervised sites into recovery centres, and use involuntary treatment for severe addiction.
questions/q_drugs/options/a/text/4: Recovery only: turn all consumption sites into treatment centres, end prescribed alternatives, and expand involuntary treatment and housing.
questions/q_drugs/options/a/text/5: End prescribed safer supply and all consumption and overdose prevention programs, turn sites into recovery centres, and use involuntary rehabilitation and housing.
questions/q_drugs/options/b/text/1: End prescribed replacement drugs, require treatment for severe addiction, ban drug use in shelters.
questions/q_drugs/options/b/text/2: End prescribed replacement drugs, let police start required treatment, and ban drug use in shelters.
questions/q_drugs/options/b/text/3: End safer supply, expand required treatment that police can start, and ban drug use in hospitals and shelters.
questions/q_drugs/options/b/text/4: End safer supply, amend the Mental Health Act so police can start mandatory treatment, and ban drug use in hospitals, shelters and supportive housing.
questions/q_drugs/options/b/text/5: End prescribed alternatives, change the Mental Health Act for officer-initiated mandatory treatment, and ban drug use in hospitals, shelters and supportive housing.
questions/q_drugs/options/c/text/1: Keep well-run drug-use sites, require treatment for the sickest, and keep drug possession illegal.
questions/q_drugs/options/c/text/2: Keep well-run sites and supervised replacement drugs, expand required treatment, and keep possession illegal.
questions/q_drugs/options/c/text/3: Keep well-run supervised sites and witnessed dosing of prescribed drugs, expand involuntary care, and do not bring back decriminalization.
questions/q_drugs/options/c/text/4: Keep supervised sites if well run, allow prescribed alternatives only when a health worker watches, expand involuntary care within court limits, and do not restore decriminalization.
questions/q_drugs/options/c/text/5: Keep supervised sites with operating conditions, require witnessed dosing for prescribed alternatives, keep involuntary care within the limits the court sets, open 132 involuntary beds, and do not restore decriminalization.
questions/q_drugs/options/d/text/1: Stop charging people for small amounts, offer safer prescribed drugs, and keep treatment voluntary.
questions/q_drugs/options/d/text/2: Stop charging people for carrying small amounts, offer safer prescribed drugs and more supervised sites, and keep treatment voluntary.
questions/q_drugs/options/d/text/3: Decriminalize carrying small amounts again, offer regulated drug alternatives and more supervised sites, and keep care voluntary.
questions/q_drugs/options/d/text/4: Restore decriminalization, offer regulated pharmaceutical alternatives, add more consumption and inhalation sites and drug checking, and rely on voluntary treatment instead of involuntary care.
questions/q_drugs/options/d/text/5: Decriminalize possession (which needs a federal exemption), offer regulated pharmaceutical alternatives, add consumption, inhalation and 24-hour sites, and keep care voluntary with no expansion of involuntary care.
questions/q_drugs/options/e/text/1: Open many more free treatment beds so people get help within two weeks.
questions/q_drugs/options/e/text/2: Add more free detox and treatment beds, offer treatment within two weeks, and seek charges for carrying drugs in public.
questions/q_drugs/options/e/text/3: Treatment first: 650 more free beds, treatment within 14 days, seek charges for public possession, and individual checks before involuntary care.
questions/q_drugs/options/e/text/4: Add 650 detox and treatment beds by 2030, offer treatment within 14 days, ask Ottawa to charge public possession, require capacity assessments before involuntary care, and leave sites and prescribed alternatives as they are.
questions/q_drugs/options/e/text/5: Add 150 detox and 500 free treatment beds by 2030, set a 14-day treatment standard, ask Ottawa to charge public and repeat possession, assess capacity individually under the Mental Health Act, and leave sites and prescribed alternatives untouched.
questions/q_drugs/party_positions/ndp/te: This party ended its test of not charging people for small amounts. It keeps drug-use sites and requires treatment for some people.

The NDP started decriminalization in 2023 and let it expire in 2026, saying it 'hasn't delivered the results' it hoped for. It now requires most people on prescribed alternatives to take their doses in front of a nurse or pharmacist, and it is expanding involuntary care. It says supervised sites 'save lives' if well run.

Decriminalization began in 2023, was narrowed in 2024 to exclude public use and expired on January 31, 2026; Health Minister Josie Osborne said it 'hasn't delivered the results' hoped for, and Eby said of decriminalized public drug use, 'It didn't work.' In December 2025 it moved to require most prescribed-alternatives clients to take doses in front of a nurse or pharmacist. It has announced 132 involuntary care beds in Prince George (up to $92 million) and Surrey (up to $57 million); the first 24 are due by December 2027. In July 2026 the BC Supreme Court found the Mental Health Act's treatment provisions breach the Charter; the Attorney General's office said it is reviewing the decision. On the campaign trail it says sites 'save lives' if 'well run'.
questions/q_drugs/party_positions/conser: This party would end prescribed replacement drugs, require treatment for severe addiction, and ban drug use in shelters.

The Conservative plan would end safer supply, amend the Mental Health Act so police can start mandatory treatment, and ban drug use in hospitals, shelters and supportive housing. It is silent on supervised sites; the 2024 platform promised to close them.

Safe Streets for BC (October 2026) would end 'safe supply', bring in compassionate intervention, amend the Mental Health Act for officer-connected mandatory treatment, ban drug use in hospitals, shelters and supportive housing, and add residential treatment. The 2024 platform promised to close all consumption sites. The party voted against the NDP's Bill 32, the Mental Health Amendment Act (No. 2), 2025, which passed 45 to 41. It has not stated costs or bed numbers.
questions/q_drugs/party_positions/green/: This party would not charge people for carrying small amounts. It wants safer prescribed drugs and voluntary treatment.

The Greens are the only party that would bring back decriminalization, which would need a federal exemption. Their plan, written with former chief coroner Lisa Lapointe, adds regulated pharmaceutical alternatives, more supervised and inhalation sites, and voluntary rather than involuntary care.

The Greens' Toxic Drugs Policy Brief (October 2, 2026) would decriminalize personal possession and offer regulated pharmaceutical alternatives, more supervised consumption sites with inhalation, mobile and 24-hour service, yearly drug-checking funding, housing with harm reduction and voluntary care. It cites the court ruling in the Drug User Liberation Front (DULF) case. The two Green MLAs cast the only votes against first reading of Armstrong's Drug Recovery and Community Safety Act, which would close all provincially funded consumption sites; it passed first reading 84 to 2 in March 2026. Green MLA Rob Botterell also voted against Bill 32 in 2025.
questions/q_drugs/party_positions/centre: This party wants many more free treatment beds, quick access to treatment, and charges for carrying drugs in public.

CentreBC's platform adds 650 free detox and treatment beds by 2030, treatment within 14 days, same-day detox for urgent cases and 12 crisis centres. It would ask Ottawa to charge public and repeat possession and would not bring back decriminalization. Voluntary care comes first, with individual checks before involuntary care. It is silent on supervised sites and safer supply.

The platform adds 150 detox and 500 treatment and recovery beds by 2030, all free, with same-day detox by 2028 and a 14-day treatment standard by 2030. Within 100 days it would ask Ottawa to change the prosecution directive so public and repeat possession is charged, and it would support an appeal in the DULF case. After the July 2026 ruling it would assess capacity individually under the Mental Health Act and keep secure care, adding 50 beds at Red Fish. It does not mention safer supply or supervised sites.
questions/q_drugs/party_positions/onebc/: This party would turn drug-use sites into recovery centres and require treatment for severe addiction.
OneBC would end safer supply and consumption programs, turn the sites into recovery centres, use involuntary treatment and housing for people with severe addiction, and roll back decriminalization.

OneBC would end safe supply and consumption programs, convert sites to recovery centres, use involuntary rehabilitation and housing for people with severe addiction, and roll back decriminalization. It has published no bed numbers or costs.
questions/q_public_safety/prompt/1: What should the government do about crime and safety?
questions/q_public_safety/prompt/2: People worry about break-ins, threats against shop owners and people who keep breaking the law. What should the province do?
questions/q_public_safety/prompt/3: What should the province do about crime and public safety?
questions/q_public_safety/prompt/4: The federal government sets bail law, while the province pays for police, prosecutors and courts. Which approach should BC take?
questions/q_public_safety/prompt/5: The province controls police funding, prosecutor and court capacity and the Mental Health Act, and can lobby Ottawa on bail (Bill C-14). Which provincial approach do you prefer?
questions/q_public_safety/context/1: The province pays for police and courts. Parties disagree on what to do about crime. One party wants to keep today's programs. Others want many more police, a special unit against threats to businesses, or a crackdown on people who keep committing violent crimes.
questions/q_public_safety/context/2: The province pays for police, prosecutors (the lawyers who charge people with crimes) and courts. The federal government sets the bail rules that decide who is released before trial, so BC parties can only ask for changes. Parties differ on whether to hire many more police, add special units, or keep and grow current programs.
questions/q_public_safety/context/3: Crime is a mid-level concern for voters. The Conservatives promise many more police, prosecutors and judges. The NDP government would keep current funding and expand a program aimed at people who commit many crimes. CentreBC promises 500 more Mounties, 60 more prosecutors and a permanent task force against extortion, which is when criminals threaten business owners for money. OneBC targets repeat violent offenders. The Greens have published no plan.
questions/q_public_safety/context/4: BC's Crime Severity Index, a Statistics Canada measure of police-reported crime, fell to 92.4 in 2025, nearly 12% below 2023. A Fraser Institute analysis says violent crime still rose 2.2% last year and about a third since 2017. Provincial figures show extortion fell 7% in 2025. Because bail law is federal, the province's main tools are funding for police, prosecutors and courts. The NDP has made no numeric police pledge. The Conservative plan for about 1,000 new positions has no published cost. CentreBC puts its whole safety chapter, which also covers housing, treatment and disaster preparedness, at about $1.8 billion over four years.
questions/q_public_safety/context/5: BC's Crime Severity Index fell to 92.4 in 2025, nearly 12% below 2023 according to the province, but the violent crime index rose 2.2% in 2025 and 31.7% since 2017, according to a Fraser Institute analysis of Statistics Canada data. Extortion fell 7% province-wide in 2025. The NDP government funded police through the $230 million Safer Communities plan in 2022 and $325 million in new funding over three years in Budget 2025 for encampments, policing and the justice system, but has made no numeric police pledge. The Conservative plan adds about 1,000 positions, has no published cost and does not mention extortion. CentreBC's plan adds 500 Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) officers and 60 Crown prosecutors; the party costs its whole safety chapter, which also covers housing, treatment and emergency preparedness, at about $1.8 billion over four years plus $255 million in capital. The Greens have published no plan. Bail and sentencing law are federal.
questions/q_public_safety/options/a/text: Hire many more police and court workers, and publish numbers on repeat crime.
Hire hundreds more police, prosecutors and judges, and publish numbers on repeat crime and on who gets bail.
Hire many more police, prosecutors and judges, and publish data on repeat offending and bail.
Create about 1,000 new positions for police, rural RCMP, prosecutors, judges and sheriffs, plus public dashboards on repeat offending and bail.
Add 250 police officers, 500 rural RCMP plus 150 civilian staff, 50 Crown prosecutors and 20 trial judges, with public reporting on repeat offending and bail.
questions/q_public_safety/options/b/text: Make the police unit against threats to businesses permanent, and add downtown safety teams.
Make the unit fighting threats against businesses permanent, add a port crime unit and prosecutors, and fund downtown safety patrols.
Make the extortion task force permanent, add a port police team and 60 prosecutors, double repeat-offender enforcement, review bail, and fund downtown safety teams.

Make the extortion task force permanent with its own budget, create a 40-officer port team, add 60 Crown prosecutors, double repeat-offender enforcement, review bail independently, and fund safety teams in 20 downtowns.

Make the extortion task force permanent, build a 40-officer port team with border services and the RCMP, hire 60 Crown prosecutors by 2030/31, double repeat-offender enforcement to $26 million a year, review bail before 2028, and fund 20 downtowns.
questions/q_public_safety/options/c/text: Keep today's police funding and programs, and ask the federal government for tougher bail.
Keep current funding, expand the repeat-offender program, press the federal government on bail, and fund protection from hate crimes.
Keep current funding, expand the repeat-offender program across BC, press the federal government on bail, and counter extremism.
Keep current funding, expand the prolific offender program province-wide, lobby Ottawa for bail reform, and fund security against hate crimes.
Maintain Budget 2025 public safety funding, expand the prolific offender program province-wide, keep pressing Ottawa on bail after Bill C-14, and fund security against hate crimes.
questions/q_public_safety/options/d/text: Get tough on people who keep committing violent crimes, and ban masks at protests.
Focus on repeat violent offenders, ban masks at protests, and refuse to take part in the federal gun buyback.
Target repeat violent offenders, ban masks at protests, and keep BC out of the federal gun buyback.
Target repeat violent offenders, pass a law banning masks at protests, and refuse the federal gun buyback, offering provincial gun storage instead.
Focus on repeat violent offenders, ban protest masks by law, stay out of the federal firearms buyback with provincial storage instead, and make no new police, Crown or court commitments.
questions/q_public_safety/party_position: This party would keep today's programs, grow the one for repeat offenders, and ask the federal government for tougher bail.

The NDP government funded police through its Safer Communities plan, set up teams for repeat violent offenders and pushed Ottawa for bail reform. In this campaign it promises security funding for the Jewish community, a summit on extremism and a wider repeat-offender program. It makes no numeric police promise and says nothing about extortion.

In government, the NDP put $230 million into Safer Communities in 2022, set up 12 hubs for repeat violent offenders in 2023 and added $325 million in new funding over three years in Budget 2025 for encampments, policing and the justice system. Its Bill 36 (2023) required Surrey to complete its switch to a municipal police force, and the province pays Surrey $30 million a year toward transition costs until 2029. It pressed Ottawa for the Bill C-14 bail reforms. In 2026 it promises $500,000 a year for Jewish community security, an extremism summit and a province-wide prolific offender program, but no numeric police pledge.
This party would hire many more police and court workers and publish numbers on repeat crime.

The Conservatives' Safe Streets plan adds 250 police officers, 500 rural Mounties plus 150 civilian staff, 50 prosecutors and help paying for 20 judges, and would report on repeat offending and bail. The plan has no published cost and does not mention extortion. Bail law is set by the federal government.

The Safe Streets plan (October 2026) adds 250 police officers through the Justice Institute of British Columbia, 500 rural RCMP officers and 150 civilian staff over five years, 50 Crown prosecutors, 20 co-funded federal trial judges and more sheriffs, about 1,000 hires in all. It would report on repeat offending, bail and court delays. It has no published cost and does not mention extortion. Several current Conservatives, including Rustad, Doerkson and Halford, voted against Bill 36 in 2023.
This party has no published safety plan, so it is not scored here. It says better housing and health care support public safety.

The Greens have published no public safety or policing plan, so they are not scored here. Their drug policy paper says more supervised drug-use sites would reduce public drug use and 'support public safety'.

The Greens have no public safety or policing commitment (BC Ballot, October 9), so this question leaves them out of the Green score. Their drug policy brief says supervised consumption and inhalation sites would 'support public safety', alongside supportive housing and voluntary care. Their two MLAs cast the only votes against first reading of Armstrong's Drug Recovery and Community Safety Act, which passed first reading 84 to 2. They take no position on police numbers, bail, extortion or courts.
This party wants more police and prosecutors, a permanent unit against threats to businesses, and safety teams downtown.

CentreBC's October 10 platform adds 500 provincial Mounties over five years and 60 prosecutors, makes the extortion task force permanent, creates a port police team, doubles repeat-offender enforcement, orders an independent bail review with public data and funds safety teams in 20 downtowns. The party puts the cost of its whole safety chapter, which also covers housing, treatment and disaster preparedness, at about $1.8 billion over four years.

The platform (pages 26-29) adds 100 provincial RCMP officers a year for five years and 60 Crown prosecutors by 2030/31. It doubles repeat-offender enforcement to about $26 million a year, makes the extortion task force permanent, and creates a 40-officer port team with border services and the RCMP. A bail review would report before 2028 with quarterly data, and a Safe Downtowns Fund would reach 20 downtowns by 2028. The party costs the whole safety chapter, including housing, treatment and emergency preparedness, at about $1.8 billion over four years plus $255 million in capital. Leader Sturko is a former RCMP officer who, as a BC United MLA, voted against Bill 36 in 2023.
This party would get tough on people who keep committing violent crimes and ban masks at protests.

OneBC would focus on repeat violent offenders, ban masks at protests, keep BC out of the federal firearms buyback and run a provincial gun storage program instead. It has no plan for police numbers, prosecutors or courts.

OneBC's priorities are to crack down on repeat and violent offenders, ban masks at protests, keep the province out of the federal firearms buyback with a provincial storage program if needed, and work with Ottawa against organized crime that smuggles drugs and firearms through ports. It has made no commitments on police numbers, Crown prosecutors, courts or extortion.
questions/q_economy_tariffs/prompt/1: The United States put extra taxes on many BC products. How can BC protect jobs?
questions/q_economy_tariffs/prompt/2: American tariffs (extra taxes on BC goods sold there) are costing jobs. How should BC protect jobs and grow the economy?
questions/q_economy_tariffs/prompt/3: With American tariffs and slow growth, what should BC's plan for the economy be?
questions/q_economy_tariffs/prompt/4: The United States has put tariffs on BC lumber, metals and other goods. Which economic strategy should the province pursue?
questions/q_economy_tariffs/prompt/5: The United States charges tariffs on goods outside the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA), on metals and on softwood lumber. Which provincial economic strategy do you prefer?
questions/q_economy_tariffs/context/1: The United States now charges extra taxes on many goods from BC, and some people have lost their jobs. Parties disagree on how to respond. Ideas include selling more natural gas, buying Canadian-made goods, helping factories, logging more, or moving away from oil and gas.
questions/q_economy_tariffs/context/2: BC sells lumber, natural gas, metals and food to other countries, and American tariffs have made many of those sales harder. Parties disagree on the answer: produce more gas and mine more, have government buy Canadian, support factories and trades, move to clean energy, or allow more logging.
questions/q_economy_tariffs/context/3: The NDP government would require Canadian-made materials in public projects, double mineral exports and lend money to businesses hurt by tariffs. The Conservatives would double natural gas production and approve big projects within 120 days. CentreBC would support factories and trades training, sell more to countries other than the United States and cut rules. The Greens would allow no new oil and gas projects and stop exports of unprocessed logs. OneBC wants an oil pipeline and more logging.
questions/q_economy_tariffs/context/4: Employment in BC is down 0.6% so far this year, while exports to countries other than the United States rose 16%. In 2025 the NDP government passed laws to fast-track major projects. The vote was tied, and the Speaker broke the tie in the government's favour, over objections from First Nations. The Conservatives voted against those laws but now propose their own fast-track rules. Both parties take credit for Phase 2 of LNG Canada, a liquefied natural gas (LNG) export project that got the go-ahead in September 2026.
questions/q_economy_tariffs/context/5: Budget 2026 assumes US tariffs of 35% on goods not covered by the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA), 50% on steel, aluminum and copper, and an extra 10% on softwood lumber. Real gross domestic product (GDP) growth of 0.9% is expected in 2026. Unemployment was 6.5% in August, and employment is down 0.6% so far this year. Exports to countries other than the US rose 16%. In May 2025, Bills 14 and 15, which fast-track energy and infrastructure projects, passed on a 46-46 tie broken by the Speaker. LNG Canada made its final investment decision on Phase 2 in September 2026, and both main parties claim credit for it.
questions/q_economy_tariffs/options/a/te: Sell much more natural gas, and approve big projects fast with fewer rules.
Double natural gas production, approve big projects within months, and cut rules for business.
Double gas production, approve major projects within 120 days, and cut red tape.
Double gas production by 2032 and triple it by 2035, issue major-project permits in 120 days, roll red tape back to 2017 levels, and pause sales tax on equipment.
Double gas by 2032 and triple it by 2035, permit projects over $250 million within 120 days, remove two rules for each new one, and exempt equipment from provincial sales tax.
questions/q_economy_tariffs/options/b/te: Buy Canadian, sell more minerals, and lend to businesses hurt by the American taxes.
Have government buy Canadian, double mineral exports, keep growing gas exports, and lend to businesses hurt by tariffs.
Buy Canadian for public projects, double mineral exports, grow liquefied natural gas, and offer relief loans to businesses hurt by tariffs.
Require Canadian content in public infrastructure, double mineral exports, grow net-zero-ready liquefied natural gas, and offer $500 million in interest-free relief loans and a youth hiring credit.

Require Canadian content in government buying, run mine permits in parallel, double critical mineral exports, grow net-zero-ready liquefied natural gas, and offer $500 million in interest-free loans and a $5,000 youth hiring credit.
questions/q_economy_tariffs/options/c/te: Support factories and trades, sell to more countries, and cut taxes for hard-hit industries.
Double factory grants, add trades training, sell beyond the United States, and halve a payroll tax for hard-hit industries.
Double the manufacturing fund, expand trades training, double exports beyond the United States, halve a payroll tax for tariff-hit industries, and cut regulations 25%.
Raise the manufacturing fund to $60 million, add $60 million for trades training, double non-US exports by 2033, halve the Employer Health Tax for tariff-hit sectors, and cut regulations 25%.

A $60 million-a-year manufacturing fund, $60 million for 3,500 trades seats, non-US exports doubled to $62 billion by 2033, the Employer Health Tax halved for forestry, metals and manufacturing, and 25% fewer regulations.
questions/q_economy_tariffs/options/d/te: Stop new oil and gas projects, charge resource companies more, and grow clean energy.
Stop new oil and gas projects, charge resource companies more, stop shipping raw logs abroad, and grow clean energy.
Allow no new fossil fuel projects, end raw log exports, raise royalties (what companies pay for public resources) and tax windfall profits.
Allow no new fossil fuel projects, end raw log exports, reject a bigger logging target, take 50% of net profits as royalties, and add a windfall tax.
Allow no new fossil fuel projects, set royalties at 50% of net profits, add a windfall tax, end raw log exports, and reject the 45 million cubic metre harvest target.
questions/q_economy_tariffs/options/e/te: Allow more logging, build an oil pipeline, and work closely with western provinces.
Allow more logging at lower fees, approve a north coast oil pipeline, and form an alliance with western provinces.
Allow more logging at lower fees, build an oil pipeline to the north coast, and form an alliance of western provinces.
Raise the allowable timber cut, lower stumpage fees, build a pipeline to Prince Rupert or Kitimat, audit 176,000 regulations, and form a Western Canada alliance.
Raise the allowable cut, reduce stumpage fees, speed up forestry permits, build a pipeline to Prince Rupert or Kitimat, audit 176,000 rules, and form a Western Canada alliance.
questions/q_economy_tariffs/party_positi: This party wants government to buy Canadian, sell more minerals abroad, and lend to businesses hurt by the American taxes.

The NDP promises buy-Canadian rules, doubled exports of critical minerals, more liquefied natural gas and $500 million in loans for small businesses. Its 2025 laws to fast-track projects passed over objections from First Nations and the opposition. Employment fell this year, while exports to countries other than the United States rose 16%.

The NDP passed Bill 7, its tariff response law, 48-44 in 2025 after the cabinet override power was removed. Bills 14 and 15, which fast-track projects, passed 46-46 on the Speaker's vote; a minister later said the government 'made an error' on consultation. It approved Ksi Lisims. For 2026 it promises buy-Canadian purchasing, double mineral exports, parallel permitting, a $500 million relief fund and a $5,000 youth hiring credit. Errors in the gas revenue forecast overstated this year's expected royalties by $306 million and about $1.46 billion over five years.
This party would sell much more natural gas abroad and approve big projects faster with fewer rules.

The Conservatives would double gas production, approve projects over $250 million within 120 days, cut red tape and pause the provincial sales tax on business equipment. They voted against the NDP's fast-track laws but propose their own. They have no forestry plan.

The September 29, 2026 plan would more than double natural gas production by 2032 and more than triple it by 2035. A 120 Day Permitting Act would cover projects over $250 million. Red tape would return to 2017 levels by the end of a first term under a one-in, two-out law, and machinery, equipment and business software would be exempt from provincial sales tax for three years. On October 10 it proposed a First Job Tax Credit for businesses that hire young people, with no amount stated. The party welcomes the Pacific Link pipeline. It voted against Bills 7, 14 and 15, and called Bill 7 'the most undemocratic, power-grabbing legislation in history'.
This party would stop new oil and gas projects, charge resource companies more, and grow clean energy.

The Greens would stop new fossil fuel development, end exports of unprocessed logs, take half of oil and gas profits in royalties and tax windfall profits. They call this their 'economic direction', not a full platform.

The Greens' Economic Vision and October forestry brief reject the Working Forest Model's 45 million cubic metre harvest target, end raw log exports and aim to direct 30 to 50% of available wood to higher-value manufacturing. They add Buy BC purchasing, a single front door for approvals, a windfall tax, a minimum corporate tax, royalties of 50% of net profits and an end to fossil fuel subsidies. The Greens voted against Bills 14 and 15. Both Green MLAs voted for the final Bill 7 after its cabinet override part was withdrawn.
This party wants to help factories and workers, sell to more countries, and cut rules.

CentreBC's October 10 platform doubles the Manufacturing Jobs Fund to $60 million, adds $60 million for trades training, aims to double exports outside the United States by 2033, halves the Employer Health Tax for tariff-hit sectors and cuts regulations 25%. If savings fall short, the fund stays at $30 million. It backs liquefied natural gas with First Nations partners.

The platform sets one review per project with 12-month provincial decisions and 10 mine decisions by 2030. The Manufacturing Jobs Fund rises to $60 million a year, though a fallback list holds it at $30 million. It adds 3,500 trades seats, aims to double non-US exports to $62 billion by 2033, halves the Employer Health Tax for tariff-hit sectors and cuts regulations 25%. It backs net-zero-ready liquefied natural gas with First Nations partners, and sets no gas target. Separately, it supports a pipeline only under five conditions it set in 2025, including Indigenous participation and safety and climate guardrails.
This party wants more logging, an oil pipeline, and closer ties with other western provinces.

OneBC would raise the allowable timber cut, lower stumpage fees (what companies pay to log public forests), approve an oil pipeline to Prince Rupert or Kitimat, audit 176,000 regulations and form a Western Canada alliance, along with 25% tax cuts. It has no plan to respond to tariffs.

OneBC would raise the annual allowable cut, reduce stumpage fees, speed up forestry permits, back a pipeline to Prince Rupert or Kitimat, audit 176,000 regulations and form a Western Canada Alliance. It also promises 25% tax cuts for every tax bracket, including corporate, and 2% off the provincial sales tax. It has no tariff-response program and no costing.
questions/q_climate_energy/prompt/1: Oil and gas create jobs, but they also add to climate change. What should BC do?
questions/q_climate_energy/prompt/2: BC sells natural gas, but it is behind on its goal to cut pollution that warms the climate. What should it do?
questions/q_climate_energy/prompt/3: What direction should BC take on climate change and energy?
questions/q_climate_energy/prompt/4: Which direction should BC take on climate targets, carbon pricing for industry and natural gas production?
questions/q_climate_energy/prompt/5: Choose a direction on emissions targets, industrial carbon pricing, liquefied natural gas (LNG) expansion and clean power.
questions/q_climate_energy/context/1: Oil and gas bring jobs and money to BC, but burning them adds to climate change. In 2025 the government stopped the carbon tax people paid on fuel. Big industry still pays a carbon charge. Parties disagree on gas exports, oil pipelines and climate goals.
questions/q_climate_energy/context/2: In 2025 BC stopped charging the carbon tax on the fuel people buy, but large industries still pay a carbon price. The province is also allowing more plants that export natural gas. BC expects to cut its climate pollution by only half of what the law requires by 2030.
questions/q_climate_energy/context/3: BC expects to cut its climate pollution 20% by 2030, which is half of the 40% target set in law. The carbon tax that people paid on fuel ended in 2025, but large industries still pay a carbon price. Parties disagree on growing natural gas exports, on oil pipelines and on whether to keep the carbon price for industry.
questions/q_climate_energy/context/4: BC's emissions are projected to be 20% below 2007 levels by 2030, while the law sets a 40% target. In 2025 the NDP government ended the consumer carbon tax, the rebates for electric vehicles and the rule that all new cars sold be zero-emission by 2035. Carbon pricing for large industry and clean fuel rules remain. LNG Canada, a liquefied natural gas (LNG) export project, approved its Phase 2 expansion in September 2026.
questions/q_climate_energy/context/5: BC law set targets of 16% below 2007 emissions by 2025 and 40% by 2030, but the 2025 accountability report projects cuts of only 2.6% and 20%. The consumer carbon tax has been zero since April 1, 2025. The Output-Based Pricing System, which charges large industrial emitters and tightens 1% a year, remains. So does the Low Carbon Fuel Standard, which requires a 30% cut in the carbon intensity of fuels by 2030. Electric vehicle rebates ended and the 2035 zero-emission vehicle mandate was dropped. LNG Canada made its final investment decision on Phase 2 in September 2026. An oil pipeline to the coast, called Pacific Link, has been proposed.
questions/q_climate_energy/options/a/tex: Produce as much oil and gas as possible, and drop climate charges and goals.
Produce as much oil and gas as possible, stop charging industry for pollution, and drop climate targets.
Maximize oil and gas, end carbon pricing for industry, and drop climate targets.
Approve a pipeline to the coast, end industrial carbon pricing, the clean fuel rules and the CleanBC climate plan, and abandon the 2030 target.
Build a pipeline to Prince Rupert or Kitimat, repeal the industrial carbon price and the Low Carbon Fuel Standard, wind down CleanBC, and set no emissions targets.
questions/q_climate_energy/options/b/tex: Sell much more natural gas overseas, protect nature, and make no new climate promises.
Sell much more natural gas abroad under existing nature rules, but make no new climate promises.
Expand natural gas exports quickly under environmental rules, and leave carbon pricing and climate targets undecided.
Double gas output by 2032 with 120-day permits that keep environmental protections, seek credit for replacing coal abroad, and make no commitment on industrial carbon pricing.

Double gas by 2032, permit projects within 120 days under environmental standards, seek credit for displacing coal, support a pipeline, and make no commitment on carbon pricing, clean fuel rules or targets.
questions/q_climate_energy/options/c/tex: Sell more natural gas, keep climate charges on big industry, and build clean power.
Keep building gas export plants that run on clean power, keep industry's pollution charges, and add wind power.
Expand gas export plants built to reach net-zero emissions, keep carbon pricing for industry, and build clean power.
Keep industrial carbon pricing and clean fuel rules with no consumer tax, grow net-zero-ready liquefied natural gas, and build wind power and power lines.

Keep the consumer carbon tax at zero and the industrial carbon price and clean fuel standard, grow net-zero-ready gas exports to 48 million tonnes a year, fund a $36 billion grid, and keep the 2030 target.
questions/q_climate_energy/options/d/tex: Stop new oil and gas projects, and spend on clean power instead.
Approve no new gas, oil or pipeline projects, and fund clean power and energy-saving home upgrades.
Allow no new fossil fuel projects or pipeline, and fund renewable power and home energy upgrades.
Allow no new fossil fuel projects or pipeline, make gas exporters pay for their own power, end fossil fuel subsidies, and expand home energy upgrades.
Allow no new fossil fuel development or pipeline, make gas exporters pay for their own power, end fossil fuel subsidies, and make electricity 35% of energy use by 2035.
questions/q_climate_energy/options/e/tex: Set a lower climate goal, keep charging big polluters, and help homes save energy.
Set a lower climate goal BC can meet, keep charging big industry, and lend money for home energy upgrades.
Lower the 2030 target in law to a 20% cut, keep industrial carbon pricing, pass a methane law, and offer home-upgrade loans.
Set a 2030 milestone of 20% below 2007 in law, keep industrial carbon pricing, pass a methane law, offer $500 million in home-upgrade loans, add highway chargers, and keep the tanker ban.
Legislate a 2030 milestone of 20% below 2007, keep the 2040 and 2050 targets and the industrial carbon price, cut methane 75% by 2030, lend $500 million for home retrofits, and keep the tanker ban.
questions/q_climate_energy/party_positio: This party ended the carbon tax on fuel people buy, but it keeps carbon charges on big industry and is growing gas exports.

In government, the NDP ended the consumer carbon tax and rebates for electric vehicles, approved more liquefied natural gas and kept carbon pricing for industry. It admits BC will miss its 2030 target by about half and has not said how it will respond.

The NDP cut the consumer carbon tax to zero in April 2025 but kept the industrial carbon price and the Low Carbon Fuel Standard. It dropped electric vehicle rebates and the 2035 zero-emission vehicle target, and signed wind power contracts. BC is projected to reach 20% below 2007 by 2030, against 40% in law. For 2026 it promises more liquefied natural gas, a north coast transmission line and a temporary 10 cent per litre fuel tax cut. It would accept a pipeline only if the tanker ban stays.
This party wants to sell much more natural gas abroad. It has made no promises on cutting pollution.

The Conservatives would double gas output by 2032, approve projects within 120 days and back an oil pipeline. Their 2026 materials do not mention carbon pricing for industry or the 2030 target. In 2025 their leader at the time called the industrial carbon tax 'punishing' and asked if it would be dropped.

The 2026 plan would more than double gas output by 2032 and more than triple it by 2035, pass a 120 Day Permitting Act while 'keeping BC's high environmental standards' and seek credit for displacing coal. The party welcomes the Pacific Link pipeline. It says nothing about the industrial carbon price, the Low Carbon Fuel Standard, CleanBC or the 2030 target. In 2024 the party promised to end the carbon tax and the Low Carbon Fuel Standard, and in March 2025 Rustad called the industrial carbon tax 'punishing' and asked whether it would be dropped. This quiz scores the party as likely to weaken industrial pricing.
This party wants to stop new oil and gas projects and spend on clean power.

The Greens would stop new fossil fuel development, oppose the oil pipeline, make gas exporters pay for their own power, end fossil fuel subsidies and fund renewable power and home upgrades. A Green MLA cast the only vote against ending the carbon tax at first reading, and both voted against the fast-track project laws.

The Greens would stop new fossil fuel development. Their October 10 climate brief would end approvals for new fracking expansion, LNG terminals and fossil fuel pipelines, oppose the Pacific Link pipeline, end fossil fuel subsidies, strengthen industrial carbon pricing, set gas royalties at 50% of net profits and cap oil and gas emissions if other rules fall short. They would make existing liquefied natural gas plants pay for their own power, restore net metering and raise electricity to 35% of energy use by 2035. In March 2025 Green MLA Rob Botterell cast the only vote against the carbon tax repeal bill at first reading, and the Greens voted against Bills 14 and 15, which fast-track projects.
This party says BC will miss its climate goal and wants a lower one in law. It would keep charging big polluters and help homes save energy.

CentreBC's October 10 platform admits BC will miss its 2030 goal and would set a 20% cut in law instead of 40%. It keeps carbon pricing for large industry with no consumer tax, and adds a methane law, home-upgrade loans, highway chargers and more BC Hydro power. It backs gas exports with First Nations partners and would seek a federal promise in writing to keep the northern tanker ban.

The platform puts a 2030 milestone of 20% below 2007 in law, down from 40%, keeps the 2040 and 2050 targets and creates a Climate Accountability Office. It keeps industrial carbon pricing, sends at least $100 million a year to the CleanBC Industry Fund and rules out a consumer carbon tax. It would cut methane 75% from 2014 levels by 2030, lend $500 million for 25,000 home upgrades and add 2,000 megawatts of BC Hydro power. It backs net-zero-ready gas exports with First Nations partners and would seek a written federal commitment to keep the northern tanker ban.
This party wants an oil pipeline to the coast and has no climate plan.
OneBC would approve a pipeline to Prince Rupert or Kitimat. Beyond general cuts to regulations, it has published no climate commitments and no position on carbon pricing.

OneBC would build a pipeline to Prince Rupert or Kitimat, scrap the Step Code (a CleanBC energy rule for buildings) and audit 176,000 regulations. It has no climate plan, targets or carbon pricing position, so this quiz places it at the deregulation end by inference.
questions/q_education_childcare/prompt/1: What should the government do about child care and schools?
questions/q_education_childcare/prompt/2: What should the province do about child care and public schools?
questions/q_education_childcare/prompt/3: What should the province's priorities be for child care and for schools from kindergarten to Grade 12?
questions/q_education_childcare/prompt/4: Which direction should the province take on child care and on schools from kindergarten to Grade 12?
questions/q_education_childcare/prompt/5: Choose the priority for ChildCareBC, the province's child care program, and for kindergarten to Grade 12 (K-12) schools.
questions/q_education_childcare/context/: Child care costs families a lot. The province pays for some low-cost spots, but it has paused adding new ones to save money. Some parties want many more low-cost spots or free child care. Others want schools to focus on reading, math and testing.

Child care can cost families as much as rent. About one in ten licensed spaces costs $10 a day, and the province has paused new $10-a-day spaces for three years to save money. Some fast-growing school districts still rely on portable classrooms. Parties disagree on whether to expand child care, focus schools on basics, or hold spending.

About 10% of licensed child care spaces cost $10 a day. In 2026 the NDP government paused new $10-a-day spaces for three years. Some fast-growing school districts still use many portable classrooms. The Greens want free child care by 2031 and CentreBC wants 20,000 more $10-a-day spaces. The Conservatives and OneBC focus on testing, grades and the basics.

About 10% of licensed child care spaces cost $10 a day. In February 2026 the NDP government paused new $10-a-day enrolment for three years to fix the program's funding model. The Affordable Child Care Benefit still helps families with incomes up to $111,000. Fast-growing school districts still use portable classrooms.

New $10-a-day enrolment has been frozen since February 2026 (reported as a three-year freeze), and Budget 2026 adds $330 million over three years for child care. There were more than 16,000 such spaces in March 2025, against a target of 20,000. The Affordable Child Care Benefit continues for family incomes up to $111,000. Budget 2026 plans $3.9 billion over three years to build, renovate and seismically upgrade schools. The Greens' expansion has no published cost. CentreBC puts its education plan at about $2.0 billion plus $750 million in capital over four years, and funds child care from federal money, by the party's own figures.
questions/q_education_childcare/options/: Test students in reading, writing and math, give parents more say, and don't expand child care.
Bring in province-wide tests in reading, writing and math, pass a parents' rights law, and don't expand child care.
Bring in standardized tests in reading, writing and math and a parental rights law, with no child care expansion.
Bring in province-wide standardized testing in reading, writing and math and a Parental Bill of Rights, with no child care expansion.

Bring in standardized provincial testing focused on reading, writing and mathematics, a Parental Bill of Rights guaranteeing informed consent and classroom transparency, and no expansion of ChildCareBC.
Focus on reading and math, bring back exams, and don't expand child care.
Focus on reading and math, bring back letter grades and provincial exams, and don't expand child care.
Put the basics first by restoring letter grades and provincial exams, with no child care expansion.
Put literacy and numeracy first, restore letter grades in Grades 4 to 9 and provincial exams in Grades 10 and 12, with no child care expansion.
Focus on literacy and numeracy, restore letter grades in Grades 4 to 9 and provincial exams in Grades 10 and 12, raise no new taxes, and make no child care commitment.
Keep today's low-cost child care spots, pause adding new ones, and keep building schools.
Keep existing $10-a-day spaces, pause new ones for three years, and keep building schools.
Protect existing $10-a-day spaces, pause new ones for three years, and keep building schools.
Protect families already in $10-a-day spaces, pause new enrolment for three years to fix funding, and build schools within a smaller budget.
Stabilize ChildCareBC for three years with no new $10-a-day sites, keep the Affordable Child Care Benefit, keep building schools within the current capital plan, and make no new 2026 pledge.
Add many more low-cost child care spots, new classrooms, letter grades and school counsellors.
Add 20,000 more $10-a-day spaces and 25,000 school seats, use letter grades from Grade 4, and hire more counsellors.
Add 20,000 $10-a-day spaces and 25,000 school seats, bring in letter grades for Grades 4 to 9, and fund a counsellor per 400 students.
Add 20,000 $10-a-day spaces by 2030 and 25,000 school seats by 2031, starting in districts with many portables, plus letter grades, a counsellor per 400 students and 1,500 education assistants.

Add 20,000 $10-a-day spaces by 2030 with federal money and 25,000 seats with $750 million in capital, letter grades for Grades 4 to 9 from 2028, a counsellor per 400 students and 1,500 education assistants.
Make child care free, pay child care workers more, and feed every student.
Lift the child care pause, make it free by 2031, raise child care workers' pay, and feed every student.
Make child care free by 2031, raise educators' pay, provide school food, and add a wealth tax.
Make child care free for all by 2031, pay early childhood educators $35 to $45 an hour, feed every student, and move private school funding to public schools.

Make child care free by 2031, pay early childhood educators $35 to $45 an hour by 2028, fund school food and a counsellor per 250 students, move private school funding to public schools, and add a wealth tax.
questions/q_education_childcare/party_po: This party made child care cheaper, then paused new low-cost spots. It has built schools, but some students still learn in portable classrooms.

The NDP created $10-a-day child care, then in 2026 froze new spaces for three years. It says it has built 250 schools, but some fast-growing districts still rely on portable classrooms. It made no new education or child care promise in 2026.

The NDP launched ChildCareBC in 2018 and had more than 16,000 $10-a-day spaces by March 2025, toward a goal of 20,000. In February 2026 it paused new enrolment and expansion, a freeze Global News reported as three years, and Budget 2026 adds $330 million over three years for child care. The party says it built 250 schools. Budget 2026 plans $3.9 billion over three years for school building and seismic upgrades. It made no education or child care commitment in 2026.
This party wants to remove a school resource on gender identity and, in 2024, promised letter grades and exams. It has made no child care promises.

The Conservatives' 2026 Safe Schools page calls for repealing SOGI 123, with no child care or school building promise. They promised letter grades and provincial exams in 2024 but have not repeated that. Their pledge of no new taxes limits new spending.

The 2026 Safe Schools page would repeal SOGI 123, a teaching resource on sexual orientation and gender identity. It has no child care, school building or post-secondary commitment. The 2024 platform promised letter grades in Grades 4 to 9 and provincial exams in Grades 10 and 12. The no-new-taxes pledge suggests school capital would be held or cut. This quiz scores the party as focused on grades and exams, with low confidence on child care.
This party wants free child care for all, better pay for child care workers, and food for every student.
The Greens would lift the freeze now, make child care free for all by 2031, pay early childhood educators $35 to $45 an hour and feed every student. They have published no cost for the plan.

On September 28, 2026, the Greens promised to lift the freeze 'immediately', make child care free for all by 2031 and pay early childhood educators $35 to $45 an hour by 2028. Their plans also include one point of registration for $10-a-day spaces, closing the inclusive education funding gap, a counsellor per 250 students, universal school food, moving private school funding into public schools and a moratorium on artificial intelligence in schools. The releases give no cost.
This party wants many more low-cost child care spots, new classrooms, letter grades and more school counsellors.

CentreBC's October 10 platform adds 20,000 $10-a-day spaces by 2030 with federal money and 25,000 school seats by 2031, starting where portables are most common. It keeps class-size limits, funds a counsellor per 400 students and 1,500 more education assistants, and brings back letter grades. The party puts the cost at about $2 billion plus $750 million in capital.

The platform adds 20,000 $10-a-day spaces by 2030, with federal funds 'secured to 2031', and 25,000 school seats by 2031 using prefab additions and $750 million in capital. It keeps and funds class-size limits, moves to a counsellor per 400 students by 2030, adds 1,500 education assistants, brings in letter grades for Grades 4 to 9 from September 2028, publishes test results by school, caps tuition increases at 2% and sets a school artificial intelligence standard in 2027. Education costs about $2.0 billion over four years (party figure).
This party wants student testing, more say for parents, and no new child care spending.

OneBC would bring in standardized testing in reading, writing and math and a Parental Bill of Rights, and would remove SOGI 123, a teaching resource on sexual orientation and gender identity. It has no child care plan.

OneBC's priorities are standardized testing focused on reading, writing and mathematics, a Parental Bill of Rights, and removing SOGI 123 (a sexual orientation and gender identity resource) and 'politicized content' from classrooms. It has no child care, school building or post-secondary commitments, and its 25% tax cuts and four-year plan to balance the budget limit new spending.
questions/q_icbc/prompt/1: How should car insurance work for people hurt in crashes?
questions/q_icbc/prompt/2: Should ICBC's current way of paying people hurt in crashes stay, change, or face private competition?
questions/q_icbc/prompt/3: Should BC keep no-fault car insurance, bring back lawsuits for serious injuries, or open insurance to competition?
questions/q_icbc/prompt/4: Should BC keep Enhanced Care, ICBC's no-fault system, adopt a hybrid that allows lawsuits for serious injuries, or open the market?
questions/q_icbc/prompt/5: Choose a model for basic auto insurance: Enhanced Care no-fault, a hybrid allowing lawsuits (tort claims) for serious injury, or private competition with lawsuits.
questions/q_icbc/context/1: In BC, people hurt in car crashes get set payments for care from ICBC, the public insurer. Most cannot sue in court, which keeps prices lower. Some parties want badly hurt people to be able to sue again. Some want private companies to compete.
questions/q_icbc/context/2: Since 2021, ICBC, the public car insurer, has paid set amounts for care and lost income instead of letting people sue after crashes. The province says this saves drivers about $500 a year. Critics say people with the most serious injuries get too little. Some parties want lawsuits back for serious injuries, which others fear would raise prices.
questions/q_icbc/context/3: In 2021 the NDP government brought in a no-fault system, which pays set care and income benefits instead of letting people sue. The province says drivers save about $500 a year, and basic rates are frozen. Critics say people with life-changing injuries get too little. No published estimate shows how bringing back lawsuits would change prices.
questions/q_icbc/context/4: Enhanced Care began in May 2021 and replaced most lawsuits with set care and income benefits. The province says basic rates fell by an average of $496, about 28%, and basic rates are frozen until spring 2027. Critics say people with catastrophic injuries, such as brain and spinal cord injuries, are not supported well enough. No published estimate shows how restoring lawsuits would affect premiums.
questions/q_icbc/context/5: Enhanced Care, in place since May 2021, pays no-fault care-based benefits instead of court awards. The province reports an average saving of $496 (about 28%) and about $2.7 billion in rebates, with about $5 billion in claims from before 2021 still to pay. Basic rates are frozen through spring 2027. Critics say support for catastrophic injuries is inadequate. The Conservatives' hybrid proposal is described differently in a September 29 letter and an October 7 party page, and neither gives a premium estimate. The NDP's claim that premiums would double has not been verified.
questions/q_icbc/options/a/text/1: Let private companies sell car insurance, and let people hurt in crashes sue.
questions/q_icbc/options/a/text/2: Let private companies sell basic car insurance, not just ICBC, and let people hurt in crashes sue.
questions/q_icbc/options/a/text/3: Open basic car insurance to private companies, and end no-fault so injured people can sue.
questions/q_icbc/options/a/text/4: Phase out ICBC's monopoly on basic insurance, let private insurers compete, and replace no-fault with the right to sue.
questions/q_icbc/options/a/text/5: Phase out ICBC's basic-insurance monopoly, end the Enhanced Care no-fault system, and restore the right to sue for crash injuries (tort liability).
questions/q_icbc/options/b/text/1: Keep public insurance, let badly hurt people sue, and allow some private competition.
questions/q_icbc/options/b/text/2: Keep ICBC, bring back lawsuits for serious injuries, and allow competition where it lowers prices.
questions/q_icbc/options/b/text/3: Keep ICBC public, restore lawsuits for serious injuries, and allow some private competition.
questions/q_icbc/options/b/text/4: Create a hybrid: ICBC stays a public insurer, people with serious injuries can sue with capped lawyer fees, and competition is allowed where it helps.
questions/q_icbc/options/b/text/5: Pass a hybrid law within one year: lawsuits for serious injury, lawyer fees under Law Society caps, ICBC kept as a public option, and competition where it improves prices.
questions/q_icbc/options/c/text/1: Keep public insurance with set care payments and no lawsuits, and keep prices frozen.
questions/q_icbc/options/c/text/2: Keep ICBC paying for care instead of lawsuits, and freeze basic rates for three more years.
questions/q_icbc/options/c/text/3: Keep public no-fault insurance and freeze basic rates until 2030.
questions/q_icbc/options/c/text/4: Keep the Enhanced Care no-fault system and ICBC's monopoly on basic insurance, and extend the basic rate freeze to spring 2030.
questions/q_icbc/options/c/text/5: Keep Enhanced Care with no lawsuits for most claims, extend the basic rate freeze to spring 2030, and keep ICBC's monopoly on basic insurance.
questions/q_icbc/options/d/text/1: Keep public insurance, cap price rises, and pay more for the worst injuries.
questions/q_icbc/options/d/text/2: Keep ICBC's care system, hold rate rises to inflation after spring 2027, and add pain-and-suffering payments for the worst injuries.
questions/q_icbc/options/d/text/3: Keep public no-fault insurance, cap rate rises at inflation after 2027, and add awards for catastrophic injuries.
questions/q_icbc/options/d/text/4: Keep Enhanced Care and ICBC's monopoly, freeze rates to spring 2027 and then hold rises at or below inflation to 2030, and add pain-and-suffering awards for catastrophic injuries from 2031.
questions/q_icbc/options/d/text/5: Keep Enhanced Care, freeze basic rates to spring 2027 and hold rises at or below inflation to 2030, add pain-and-suffering awards for brain and spinal injuries from 2031, and act on the committee review.
questions/q_icbc/party_positions/ndp/tex: This party set up care payments without lawsuits and wants to keep prices frozen longer.

The NDP brought in no-fault 'Enhanced Care' in 2021, says the average driver saves about $500 a year, and has frozen basic rates for seven years. It promises to extend the freeze to spring 2030 but has not said what that would cost.

The NDP brought in Enhanced Care in May 2021 and froze basic rates for seven years through spring 2027. ICBC paid about $2.7 billion in rebates and the province reports an average saving of $496 (about 28%), with about $5 billion in older claims still to pay. On October 8, 2026, the party promised to extend the freeze to spring 2030, with no cost stated. It says the Conservative plan would open private competition and double premiums, a claim that has not been verified.
questions/q_icbc/party_positions/conserv: This party would keep public insurance but let badly hurt people sue, and allow some private competition.

A leaked letter commits the Conservatives to a 'hybrid' law within a year that restores lawsuits for serious injuries. The party's web page keeps ICBC public and caps lawyer fees. The two describe the plan differently, and neither gives a premium estimate.

A September 29, 2026 letter promised hybrid legislation within a year giving people the 'right to recover for their serious injuries', and said 'everything's on the table', including limits on minor-injury claims, with private competition an option under consideration. The October 7 party page caps fees under Law Society limits, says it 'eliminates the overwhelming majority of litigation' and keeps ICBC as a public option. There is no premium estimate.
questions/q_icbc/party_positions/green/t: This party has not shared a car insurance plan, so it is not scored here.
The Greens have published no 2026 position on ICBC or no-fault insurance, so this quiz does not score them on this question.
No ICBC or car insurance commitment appears on the Green plan page, in the party's economic vision or in BC Ballot's list of its commitments, so this question is left out of the Green score.
questions/q_icbc/party_positions/centreb: This party would keep public insurance and set care payments, limit price rises, and pay more to people with the worst injuries.

CentreBC's October 10 platform keeps ICBC public, freezes basic rates to spring 2027 and then holds them at or below inflation to 2030, and gives pain-and-suffering awards to people with catastrophic injuries from 2031. It otherwise keeps Enhanced Care, will act on the legislative committee's review, and allows no private competition.

The platform says 'BC Hydro and ICBC stay public'. Basic rates stay frozen until spring 2027, then rise at or below inflation through 2030. From 2031, people with catastrophic brain and spinal cord injuries get pain-and-suffering awards, built into rates once the cap ends. The party will 'act on the legislative committee's review of Enhanced Care' and set ICBC efficiency targets. It does not restore lawsuits in general or allow competition. Calling this a partial step back from no-fault is this quiz's reading, not the platform's wording.
questions/q_icbc/party_positions/onebc/t: This party would let private companies sell car insurance and let people hurt in crashes sue.
OneBC would phase out ICBC's monopoly and end no-fault insurance, letting private insurers compete and injured people sue.
OneBC's priorities include phasing out the ICBC monopoly and ending no-fault insurance. It has published no transition plan or costing.
questions/q_democracy_power/prompt/1: How much power should the government use, and should the way we vote change?
questions/q_democracy_power/prompt/2: How fast should the province push big decisions through, and should the way we vote change?
questions/q_democracy_power/prompt/3: How much power should the province use, and should BC change its voting system?
questions/q_democracy_power/prompt/4: What balance between fast decisions and checks on government do you want, and should voting rules change?
questions/q_democracy_power/prompt/5: Choose a direction on provincial powers, approval speed, government oversight and electoral rules.
questions/q_democracy_power/context/1: The government has used strong powers to approve homes and projects quickly. It also called this election two years early. Some like fast action. Others want more checks on government, or a new voting system. In 2018, voters chose to keep the current voting system.
questions/q_democracy_power/context/2: The NDP government used strong powers to speed up housing and big projects, sometimes over objections from cities. It called this election two years early. In 2018, BC voters chose to keep the current voting system, where the candidate with the most votes in each riding wins. Parties now propose different rules for approvals, oversight and voting.
questions/q_democracy_power/context/3: The NDP government passed laws that let cabinet fast-track projects, override local zoning to allow more housing, and use emergency powers in response to tariffs. It called the election two years early. In a 2018 referendum, 61% of voters rejected proportional representation, a system that gives parties seats in line with their share of the vote. Parties now propose changes to approvals, oversight and voting rules.
questions/q_democracy_power/context/4: The NDP government used provincial zoning rules, fast-track approvals by cabinet and emergency powers to respond to tariffs. Its fast-track laws passed only because the Speaker broke a 46-46 tie. It called the election two years early, and a Leger poll found 57% disapproved. In 2018, voters rejected proportional representation, which gives parties seats in line with their vote share, by 61% to 39%.
questions/q_democracy_power/context/5: Bill 7 gave cabinet tariff response powers and passed 48-44 after Part 4, a clause letting cabinet override laws, was withdrawn and a one-year sunset added. Bills 14 and 15, which fast-track projects, passed 46-46 on the Speaker's deciding vote, and a June 2025 order extended Bill 14 to all wind and solar projects. Bill 44, the 2023 zoning law, passed under time allocation, which limits debate. The snap election was called on September 22, 2026, and Angus Reid found two-thirds said it came 'too soon'. In the 2018 referendum, 61.3% voted to keep first-past-the-post. A 2017 law banned corporate and union donations and set a $1,200 cap.
questions/q_democracy_power/options/a/te: Let the province approve homes and projects fast, even when cities and towns object.
Use the province's full powers to speed up homes and projects, even over local objections.
Use full provincial powers to speed up housing and major projects, even over local objections.
Keep a strong provincial role: province-wide zoning rules, cabinet fast-track approvals and emergency trade powers, with voters judging the results at elections.
Use provincial zoning rules like Bill 44, fast-tracking by regulation under Bills 14 and 15, and Bill 7 trade powers with a sunset, with accountability through elections.
questions/q_democracy_power/options/b/te: Set firm deadlines to approve big projects, but give cities and towns more say.
Set legal deadlines for fast project approvals, but override cities and property owners less often.
Pass a law with fixed approval deadlines, but override local governments and property owners less.
Pass a 120-day permit law for major projects, remove two regulations for each new one, return regional powers to cities and the province, and oppose cabinet rule-making by regulation.
Pass a 120-day permitting law and a one-in, two-out regulation law, cut Metro Vancouver back to utilities, oppose the Bill 7 and Bill 15 powers, and keep the current voting system.
questions/q_democracy_power/options/c/te: Add a budget watchdog, publish big contracts, and make major deals public before signing.
Create a budget watchdog, make information requests free, publish big contracts, and publish First Nations deals before signing.
Create an independent budget officer and a balanced-budget law, publish scorecards and big contracts, make information requests free, and publish major agreements before signing.

Create an Independent Budget Officer and a balanced-budget law that puts ministers' pay at risk, scrap the $10 freedom-of-information fee, publish contracts over $10 million, and publish draft First Nations agreements before signing.

Pass a balanced-budget and spending control law, create an Independent Budget Officer, publish an audited quarterly scorecard, scrap freedom-of-information fees, publish contracts over $10 million, and table land agreements before signing.
questions/q_democracy_power/options/d/te: Change the voting system so each party's seats match its share of votes.
Change the voting system so each party wins seats in line with its share of the vote.
Switch to proportional representation, so seats match votes and parties must work together.
Pass proportional representation into law within 100 days so seats track votes, despite the 2018 referendum result.
Pass proportional representation legislation within the first 100 days, although 61.3% voted to keep first-past-the-post in 2018.
questions/q_democracy_power/options/e/te: End voting by mail and early voting, so people vote in person on election day.
End voting by mail and early voting, so everyone votes in person on election day.
End mail-in and early voting, so all ballots are cast in person on election day.
Allow voting only in person on election day by ending mail-in and advance voting.
End mail-in and early voting so that all ballots are cast in person on election day (a June 2025 position).
questions/q_democracy_power/party_positi: This party used strong powers to act fast and called an early election. It has changed course when people pushed back.

The NDP used cabinet fast-tracking, tariff rules made by regulation and overrides of local zoning, and called the election two years early. It dropped a clause letting cabinet rewrite laws after criticism. In 2017 it banned corporate and union donations. It has no 2026 reform pledge.

The NDP banned corporate and union donations with the Election Amendment Act in 2017. In 2023 it passed the Bill 44 zoning law under time allocation, which limits debate. In 2025 it passed Bill 7 after withdrawing Part 4, and Bills 14 and 15 on the Speaker's vote, later extending Bill 14 by order. It exempted the north coast transmission line from environmental assessment and utilities commission review. A Leger poll found 57% disapproved of the snap election. It has made no 2026 reform commitment.
This party wants firm deadlines for big projects and more say for cities, towns and families.

The Conservatives voted against the NDP's fast-track and tariff laws and called the tariff law 'undemocratic', but promise their own 120-day permitting law and a rule to remove two regulations for each new one. They would cut Metro Vancouver back to water and sewer. They have no voting-system proposal.

The Conservatives voted against Bills 7, 14 and 15. The party called Bill 7 'the most undemocratic, power-grabbing legislation in history', and Rustad said it gave cabinet 'almost unlimited powers with zero oversight'. The party promises a 120 Day Permitting Act for projects over $250 million, a one-in, two-out regulation law, and cutting Metro Vancouver back to drinking water and sewage treatment. In 2024 it promised voter approval for any new tax, but has not repeated that.
This party wants each party's seats to match its share of the votes.

The Greens would bring in proportional representation within their first 100 days so seats match votes, although voters rejected it in 2018. They helped win the 2017 donation ban and voted against the NDP's fast-track laws, citing weak oversight.

The Greens would pass proportional representation legislation in their first 100 days. Their 2017 Confidence and Supply Agreement with the NDP brought the donation ban and the 2018 referendum, which lost 61.3% to 38.7%. They voted against Bills 14 and 15 over oversight, and voted for the final Bill 7 after its cabinet override part was withdrawn. On February 9, 2026 they said they would not renew their accord with the NDP, citing 'stalled or undelivered' commitments.
This party wants a budget watchdog, public report cards, and big deals shown to the public before signing.

CentreBC's October 10 platform creates an Independent Budget Officer and a balanced-budget law that docks ministers' pay, publishes a scorecard checked by the Auditor General, scraps the $10 freedom-of-information fee, publishes contracts over $10 million and posts draft First Nations agreements 60 days before signing. It takes no position on proportional representation.

The platform passes a Balanced Budget and Spending Control Act, creates an Independent Budget Officer and cuts ministers' pay if targets are missed. A scorecard would appear within 100 days, then quarterly with a yearly audit, and cabinet decision summaries within 30 working days. It scraps freedom-of-information fees, aims for 90% on-time responses, publishes contracts over $10 million in full, posts draft First Nations agreements at least 60 days before signing, and tables title and land agreements in the legislature before they are signed. It does not mention electoral reform, recall or free votes. Sturko called the snap election 'quite insulting'.
This party has called for everyone to vote in person on election day.
In June 2025 OneBC called for ending mail-in and early voting, but this is not in its 2026 materials. It wants to audit all provincial regulations. It has no position on proportional representation.

In June 2025 OneBC's leader pledged to 'end mail-in and early voting', but this is not on its 2026 priorities page. It would audit 176,000 regulations and ban masks at protests. It has no position on proportional representation.
questions/q_local_skytrain/prompt/1: SkyTrain is being extended to Fleetwood. What should happen with trains and buses?
questions/q_local_skytrain/prompt/2: SkyTrain reaches Fleetwood in 2029, and the regional transit system needs new money from 2028. What should the province do?
questions/q_local_skytrain/prompt/3: How should the province finish the SkyTrain line and fund TransLink, the regional transit agency, after 2028?
questions/q_local_skytrain/prompt/4: How should the province finish the Surrey-Langley SkyTrain and close TransLink's funding gap from 2028?
questions/q_local_skytrain/prompt/5: The Surrey-Langley SkyTrain costs $5.996 billion and opens in late 2029, and TransLink faces a gap of at least $112 million a year from 2028. Which approach?
