questions/q_local_skytrain/context/1: A new SkyTrain line through Fleetwood is set to open in 2029. TransLink, which runs buses and trains in the region, will be short of money from 2028. Parties disagree on how to pay for transit, and on whether some people should ride free.
questions/q_local_skytrain/context/2: The federal and provincial governments are paying for the SkyTrain line to Fleetwood and Langley, which should open in late 2029. TransLink, the regional transit agency, will be short at least $112 million a year from 2028. The NDP government has ruled out a yearly fee on vehicles, and the Conservatives oppose one. Parties disagree on who should pay, and on free fares.
questions/q_local_skytrain/context/3: The NDP government is building the line, rules out a yearly vehicle fee and promises a 2027 law to find new money for TransLink, without saying what it would be. The Conservatives criticized the cost in 2024 but made no 2026 pledge. The Greens want free transit for people under 25 and over 65. CentreBC calls the line a priority and adds rapid buses and a transit pass credit, but says nothing on the funding gap. OneBC has no position.
questions/q_local_skytrain/context/4: The line now costs $5.996 billion, up from $4 billion in the 2022 business case. TransLink needs at least $112 million a year more from 2028. The NDP has ruled out a vehicle levy and the Conservatives oppose one. The other ways to close the gap are fuel or sales taxes, tolls, a provincial subsidy or service cuts, and no party has said which it would choose.
questions/q_local_skytrain/context/5: The Surrey-Langley SkyTrain will run 16 km with eight stations, three of them in or near the riding. It is budgeted at $5.996 billion, against $4.01 billion in the 2022 business case, and $2.508 billion had been spent by April 2026. The province gave TransLink $479 million in March 2023 and $312 million for 2025 to 2027, but a gap of at least $112 million a year remains from 2028. On October 2 the NDP ruled out a vehicle levy of about $150 per vehicle and promised a revenue law in 2027.
questions/q_local_skytrain/options/a/tex: Finish the SkyTrain line, and find new transit money without a yearly car fee.
Finish SkyTrain as planned, and pass a law in 2027 to find transit money, without a yearly car fee.
Finish SkyTrain and pass a new law to fund TransLink from 2028, with no vehicle levy.
Finish SkyTrain on schedule, keep temporary TransLink funding, rule out a vehicle levy, and pass a law in 2027 creating a new revenue source.
Deliver the line at $5.996 billion for late 2029, support TransLink to 2027, rule out a vehicle levy, and pass a 2027 law for new revenue from 2028.
questions/q_local_skytrain/options/b/tex: Finish the SkyTrain line, keep costs down, and add no new taxes.
Finish SkyTrain, control costs, add no new taxes or fees, and shrink the regional government.
Finish SkyTrain with tight cost control, add no new taxes, and shrink Metro Vancouver's regional government.
Finish the line affordably, add no new taxes or levy, cut Metro Vancouver back to utilities, and cover TransLink's gap within existing budgets.
Add no new taxes or levies this term, finish the line with close cost scrutiny, cut Metro Vancouver to utilities only, and cover the 2028 gap within existing budgets.
questions/q_local_skytrain/options/c/tex: Make transit free for young people and seniors, paid for by taxing the richest.
Make transit free for people under 25 and over 65, add more rail, and tax the richest to pay.
Start with free transit for people under 25 and over 65, add more rail, and fund it with a wealth tax.
Use a wealth tax to fund free passes for people under 25 and over 65, then wider free transit, regional rail and more rapid transit.

Phase in fare-free transit starting with people under 25 and over 65, add regional passenger rail, starting with support for restoring the Squamish to 100 Mile House rail corridor, expand rapid transit, and fund it with a wealth tax.
questions/q_local_skytrain/options/d/tex: Finish the SkyTrain line, add fast buses, and give riders money back on passes.

Make SkyTrain a priority, add six rapid bus lines and 15% more service, offer a 15% transit pass credit, and study more rapid transit.

Make the line a priority in a $15 billion three-year plan, borrow $3.5 billion more for transportation and port links, add six rapid bus lines and 15% more service by 2030, and offer a refundable 15% credit on passes.
questions/q_local_skytrain/party_positio: This party is building the SkyTrain line and has ruled out a yearly car fee.

The NDP is building the SkyTrain for late 2029. The cost rose from $4 billion to $6 billion and the opening slipped a year. It has ruled out a vehicle levy and promises a 2027 law for new revenue, without saying where the money would come from.

The line costs $5.996 billion, opens in late 2029 and has three stations in the Fleetwood area; $2.508 billion had been spent by April 2026. The NDP gave TransLink $479 million in March 2023 and $312 million to the end of 2027, ruled out a vehicle levy on October 2, 2026, and promises a 2027 law for a 2028 revenue source. The cost rose in August 2024. Candidate Jagrup Brar lists 'a SkyTrain extension' with no timeline.
This party made no SkyTrain promise this time. In 2024 it said it would finish the line for less.

The Conservatives have no 2026 transit commitment. In 2024 they called the $6 billion cost a 'debacle' and said they would 'get it done in an affordable way', but never pledged to cancel it. Their pledge of no new taxes affects how TransLink's gap could be closed.

No 2026 Conservative SkyTrain or TransLink commitment was found on the party's site as of October 12. In August 2024 Rustad called it 'the $6 billion Surrey Skytrain debacle' and said a Conservative government would 'get it done in an affordable way'. The NDP claim that Rustad would cancel it is unconfirmed. For 2026 the party pledges no new taxes and would cut Metro Vancouver back to water and sewage. Its October 2 release attacked the reported vehicle levy and offered no alternative. Candidate Purewal has published only party themes.

The Greens promise 'fast, frequent and free' transit, starting with free passes for people under 25 and over 65, plus regional passenger rail, paid for by their wealth tax. They have no position on the SkyTrain line itself but support expanding transit.

They have no position on the SkyTrain line itself. The Greens say their proposed Fair Share Act would help pay for free transit. Candidate Binnema has no published transit position.
This party treats the SkyTrain line as a priority, and would add fast buses and give riders money back on passes.

CentreBC's October 10 platform makes the Surrey-Langley SkyTrain a priority in a $15 billion transportation plan, with about six rapid bus lines, 15% more transit service by 2030, a 15% tax credit on transit passes and a study of more rapid transit south of the Fraser. The platform names the line alongside the Fraser River Tunnel and Highway 1 widening in a $15 billion three-year plan, plus $3.5 billion more borrowed for transportation, rapid bus and port connections. It adds about six rapid bus lines, 15% more service by 2030, a refundable 15% BC Commuter Credit on transit passes and ferry fares, and a study of rapid transit south of the Fraser. It gives no dollar figure for the line and no position on the 2028 TransLink gap or a vehicle levy. Candidate Paul Brar has published no positions.
This party has said nothing about trains or buses, so it is not scored here.
OneBC has no transit position, so it is not scored on this question.
OneBC has no transportation commitment on its priorities page, so this question is left out of its score. Candidate Hofbauer has published no positions.
questions/q_local_extortion/prompt/1: Some Surrey business owners get threats demanding money. How can the province protect them?
questions/q_local_extortion/prompt/2: Criminals are threatening Surrey businesses for money while Surrey switches to its own police. What should the province do?
questions/q_local_extortion/prompt/3: How should the province respond to extortion, threats demanding money, in Surrey while the city changes police forces?
questions/q_local_extortion/prompt/4: Extortion mainly targets South Asian business owners in Surrey, while the city's switch to its own police force continues. Which provincial approach do you prefer?
questions/q_local_extortion/prompt/5: Surrey had 133 extortion cases and 49 shots-fired incidents in 2025, and 142 cases and 21 shots-fired incidents in 2026 to September 28. Which provincial approach?
questions/q_local_extortion/context/1: Criminals in Surrey have been threatening business owners to get money, sometimes with shootings. The province pays for police and courts. Some parties want a permanent special police unit. Some want many more police across BC. Others want tougher action on repeat offenders.
questions/q_local_extortion/context/2: Since 2025, criminals have threatened many Surrey business owners for money, sometimes with shootings. The province pays for police and courts, while the federal government sets bail rules. A 2023 provincial law made Surrey replace the Mounties with its own city police force, and that switch is still under way.
questions/q_local_extortion/context/3: Extortion means threatening someone to get money. CentreBC would make the police task force on extortion permanent and add 60 prosecutors and 500 Mounties. The Conservatives would add nearly 1,000 police and justice staff across BC, but their plan does not mention extortion. The NDP government set up the task force but has made no 2026 pledge. OneBC targets repeat offenders. The Greens have no plan.
questions/q_local_extortion/context/4: Surrey had 133 extortion cases and 49 shots-fired incidents in 2025, and 142 cases and 21 shots-fired incidents in 2026 up to September 28. Police credit steady enforcement for the drop in shootings, but no independent analysis exists. Bill 36, the 2023 law that made Surrey replace the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) with its own police service, passed over the city's objection. BC Liberal members, including Doerkson and Sturko, voted against it.
questions/q_local_extortion/context/5: Surrey Police Service (SPS) figures show 9 extortion cases and 2 shots-fired incidents in 2024; 133 cases, 49 shootings and 88 victims in 2025; and 142 cases, 21 shootings, 3 arsons and 76 victims in 2026 up to September 28. An RCMP-led task force of about 40 members has worked since September 2025, and Project E_Pursuance made arrests on October 2. Under Bill 36, the SPS became the police of jurisdiction on November 29, 2024. No completion date is published: the RCMP says November 2026 and the SPS says late 2027.
questions/q_local_extortion/options/a/te: Make the special police unit permanent, and add a port crime unit and prosecutors.
Make the extortion task force permanent, add a port crime unit and prosecutors, and double repeat-offender enforcement.
Make the extortion task force permanent, add a joint port unit and 60 prosecutors, double repeat-offender enforcement, and leave the police switch alone.

Make the extortion task force permanent, create a 40-officer port team with border services and the RCMP, add 60 Crown prosecutors, double repeat-offender enforcement, and leave the city police switch as is.

Make the extortion task force permanent with its own budget, create a 40-officer port team by 2028, hire 60 Crown prosecutors by 2030/31, double repeat-offender enforcement to $26 million, and leave the city police unchanged.
questions/q_local_extortion/options/b/te: Hire more police across BC, and send them where crime is worst.
Hire hundreds more police, prosecutors and judges across BC, send them to high-crime areas, and require addiction treatment.
Hire hundreds more police and prosecutors across BC, send them to the hardest-hit neighbourhoods first, and require addiction treatment.
Across BC, add 250 police, 500 rural RCMP, 50 prosecutors and 20 judges, send officers to hot spots, use Mental Health Act powers, and report on bail.

A province-wide plan: more police trained at the Justice Institute, rural RCMP, more Crown prosecutors and judges, neighbourhood deployment, Mental Health Act enforcement, and public data on repeat offending and bail.
questions/q_local_extortion/options/c/te: Keep today's approach, finish Surrey's switch to its own police, and seek stricter bail.
Keep the task force and community advisory group, finish the switch to Surrey's own police, and seek stricter bail.
Stay the course: keep the task force and advisory group, finish the police switch, and lobby for stricter bail.
Keep the task force, victim fund, advisory group and joint police board, fund the Surrey Police Service to 2029, expand repeat-offender programs, and seek bail reform.

Keep the task force, victim support and advisory group, fill police board vacancies by agreement of the mayor and minister, fund the Surrey Police Service at $30 million a year to 2029, and back Bill C-14.
questions/q_local_extortion/options/d/te: Get tough on people who keep committing violent crimes, and protect legal gun owners.
Target repeat violent offenders, ban masks at protests, and keep BC out of the federal gun buyback.
Target repeat violent offenders, ban masks at protests, and stay out of the federal gun buyback.
Focus on repeat violent offenders, ban masks at protests, and refuse to run the federal gun buyback, saying legal owners are not the problem.
Crack down on repeat and violent offenders, ban protest masks, refuse the federal buyback and offer provincial gun storage, with no measures specific to extortion or the city police.
questions/q_local_extortion/party_positi: This party set up the special police unit and passed a law making Surrey switch to its own police force.

The NDP passed a law ordering Surrey's police switch, created the task force and an advisory group, replaced its own police board appointees after criticism, and pressed Ottawa on bail. Eby said 'we need better results'. It has no 2026 extortion pledge.

Bill 36 passed 56-27 in 2023, with Brar voting yes. The government funds the Surrey Police Service at $30 million a year to 2029. It created the Extortion Task Force in September 2025 and put $500,000 toward victim support, matched by Ottawa, in November 2025. It did not renew four provincial police board members, appointed five new ones in March 2026, agreed that future vacancies be filled by agreement of the mayor's office and the public safety minister, and pressed Ottawa for Bill C-14. Eby said 'we need to see more arrests'. It has no 2026 extortion or police commitment. Brar has never broken ranks and has made no extortion statement.
This party wants many more police officers across BC.

The Conservatives' province-wide plan adds nearly 1,000 police, prosecutors and court staff and targets the hardest-hit neighbourhoods, but does not mention extortion or the Surrey Police Service. At its Surrey candidate launch the party criticized the NDP on extortion.

The Safe Streets for BC plan (October 6, 2026) has no extortion item. The party's September 29 Surrey candidate release said small business owners face 'a wave of extortion and violence that has left many afraid to open their doors'. It has no position on the Surrey Police Service. BC Liberal members, including Doerkson, voted against Bill 36. Candidate Purewal has published only party themes.
This party has no plan on this issue, so it is not scored here.
The Greens have no public safety or extortion position, so they are not scored on this question.

The Greens' platform page lists no commitment on policing, extortion or the Surrey Police Service, so this question is left out of the Green score. Candidate Binnema has made no local safety statement.
This party would make the special police unit permanent, and add a port crime unit and more prosecutors.

CentreBC's October 10 platform makes the extortion task force permanent with its own budget and adds a 40-officer port team, 60 more Crown prosecutors, doubled repeat-offender enforcement, 500 more provincial Mounties and a bail review with public data. Its 2025 Surrey-only ideas are not in the platform. It says nothing about the Surrey Police Service.

The platform makes the extortion task force permanent 'so the capacity built in 2025-26 isn't lost'. It adds a 40-officer port team with border services and the RCMP by 2028, 60 Crown prosecutors by 2030/31, doubled repeat-offender enforcement and 100 provincial RCMP officers a year for five years, plus a bail review before 2028. Its November 2025 Surrey plan, with a federal financial crimes cell, small security grants and a 48-hour protection standard, is not repeated. It has no Surrey Police Service position. Sturko, running in Surrey South, voted against Bill 36 in 2023.
This party would get tough on people who keep committing violent crimes and protect legal gun owners.
OneBC would target repeat violent offenders, ban masks at protests and keep BC out of the federal firearms buyback. It has no position on extortion or Surrey policing.

OneBC's priorities are repeat and violent offenders, a ban on masks at protests, no part in the federal buyback and a provincial gun storage program. It has no position on extortion or the Surrey Police Service. Candidate Hofbauer has published no positions.
questions/q_local_hospital_schools/promp: Surrey has a half-built hospital and crowded schools. What should the province do first?
Surrey's new hospital opens in 2030, its emergency room is busy and schools keep growing. What should the province focus on?
How should the province handle Surrey's half-built hospital, overloaded emergency room and crowded schools?
How should the province handle Surrey's hospital, emergency room and school space as the city grows?

The Cloverdale hospital (about $2.88 billion) opens in 2030, 8.4% of Surrey Memorial emergency patients left without being seen in 2024, and the school district expects 700 to 800 more students a year. Choose the approach.
questions/q_local_hospital_schools/conte: A new hospital is being built in Cloverdale, but it will not open until 2030. More patients now leave the busy Surrey Memorial emergency room before a doctor sees them. Many students learn in portable classrooms. Parties disagree on how to pay for more.

The province pays to build hospitals and schools. The new Cloverdale hospital will open in 2030, three years later than first planned. At Surrey Memorial, more emergency patients now leave before being seen. Surrey schools had 361 portables in 2023. The province is borrowing heavily, and parties disagree on how fast to build and how to pay.

The NDP government is building the Cloverdale hospital and new school seats, and promises 20 clinics and faster licensing for doctors trained abroad. The Conservatives say they are 'contemplating' the hospital and offer emergency room funding and a wait-time commission. The Greens want a health centre in every riding. CentreBC would build a new tower at Surrey Memorial, plan a children's hospital and add 25,000 school seats across BC. OneBC would allow private clinics.

The Cloverdale hospital's cost rose from $1.72 billion to about $2.88 billion, and its opening slipped from 2027 to 2030. In 2024, Surrey Memorial's emergency doctors said 8.4% of patients leave without being seen. The Surrey school district has asked for $5.49 billion and had 361 portables in 2023. In 2016 the NDP promised to remove all of Surrey's portables within four years of taking office, and that pledge was not met.

The Cloverdale hospital was half built in March 2026, with completion in August 2029, patients in 2030 and a cost of about $2.88 billion, up from $1.72 billion. In a September 2024 letter, Surrey Memorial emergency doctors said 8.4% of patients leave without being seen, up from 2.9% in 2020-21. Surrey enrolment passed 83,000 in 2024-25; the district expects 700 to 800 more students a year and about 87,000 by 2035, has asked for $5.49 billion for 76 projects, and had 361 portables in 2023. About 2,300 seats were under construction in August 2025; an 800-seat addition at Fleetwood Park Secondary is in design, with building due to start in winter 2027. Budget 2026 set provincial capital spending at $18.7 billion, below the $20.4 billion forecast.
questions/q_local_hospital_schools/optio: Keep building the hospital and schools, add clinics, and borrow and tax top earners.
Finish the hospital and classrooms, add clinics, fast-track doctors trained abroad, and borrow and tax top earners.
Build the hospital, school seats and clinics, fast-track doctors trained abroad, and pay through borrowing plus a tax on top earners.
Keep building the hospital for 2030 and new school seats, add 20 clinics, help foreign-trained doctors qualify, and expand diagnostics, funded by deficits and a new top tax bracket.

Build the Cloverdale hospital and schools within the $18.7 billion capital plan, add 20 clinics, 1,000 training seats and diagnostics, and fund it with deficits and top tax rates of 18.8%, 22.5% and 24.5%.
Keep emergency rooms open, let families choose care homes, and raise no taxes.
Fund emergency rooms, let seniors choose their care home, focus schools on basics, and raise no taxes.
Fund emergency rooms, set up a wait-time commission, let care funding follow the senior, and focus schools on basics.
Add no new taxes, fund emergency rooms, run a 100-day wait-time commission, review care-home design rules, let funding follow seniors to non-government providers, and focus schools on basics.
Create a $50 million emergency fund and a 100-day commission, review long-term care design rules, let care funding follow the senior, make no health cuts, and raise no new taxes.
Open a local health centre, feed every student, and tax the richest to pay.
Open a Fleetwood health centre, fully fund help for students with extra needs, feed every student, and tax the richest.
Open a Fleetwood health centre, fully fund inclusive education for students with extra needs, provide school food and counsellors, and add a wealth tax.
Put a community health centre in every riding, close the inclusive education funding gap, fund a counsellor per 250 students and food for every student, and add a wealth tax.

Open an integrated health centre in every riding, fully fund inclusive education, fund a counsellor per 250 students, school food and supplies, and a wage grid for early childhood educators, with a wealth tax.
Build a new Surrey Memorial tower and a children's hospital, and add classrooms.
Build a Surrey Memorial tower, plan a children's hospital, add school seats, and give everyone a regular doctor or nurse.
Build a Surrey Memorial tower, plan a children's hospital, add 25,000 school seats, and give everyone a regular doctor or nurse.

Start building a Surrey Memorial acute-care tower by 2030, plan a Surrey-Langley children's hospital, add 25,000 school seats by 2031, give everyone primary care by 2031, and pay with administrative savings.

Publish a budget for the Surrey Memorial tower and open it about 2035, start a children's hospital in 2031, add 25,000 seats and have 2,500 long-term care beds under construction by 2031, and pay with administrative savings.
Let private clinics open beside public hospitals, and test students more at school.
Let private clinics open alongside public hospitals to shorten waits, and add province-wide school tests.
Allow private clinics beside public hospitals to cut waits, and bring in standardized school testing.
Allow private clinics alongside public care to relieve Surrey hospitals, repeal the Health Professions and Occupations Act, and bring in standardized testing.
Allow private clinics alongside public care to relieve Surrey hospitals, repeal the Health Professions and Occupations Act, and bring in standardized testing in schools.
questions/q_local_hospital_schools/party: This party is building the new hospital and new classrooms, and wants more clinics.

The NDP is building the Cloverdale hospital and new Surrey school seats, and promises 20 clinics and faster licensing for doctors trained abroad. The hospital's cost rose about $1 billion and its opening slipped three years. It did not meet its 2016 promise to end Surrey's portables within four years.

The Cloverdale hospital now costs about $2.88 billion, up from $1.72 billion, with completion in August 2029 instead of 2027. The NDP is building a medical school at Simon Fraser University in Surrey and 60 mental health beds in Surrey, including involuntary care, due in spring 2028. About 2,300 school seats are under construction and 19 of 40 modular buildings replaced portables, but the district had a $16 million budget shortfall in 2025-26. For 2026 it promises 20 clinics, help for foreign-trained doctors, 1,000 training seats, and eight MRI machines and 10 CT scanners across BC. Candidate Brar promises 'a new hospital' with no timeline.
This party wants to keep emergency rooms open and is still deciding about the new hospital.

Asked about the hospital on October 7, Doerkson said 'we're contemplating all of that for our platform rollout'. Its health plan offers emergency room funding, a 100-day wait-time commission, no cuts, and long-term care funding that follows the senior. It has no Surrey school pledge.

Asked about the hospital on October 7, Doerkson said 'we're contemplating all of that for our platform rollout'. Its Keep Emergency Rooms Open plan (October 5) offers a $50 million emergency fund, a 100-day expert commission and a promise to keep current health care spending in place; on October 12 the party restated that care would stay universal and publicly funded. Its seniors plan (October 9) reviews long-term care design rules, lets care funding follow the senior and offers a choice of home care provider. It has no position on school capital or Surrey Memorial. Candidate Purewal has published only party themes.
This party wants a local health centre, food for every student, and full support for students with extra needs.

The Greens would put a community health centre in every riding, including Fleetwood, close the funding gap for inclusive education, add counsellors and feed every student. They say their wealth tax would help fund schools. They have no position on the hospital itself.

The Greens would open an integrated community health centre in every riding, close the inclusive education funding gap, fund a counsellor per 250 students and provide school food and supplies for all. They have no position on the hospital or on the pace of building. Candidate Binnema has published no local position.
This party would build a hospital tower and a children's hospital, add classrooms, and give everyone a regular doctor or nurse.

CentreBC's October 10 platform builds the Surrey Memorial acute-care tower with a published budget, starting by 2030 and opening about 2035. It plans a Surrey-Langley children's hospital, adds 25,000 school seats by 2031 and promises everyone a regular doctor or nurse. It pays through attrition and administrative cuts, not new taxes, and does not mention the Cloverdale hospital.

The platform builds the Surrey Memorial tower announced in 2024, with new operating rooms and cardiac intensive care. It completes the business case, site and design for a children's hospital south of the Fraser in its first term, with construction in 2031. It adds 25,000 school seats by 2031 with $750 million and promises primary care for all by 2031 with 600 nurse practitioners. It would have 2,500 long-term care beds under construction and 1,000 open by March 2031, and plans $3.2 billion in health capital over four years. It does not name the Cloverdale hospital or Surrey's school district.
This party would allow private clinics next to public hospitals, and more testing in schools.

OneBC would allow private health care alongside the public system, repeal the Health Professions and Occupations Act and bring in standardized testing. It has no position on building hospitals or schools.

OneBC would allow private care alongside the public system, repeal the Health Professions and Occupations Act and bring in standardized testing. It has made no commitments on building hospitals or schools. Candidate Hofbauer has published no positions.
questions/q_local_metro_translink/prompt: Metro Vancouver's buses and trains will run short of money soon. What should the province do?
TransLink, which runs Metro Vancouver's buses and trains, needs new money from 2028. What should the province do?
TransLink needs at least $112 million a year in new money from 2028. How should the province fund transit in Metro Vancouver?
TransLink's provincial top-up ends in 2027, and it needs at least $112 million a year more from 2028. How should the gap close?
The province's $312 million subsidy carries TransLink to the end of 2027; the agency needs at least $112 million a year from 2028 and the government has ruled out a vehicle levy. Which approach?
questions/q_local_metro_translink/contex: TransLink runs the buses and trains in Metro Vancouver. The province gives it extra money now, but that runs out after next year. Parties disagree on who should pay after that, and on whether some riders should travel free.

TransLink, the regional transit agency, gets a provincial top-up that ends in 2027. From 2028 it needs at least $112 million a year more. In October the government ruled out a yearly fee on vehicles and a charge for using roads. Parties disagree on where the money should come from, and on free fares for young people and seniors.

The province's $312 million subsidy carries TransLink to the end of 2027. From 2028 the agency needs at least $112 million a year more. In October the NDP government ruled out a vehicle levy and road pricing and promised a law in 2027 to find another source, without naming one. The Conservatives oppose any new tax or levy. The Greens want free fares for riders under 25 and over 65. CentreBC promises more service and a pass credit.

The province gave TransLink $312 million in 2025, about half of its shortfall to the end of 2027. TransLink needs at least $112 million a year in new revenue from 2028 and says the province chooses the tool. Fuel use per vehicle has fallen about 45% since 2002, which erodes the fuel tax that funds transit. On October 2 the NDP ruled out a vehicle levy and road pricing and promised a 2027 revenue law. The Conservatives oppose any new tax. The Greens and CentreBC would spend more on service but name no new regional revenue source.

TransLink received $479 million from the province in March 2023 and $312 million for 2025 to 2027, and needs at least $112 million a year from 2028. A reported $100 to $150 yearly vehicle levy, collected at ICBC renewal, was never confirmed. On October 2, 2026 Eby said a vehicle levy or road pricing 'are not options we would proceed with' and promised legislation in 2027 for a 2028 revenue source, unnamed. The same week the NDP pledged a 10 cent a litre fuel tax cut, which the Greens say undercuts transit funding. The Conservatives' October 2 release opposed the levy and proposed no alternative. CentreBC's October 10 platform funds 15% more service inside a $15 billion three-year plan. OneBC has no transit position.
questions/q_local_metro_translink/option: Keep funding transit, with no yearly car fee, and cut the gas tax.
Keep the top-up, pass a law in 2027 to find transit money with no car fee, and cut fuel tax.
Pass a 2027 law for new transit revenue, rule out a vehicle levy and road pricing, and cut fuel tax 10 cents a litre.
Keep provincial support to 2027, legislate a new TransLink revenue source in 2027 with no vehicle levy or road pricing, and cut the provincial fuel tax 10 cents a litre.

Keep the $312 million subsidy to 2027, legislate an as yet unnamed TransLink revenue source in 2027 for 2028, rule out a vehicle levy and road pricing, and cut the provincial motor fuel tax by 10 cents a litre.
Add no new taxes or fees for transit, and cut regional government waste.
Add no new taxes, fees or road charges, cut waste at the regional government, and grow door-to-door service for seniors.
Rule out any new tax, levy or road charge, shrink Metro Vancouver's regional government to core services, and expand HandyDART where demand is highest.
Add no new taxes or levies, cover TransLink's gap within existing budgets, cut the Metro Vancouver regional district back to core services, and expand HandyDART.

No new taxes, levies or road pricing this term; fund TransLink within existing budgets; audit and cut the Metro Vancouver regional district to utilities and core services; expand HandyDART where demand is highest.
Double the buses, free rides for youth and seniors, and tax oil companies.
Double the bus fleet, make transit free under 25 and over 65, extend SkyTrain to UBC, and tax oil profits.
Double the bus fleet, phase in free fares starting under 25 and over 65, build SkyTrain to UBC, and tax fossil fuel windfalls.
Fund TransLink with provincial money and a fossil fuel windfall tax, double buses in a term, phase in free transit starting with under 25s and over 65s, build SkyTrain to UBC.

Fund TransLink from provincial revenue and a fossil fuel windfall tax, double the bus fleet in one term, phase in fare-free transit starting under 25 and over 65, build SkyTrain to UBC, and have an all-party committee set funding.
Add fast bus lines and more service, and give riders money back on passes.
Add about six rapid bus lines and more service by 2030, and give riders part of their pass cost back.
Fund 15% more transit service by 2030 and about six rapid bus lines, and give riders a refundable 15% credit on passes.
Fund 15% more service by 2030 and about six rapid bus lines in a $15 billion three-year transportation plan, plus a refundable 15% tax credit on transit passes.

Fund 15% more TransLink and BC Transit service by 2030, about six rapid bus lines and a refundable 15% credit on passes, within a $15 billion three-year plan that borrows $3.5 billion more, with no new regional revenue tool.
Charge drivers a yearly fee or tolls so transit has its own steady money.
Give the region its own steady transit money, such as a yearly vehicle fee or road pricing, not yearly top-ups.
Create a stable regional revenue source, such as a vehicle levy or road pricing, so TransLink stops depending on yearly provincial top-ups.
Legislate a permanent regional revenue tool, such as a vehicle levy or road pricing, so TransLink stops relying on year-to-year provincial subsidies.
Legislate a permanent regional revenue tool, such as a vehicle levy collected at insurance renewal or road pricing, so TransLink stops depending on year-to-year provincial subsidies and fuel tax.
questions/q_local_metro_translink/party_: This party gives transit extra money now, rules out a yearly car fee, and promises a new money plan in two years.

The NDP government gave TransLink $312 million in 2025, enough to the end of 2027. On October 2 it ruled out a vehicle levy and road pricing and promised a 2027 law to create a new revenue source, without saying what. It also promises a 10 cent a litre fuel tax cut.

Record: $479 million to TransLink in March 2023 and $312 million for 2025 to 2027, about half the shortfall. On October 2, 2026 Eby said 'a vehicle levy or road pricing are not options we would proceed with' and promised 2027 legislation for a 2028 revenue source, unnamed. The NDP also pledges a 10 cent a litre fuel tax cut and a price cap through the Utilities Commission; the Greens say that erodes the fuel tax that funds TransLink.
This party says no new taxes or fees, and wants to cut waste in the regional government.

The Conservatives attacked the reported vehicle levy as a 'secret vehicle tax plan' and promise no new or higher taxes. They have published no TransLink funding plan. Their October 5 plan would audit and shrink the Metro Vancouver regional district. They would grow HandyDART where demand is highest.

The October 2 release 'Eby Must Answer on Secret Vehicle Tax Plan' opposes a levy and proposes no alternative revenue. On September 27 Doerkson promised not to raise existing taxes or introduce new ones. Its October 5 Metro Vancouver plan would audit the North Shore wastewater plant, create 'a smaller, professional board' and return housing, economic development and climate functions to cities and the province. Its October 9 seniors plan expands HandyDART. No 2026 commitment on TransLink's 2028 gap or on SkyTrain to UBC.
This party wants free rides for young people and seniors, many more buses, and oil companies to pay for it.

The Greens' October 9 transit brief promises to fully fund transit, double the bus fleet in a first term, phase in free fares starting under 25 and over 65, extend SkyTrain to UBC and have an all-party committee set long-term funding. They oppose the fuel tax cut and want a windfall tax on fossil fuel companies.

Transit and Transportation Policy Brief (October 9, 2026): fully fund TransLink and BC Transit, double the bus fleet within the first term, phase in fare-free transit starting with riders under 25 and over 65, SkyTrain to UBC, end outsourcing, and an all-party legislature committee on a long-term funding model. No dollar costing. In a statement on the NDP fuel tax cut, the party said relief should come 'without decreasing our revenue and undercutting the services those people depend on', and called for 'taxing the enormous windfalls fossil fuel companies are making right now'.
This party would add fast bus lines and more service, and give riders some money back on passes.

CentreBC's platform funds 15% more transit service by 2030 and about six rapid bus lines inside a $15 billion three-year transportation plan, and gives a refundable 15% credit on monthly and annual passes. It says nothing about a vehicle levy or how to close TransLink's 2028 gap.

Platform (October 10, pages 11 and 13): with TransLink and BC Transit, fund a 15% service increase by 2030; about six new rapid bus lines; a refundable BC Commuter Credit returning 15% on passes and ferry multi-trip fares; $15 billion over three years with $3.5 billion more borrowed; the Surrey-Langley SkyTrain and the Fraser River Tunnel as priorities. No position on a vehicle levy, road pricing or a new TransLink revenue source.
This party has said nothing about buses or trains, so it is not scored here.
OneBC has no transit or transportation position, so it is not scored on this question.
OneBC's priorities page lists no transportation commitment, so this question is left out of its score.
questions/q_local_metro_title_homes/prom: A court says a First Nation owns Richmond land with homes on it. What should happen?
A court recognized a First Nation's title to Richmond land with private homes. How should owners be protected and claims settled?
A 2025 ruling recognized Cowichan title over Richmond land with private homes. How should owners be protected and claims settled?
The Cowichan title ruling over Richmond land with homes is under appeal. How should owners be protected and title settled?

In August 2025 the BC Supreme Court recognized Cowichan Tribes' Aboriginal title over Richmond land including privately held parcels; the province, Ottawa and Richmond have appealed. Which approach to homeowners and title?
questions/q_local_metro_title_homes/cont: A judge decided that a First Nation owns some land in Richmond, including land under people's homes. The province is fighting that decision in a higher court. Parties disagree on how to protect the people who live there, and on how to settle these claims.

In 2025 the BC Supreme Court recognized Cowichan Tribes' title over land in Richmond, including private homes. The province, the federal government and the City of Richmond have appealed. Parties disagree on whether to promise homeowners money if their home loses value, whether to change the Indigenous rights law, and whether claims should be settled by treaty or in court.

The August 2025 Cowichan ruling recognized Aboriginal title over Richmond land that includes private homes. The province is appealing and Eby says it will 'go to the wall' for owners. CentreBC would pass a law promising owners compensation for lost value. The Conservatives and OneBC would repeal the Indigenous rights law and put property rights first. The Greens would keep the law and settle claims by negotiation. A March poll found most people would put private property first.

The Cowichan decision (BC Supreme Court, August 2025) recognized Aboriginal title over part of Richmond including privately held parcels; the province, Canada, Richmond and others have appealed. A separate 2025 Court of Appeal ruling made DRIPA obligations enforceable, and the two cases are often confused. Eby calls the rulings 'overreaching' and promises to protect owners, without a compensation law. CentreBC's homeowner guarantee would compensate owners up to assessed value and keep homes mortgageable. The Conservatives and OneBC would repeal DRIPA. The Greens would legislate how DRIPA is carried out. Angus Reid (March 2026): 65% put private property first.

Cowichan Tribes v. Canada (BC Supreme Court, August 2025) recognized Aboriginal title over land in Richmond including privately owned parcels; CentreBC's platform says about 145 private properties are affected. Cowichan Tribes, the province, Canada and Richmond have all appealed. The Court of Appeal's December 2025 Gitxaala decision made Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act duties enforceable; on April 20, 2026 Eby dropped plans to amend or suspend the Act for the spring session. On September 25 he said responding to the court 'is not up for debate'. Angus Reid, March 11 to 17, 2026 (n=499): 53% say the Act goes too far, 65% put private property rights first. OneBC's Property Rights Protection Act was defeated 40 to 48 on October 29, 2025, with Conservatives voting in favour.
questions/q_local_metro_title_homes/opti: Pay homeowners for any lost value from a ruling, and settle claims by treaty.
Pass a law paying homeowners for lost value, make no land deals until appeals end, and settle claims through treaties.
Legislate a homeowner guarantee for lost value and the right to sell, no private-land deals until appeals end, and settle title by treaty.
Legislate a guarantee for owners' title-related losses and right to sell or mortgage, sign no private-land deals until appeals end, and move to a treaty-based law.

Legislate compensation up to assessed value for title-related losses and preserve owners' ability to sell or mortgage, keep private land out of title deals unless the owner sells, finalize nothing until Cowichan appeals end, and move to a treaty-based law.
Keep fighting the ruling in court, protect homeowners in talks, and fix the law.
Keep appealing, promise private property is protected in any talks, and change the Indigenous rights law rather than scrap it.
Keep appealing the Cowichan ruling, protect private property in any negotiation, and amend rather than repeal the Indigenous rights law, with no compensation law.
Pursue the appeal, protect private owners in any talks, and amend rather than repeal the Indigenous rights law so it cannot override other laws, with no compensation law.

Pursue the Cowichan appeal, pledge to protect private property owners in any negotiation, and amend the Declaration Act in consultation with First Nations so it cannot be used to strike down other legislation, with no statutory compensation guarantee for homeowners.
Scrap the Indigenous rights law, put property rights first, and let elected people decide.
Repeal the Indigenous rights law, put property rights first in provincial law, and let the elected legislature decide, not courts.
Repeal the Indigenous rights law, put property rights first in statute, let the legislature, not courts, decide how title applies, and keep resource partnerships.
Repeal the Indigenous rights law, put property rights in statute, let legislators, not courts, decide how title applies, and build resource projects in partnership with First Nations.

Repeal the Declaration Act, enact statutory protection for private property rights, return decisions on how title applies to the elected legislature rather than the courts, and build resource projects in partnership with First Nations.
Scrap the Indigenous rights law, stop giving land and money to First Nations governments.
Repeal the Indigenous rights law, void the UN declaration in BC, and stop land and money transfers to band governments.
Repeal the Indigenous rights law, void the UN declaration, halt land and money transfers to band governments, and seek repeal of the Indian Act.
Repeal the Indigenous rights law, void the UN declaration in BC, halt transfers of cash, land and resource control to band governments, and seek repeal of the Indian Act.

Repeal the Declaration Act, declare UNDRIP of no force and effect in BC, halt voluntary transfers of cash, land and control over public resources to band governments, and seek repeal of the Indian Act through constitutional reform.
Keep the Indigenous rights law, settle claims by negotiation, and explain the law publicly.
Keep the Indigenous rights law and spell out how it works, settle title by negotiation, and fund public education.
Keep the Indigenous rights law and legislate how it is carried out, co-develop a way to settle disputes without litigation, and fund public education.
Keep and implement the Indigenous rights law, co-develop a way to settle title by negotiation rather than in court, improve modern treaties, and fund public education.

Implement the Declaration Act through implementing legislation, create an expert advisory committee, co-develop an Indigenous-Crown dispute resolution process to avoid litigation, support and improve modern treaties, and fund public education on the Act to counter misinformation.
questions/q_local_metro_title_homes/part: This party is fighting the ruling in a higher court and promises to protect homeowners, but offers no payment law.

The NDP government appealed the Cowichan ruling. Eby calls the Cowichan and Gitxaala decisions 'dramatic, overreaching and unhelpful', says the government will 'go to the wall' for private property owners, and says it must respond by amending the law. It proposes no compensation law and no repeal.

Record: the province appealed Cowichan; in April 2026 Eby and the First Nations Leadership Council agreed to no Declaration Act amendments in the spring session, after a withdrawn suspension bill. On September 25, 2026 Eby said responding to the court decision 'is not up for debate'; he has also promised to 'go to the wall' for private owners. No 2026 platform commitment, no compensation guarantee, no repeal. The province-wide question scores the amendment pledge; this one scores the homeowner response.
This party would scrap the Indigenous rights law and put property rights first, with elected people deciding.

The Conservatives promise to repeal DRIPA, 'protect property rights, and put important decisions back in the hands of elected representatives', and say they want to build projects in partnership with First Nations. They voted for OneBC's property rights bill at first reading. They have no statement on the Cowichan ruling or on compensation.

Plan page 'Repeal DRIPA, Promote Economic Reconciliation' (October 7): Doerkson says DRIPA 'has to be repealed' and that he wants 'partnerships with First Nations' on projects. Doerkson on X, October 7: 'Repeal DRIPA, protect property rights, and put important decisions back in the hands of elected representatives.' On October 29, 2025 the caucus voted yea at first reading on the Property Rights Protection Act (lost 40 to 48). No published position on the Cowichan appeal, a compensation guarantee or a treaty replacement law.
This party would keep the Indigenous rights law, settle claims by talking, and explain the law to the public.

The Greens would implement DRIPA 'through legislation to remove uncertainty', fund public education 'to combat misinformation', set up an expert advisory committee, improve modern treaties and co-develop a way to settle Indigenous-Crown disputes 'to avoid litigation'. They have no published position on the Cowichan ruling or on homeowner compensation.

Indigenous Rights Policy Brief and statement (September 30, 2026): implementing legislation for the Declaration Act, an expert advisory committee, public education against misinformation, support for modern treaties and a co-developed Indigenous-Crown dispute resolution process to avoid litigation. The party welcomed the April 2026 pause on amendments. No Cowichan-specific position and no compensation proposal; option e is their general approach applied to a title dispute.
This party would pass a law paying homeowners for lost value and settle claims through treaties.

CentreBC's platform has a 'homeowner guarantee' law: the province compensates owners for any loss in value from a title ruling, up to assessed value, and keeps them able to get a mortgage or sell. No deals touching private land until the Cowichan appeals are settled. It would also replace DRIPA with a treaty-based law.

Platform (October 10, pages 35 to 36): homeowner guarantee legislation compensating owners up to assessed value for title-related losses and preserving the ability to mortgage or sell,; private land off the table in treaty and title deals unless the owner chooses to sell; nothing finalized until the Cowichan appeals end; title deals tabled in the legislature before signing; a first-session bill repealing DRIPA and section 8.1 of the Interpretation Act for a law 'built on negotiated treaties', with $30 million a year for faster treaty talks.
This party would scrap the Indigenous rights law and stop transfers of land and money to First Nations governments.

OneBC would repeal DRIPA and declare the UN declaration of 'no force and effect in BC', halt voluntary transfers of cash, land and resource control to band governments, and 'defund the Reconciliation Industry'. Its MLAs introduced a property rights protection bill in 2025, which was defeated.

Priorities page: repeal DRIPA and declare UNDRIP of no force and effect; halt voluntary transfers of cash, land and control over public resources to band governments; seek Indian Act repeal through constitutional reform; end mandatory land acknowledgements. X, September 26, 2026: repeal DRIPA and 'defund the Reconciliation Industry'. The Property Rights Protection Act (October 2025) lost 40 to 48. No Cowichan-specific statement and no compensation proposal.
questions/q_local_metro_density/prompt/1: Who should decide how many homes fit on a lot: the province or city councils?
questions/q_local_metro_density/prompt/2: The province makes cities allow several homes per lot and towers near transit. Keep that power, or give it back to councils?
questions/q_local_metro_density/prompt/3: Sixteen Metro Vancouver mayors want the 2023 density laws undone. Keep the rules, add to them, or give councils back the say?
questions/q_local_metro_density/prompt/4: Sixteen Metro Vancouver mayors asked in 2025 to repeal or revise the multi-unit, transit-area and housing-target laws. What now?
questions/q_local_metro_density/prompt/5: Bill 44 (small-scale multi-unit housing, passed 45 to 29) and Bill 47 (transit-oriented areas, 65 to 0) override municipal zoning; sixteen Metro mayors sought repeal or revision in November 2025. What now?
questions/q_local_metro_density/context/: The province recently made cities allow more homes on each lot and taller buildings near train stations. City councils used to decide this alone. Many mayors want that power back. Parties disagree on who should decide, and on what the province should do instead.

In 2023 the province passed laws making cities allow three or four homes on most lots and tall buildings near transit, and set housing targets for cities. Sixteen Metro Vancouver mayors have asked the province to repeal or change those laws. A recent poll found slightly more people back the province than councils. Parties disagree on who should decide.

The province's 2023 laws require three or four homes on most lots, higher density near transit and housing targets for named cities. Sixteen Metro Vancouver mayors asked in November 2025 to repeal or revise them. The NDP government has kept the laws. CentreBC would keep the transit rules and add provincial approval deadlines. The Conservatives promised in 2024 to scrap the lot rule and pay cities that allow more homes instead, and have no 2026 position. The Greens voted against the lot law.

Bill 44 (small-scale multi-unit housing) and Bill 47 (transit-oriented areas) passed in November 2023, with housing target orders for named cities. In late November 2025 sixteen Metro Vancouver mayors asked Premier Eby to repeal and revise all three. A Liaison Strategies poll (September 26 to 27, 2026, n=1,000) found 43% would give the province the final say over minimum housing allowances and 37% the council. The NDP has kept the laws. CentreBC keeps transit-area density and adds a provincial approval standard. The Conservatives' 2024 platform pledged to scrap Bill 44 and fund cities that allow multi-unit housing; nothing in 2026. The Greens voted against Bills 44 and 46.

Bill 44 passed third reading 45 to 29 on November 29, 2023, with Furstenau, Olsen, Rustad and Banman among the nays; Bill 47 passed 65 to 0 on November 30, 2023. Housing Supply Act target orders cover named Metro municipalities. In late November 2025, sixteen mayors (including Burnaby, Richmond, Coquitlam and Delta) wrote to Eby seeking repeal and revision of all three. Liaison Strategies, September 26 to 27, 2026 (n=1,000, plus or minus 3.1): province 43%, council 37% on final say; 56% support more homes nearby. The NDP has no 2026 change; its housing pledges are tax measures. CentreBC's platform sets six-month rezoning and eight-week permit standards with one rulebook by January 1, 2028, a $125 million a year performance fund and a $240 million growth fund. OneBC has no density position.
questions/q_local_metro_density/options/: Keep the provincial rules making cities allow more homes per lot and near transit.
Keep the provincial rules on more homes per lot, towers near transit and housing targets, and do not unwind them.
Keep the 2023 provincial rules on small-scale multi-unit housing, transit-area density and housing targets, and refuse the mayors' request to unwind them.
Keep Bill 44, Bill 47 and the housing target orders as they stand, refuse the mayors' request to repeal or revise them, and keep enforcing targets on named municipalities.

Keep Bill 44 (small-scale multi-unit housing), Bill 47 (transit-oriented areas) and Housing Supply Act target orders unchanged, refuse the sixteen mayors' request, and continue provincial enforcement against municipalities that miss targets.
Keep the rules near transit, and set deadlines for how fast cities approve homes.
Keep density rules near transit, set provincial deadlines for city approvals with one rulebook, and pay cities that meet targets.
Keep transit-area density rules, set provincial deadlines of six months for rezonings and eight weeks for permits, and fund cities meeting targets.
Keep transit-area rules, require rezonings in six months and permits in eight weeks under one rulebook by 2028, refund fees if missed, and fund cities that meet targets.

Keep transit-oriented area rules, legislate six-month rezoning and eight-week permit standards with one rulebook across municipalities by January 1, 2028 (fees refunded if missed), a $125 million a year performance fund for cities meeting targets, plus a growth fund.
Let councils decide homes per lot, and pay cities that choose to allow more.
Give councils back the say on homes per lot, pay cities that allow more, and keep transit rules with changes.
End the provincial homes-per-lot order, pay cities that allow small-scale multi-unit housing and pre-zone land, and amend transit-area rules to require shops nearby.
Swap the multi-unit mandate for a yearly fund for municipalities allowing such housing on most residential land and pre-zoning, and require shops near transit-area housing.

Repeal the Bill 44 mandate and replace it with a $1 billion a year fund for municipalities allowing small-scale multi-unit housing on at least two-thirds of residential land, pre-zone with cities, and amend Bill 47 to require nearby shops.
Stop ordering cities on zoning; have the province build non-profit homes and protect renters.
Put provincial effort into non-profit homes and renter protection instead of zoning orders, leaving most zoning to councils.
Shift provincial effort from zoning mandates to building 26,000 non-market homes a year and rent limits between tenants, leaving most zoning to councils.
Shift from zoning mandates to building or protecting 26,000 non-market homes a year, restart community housing funding, add vacancy control, and leave most zoning to councils.

Shift provincial effort from the Bill 44 mandate to building or protecting 26,000 non-market homes a year, restarting the Community Housing Fund, legislating vacancy control and faster approvals for all housing forms, while leaving most zoning decisions with councils.
questions/q_local_metro_density/party_po: This party made the rules and has kept them, even after many mayors asked for them to go.

The NDP passed the 2023 laws on homes per lot, transit-area density and housing targets, and has kept them despite the sixteen mayors' letter. Its 2026 housing pledges are tax measures: a higher speculation tax and an unsold condo tax. No 2026 commitment to change the density rules.

Record: Bill 44 (45 to 29), Bill 46 and Bill 47 (65 to 0) in November 2023, plus Housing Supply Act target orders; the government did not act on the November 2025 mayors' letter. 2026 pledges: speculation and vacancy tax from 1% to 2% (4% to 5% foreign) and an Unsold Condo Tax starting at 2% (September 25). No 2026 statement on small-scale multi-unit housing, transit-oriented areas or targets; option a is the standing record.
This party promised in 2024 to scrap the lot rule and pay cities that allow more homes. It has said nothing about it this time.

In 2024 the Conservatives pledged to scrap the homes-per-lot law and replace it with a $1 billion a year fund for cities that allow such housing, pre-zoning with cities and changes to the transit-area law. They have published no 2026 position on the density laws, so option c is inferred from 2024 and is low confidence.

2024 platform (Global News, September 27, 2024): repeal Bill 44 and create a $1 billion a year fund for municipalities allowing small-scale multi-unit housing on at least two-thirds of residential land, pre-zoning with cities, and amending Bill 47 to require shops and services within walking distance. 2026: only 'bring down the cost of building and buying a home' and a Metro Vancouver plan returning housing functions from the regional district to cities and the province. Inferred, low confidence.
This party voted against the lot rule and wants the province to build non-profit homes instead.

The two Green MLAs voted against the homes-per-lot law in 2023. The 2026 plan is to build or protect 26,000 non-market homes a year, restart the Community Housing Fund, bring in vacancy control and make it 'easier and quicker to build all forms of housing'. It takes no stated position on the mayors' letter, so option d is inferred.

Record: Furstenau and Olsen voted nay on Bills 44 and 46 at third reading (November 29, 2023). Platform and Rights for Renters brief (September 29, 2026): 26,000 non-market homes a year, Community Housing Fund restart, vacancy control, faster approvals for all housing forms. No 2026 statement on the small-scale multi-unit mandate, transit-oriented areas, target orders or the mayors' request. Option d combines the 2023 vote with the 2026 priorities; inferred, low confidence.
This party would keep the rules near transit and make cities approve homes faster, with one rulebook.

CentreBC's platform builds on 'provincial rules that allow more homes near transit' and adds a provincial standard of six months for rezonings and eight weeks for building permits, with one set of rules across municipalities by 2028 and fees refunded if missed, plus a $125 million a year fund for cities that meet timelines and targets.

Platform (October 10, pages 7, 11 and 13): provincial approval standard of six months for rezonings and eight weeks for building permits, one set of rules across municipalities by January 1, 2028, fees refunded when missed; a $125 million a year housing performance fund for cities meeting timelines and targets; a $240 million a year growth fund; buying land near new transit stations before announcement. It keeps transit-area density rules and does not mention repealing the small-scale multi-unit mandate or the mayors' letter.
This party has not said who should decide zoning, so it is not scored here.
OneBC would scrap the Step Code building rules and block city rent control, but has no position on the provincial density laws, so it is not scored on this question.

Priorities page: open new land for development, eliminate the Step Code, block municipal rent control programs, remove taxes that inflate prices. Nothing on Bill 44, Bill 47, target orders or the mayors' request; this question is left out of its score.
questions/q_local_fraser_valley_farmland: Should food factories be allowed on some weaker farmland in the Fraser Valley?
The province proposed letting food processing plants build on some lower-quality protected farmland. What should happen?
The province proposed letting food plants use some lower-quality land in the Agricultural Land Reserve. What should happen?
A July 2026 proposal would let food processors use Class 5 to 7 reserve soil, up to 0.25% of private reserve land. What now?
The July 2026 proposal would let food processors build on Agricultural Land Reserve Class 5 to 7 soil, capped at 0.25% of private reserve land, with a 5% local-product minimum. Which approach?

Much of the Fraser Valley is protected farmland that can only be used for farming. The province wants to let food factories build on some of the weaker soil, so more food can be made nearby. Farm groups say the land would be lost.

Much of the Fraser Valley is in the farmland reserve, where building is limited to farm use. In July 2026 the province proposed letting food processing plants build on lower-quality reserve soil, with a cap on the area and a lower local-content rule. Business groups support it; the farmland commission and farm groups oppose it. The election paused the decision.

On July 23, 2026 the NDP government proposed letting food processors build on Agricultural Land Reserve land with poorer soil, capped at a small share of private reserve land, with the local-product minimum cut from 50% to 5%. The province says 500 to 1,000 hectares in the Lower Mainland and Fraser Valley could qualify. The Abbotsford Chamber and food manufacturers back it; the Agricultural Land Commission and the BC Agriculture Council oppose it. The election paused the decision.

The July 23, 2026 proposal would allow food processing on Agricultural Land Reserve Class 5 to 7 soil, cut the local-product minimum from 50% to 5%, and cap the total at 0.25% of the 2.1 million hectares of private reserve land. The province says the soil test excludes about 90% of Fraser Valley farmland and that 500 to 1,000 hectares could qualify. Food manufacturers, the Board of Trade and the Abbotsford Chamber support it. The Agricultural Land Commission and the BC Agriculture Council oppose it. Consultation closed September 18 and the election paused the decision. Eby calls it a food security measure; the Conservatives declined to state a position.

The July 23, 2026 proposal would let food processors build on Agricultural Land Reserve Class 5 to 7 soil, cut the local-product minimum from 50% to 5%, and cap the total at 0.25% of the 2.1 million hectares of privately owned reserve land. The province says the soil condition would exclude about 90% of Lower Mainland and Fraser Valley reserve farmland and 500 to 1,000 hectares could qualify. Supporters include BC Food and Beverage, the Board of Trade and the Abbotsford Chamber of Commerce. The Agricultural Land Commission called it one of the most significant policy shifts in decades; the BC Agriculture Council supports food processing but opposes the proposed rule changes. Consultation closed September 18, 2026 and the election call paused the decision. Eby says it affects 0.3% of the reserve; the Agriculture Council's figure is far larger and the two do not reconcile.
Keep farmland for farming, and limit who can buy it.
Keep the farmland rules, limit farmland buyers to citizens and residents, create a public land bank, and tax unused farmland.
Keep the reserve rules, limit larger farmland purchases to citizens and permanent residents, create a public land bank, and tax unused farmland.
Reject reserve processing, limit owners of reserve parcels over four hectares to citizens and permanent residents, start a public farmland bank, and tax unused farmland.

Withdraw the processing proposal; restrict ownership of Agricultural Land Reserve parcels over 4 hectares to citizens and permanent residents of BC; create a public land bank for new farmers; let municipalities tax idle farmland; add food sovereignty to the Agricultural Land Commission's mandate.
Keep the farmland rules, and help food makers with loans and grants instead.
Keep the farmland rules, and help processors with loan guarantees and a food-processing fund on regular industrial land.
Keep the reserve rules, and support processors with loan guarantees and a food stream in a manufacturing fund, with faster approvals on industrial land.
Keep reserve processing rules, offer processing and equipment loan guarantees, add a food stream to a manufacturing fund, and update farm classification so farmland is farmed.

Leave the reserve's processing rules unchanged; provide loan guarantees for processing and equipment; add a food stream to a Manufacturing Jobs Fund doubled to $60 million a year; set ten-year farm targets; update farm classification rules so farmland is farmed.
Allow food factories on a small amount of weaker farmland, after a soil check.
Allow food processing plants on a small, capped share of lower-quality farmland, with a soil test and local permits.
Allow food processing on a small capped share of lower-quality reserve land, with a soil test, and let processors use food from anywhere.
Adopt the proposal: processing on Class 5 to 7 reserve soil, capped at 0.25% of private reserve land, with a soil assessment and a 5% BC-product minimum.

Proceed with the July 2026 proposal: processing on Class 5 to 7 soil and serviced Class 4, capped at 0.25% of the 2.1 million private reserve hectares, soil assessment required, local-product minimum cut from 50% to 5%.
Loosen the rules more, letting landowners and councils decide what goes on weak soil.
Go further than the proposal: let landowners and local governments decide what is built on reserve land with weak soil.
Go further than the proposal: remove the area cap and let landowners and local governments decide what is built on weak-soil reserve land.
Go further: drop the 0.25% cap and soil-class test, and let landowners and local governments decide what is built on lower-quality reserve land, including non-food industry.

Go beyond the July 2026 proposal: remove the 0.25% cap and the Class 5 to 7 soil test, allow non-food industrial uses, and devolve decisions on lower-quality reserve land to landowners and local governments rather than the Agricultural Land Commission.
This party made the proposal. It says food made here means safer supply and lower prices.

The NDP government proposed the change in July 2026 and Eby defends it as a food security and cost-of-living measure: 'food processing is part of that'. No 2026 campaign commitment on it was found, and the election paused it. The agriculture minister who sponsored it is not running again.

Record: news release 2026AF0017 (July 23, 2026) proposed processing on Class 5 to 7 soil, a 5% local-product minimum and a 0.25% cap; consultation closed September 18. Eby told The Tyee the change affects 0.3% of the reserve and is about food security. No 2026 campaign commitment on the proposal was found, and Agriculture Minister Popham is not seeking re-election. Other 2026 food pledges (October 2) are a price guard capping profit margins on grocery essentials and a Lower Mainland wholesale food terminal with Ottawa.
This party has not said what it would do about this, so it is not scored here.

Leader Lorne Doerkson declined to state a position on the farmland proposal; he said the party would do 'everything in our power' and that 'there will be more on that' in its platform. With no published position, the party is not scored here.

The Tyee (October 7, 2026): Leader Lorne Doerkson declined to give the party's position on the proposal; he said 'We're going to do everything in our power' and 'There will be more on that for certain in the coming days in our platform.' The 'Our Plan' page has no farmland or agriculture item as of October 12, and the party pointed only to a temporary PST removal on beer and wine. No_position; recheck if a platform appears.
This party says weaker farmland is still farmland and should not become factory land.

A Green spokesperson told The Tyee that much of the land in the proposal is farmable and 'shouldn't be turned into industrial lands'. The October 2 food plan limits ownership of reserve parcels over four hectares to citizens and permanent residents, creates a public land bank, taxes unused farmland and adds food sovereignty to the commission's mandate.

The Tyee (October 7, 2026): a Green spokesperson opposed turning farmable reserve land industrial. Food plan (October 2, 2026): restrict ownership of Agricultural Land Reserve parcels over 4 hectares to citizens and permanent residents of BC, create a public land bank, let municipalities tax idle farmland, and add food sovereignty to the Agricultural Land Commission's mandate. The plan does not address processing directly, so option a pairs the stated opposition with the ownership measures.
This party would help food makers with loans and a fund, and has not said whether farmland rules should change.

CentreBC's platform offers loan guarantees for processing and equipment, a food stream in its Manufacturing Jobs Fund 'to help process more BC food here', ten-year farm targets and updated farm classification rules. It takes no stated position on the reserve proposal, so option b is inferred from its funding approach.

Platform (October 10): loan guarantees for processing and equipment, a food stream in a Manufacturing Jobs Fund doubled to $60 million a year, ten-year farm production targets, updated farm classification rules 'so farmland is farmed', a permanent farm recovery program and a farm water stream. The platform does not mention the Agricultural Land Reserve processing proposal. Option b is inferred from funding processors without changing reserve rules; low confidence.
This party has said nothing about farmland, so it is not scored here.
OneBC has no agriculture or farmland position, so it is not scored on this question.
OneBC's priorities page lists no agriculture or farmland commitment, so this question is left out of its score.
questions/q_local_fraser_valley_highway1: Highway One is being widened to Abbotsford. What should the province build next in the valley?
Highway 1 widening is funded to Abbotsford and only planned east of there. Where should the next transportation money go?
Highway 1 widening is funded to Highway 11 in Abbotsford by 2031 and only planned to Chilliwack. Where should the next money go?
Highway 1 widening to Highway 11 is funded ($2.65 billion, due 2031); the Chilliwack phase is not. What should be funded next?
Phase 3B of Highway 1 ($2.65 billion, due 2031) is in procurement; Phase 4 to Chilliwack is unfunded and the 2024 West Coast Express promise has no plan. What next?

October 11 post and video: reinstate, with back pay, nurses and front-line health workers still out of work over COVID-era mandates. October 5 plan graphic: 'Reduce wait times, grow services, and attract medical professions to B.C.' BC Ferries has cancellations, long waits and rising demand, and chose a Chinese state-owned yard for new ships. What comes first?

BC Ferries faces cancelled sailings, long waits and rising demand; in May 2025 it chose a Chinese state-owned shipyard for four hybrid vessels after no local yard bid. Which provincial change should come first?
questions/q_local_island_coast_ferries/c: Ferries are the only road for many Island and coast towns. Sailings get cancelled, waits are long, and fares keep rising. The province sets the ferry company's rules and money, and where new ships are built. Parties disagree on what to fix first.

BC Ferries is a provincially owned company that runs under rules and funding set by the province. Sailings get cancelled, waits are long and demand keeps rising. In 2025 the company ordered four new ships from a Chinese state-owned shipyard. In October four parties made ferry promises, none of them a fare cut. Parties disagree on what to fix first.

BC Ferries runs under a provincial mandate, with provincial funding and a provincially set board. Cancellations, long waits and rising demand are the common complaints. In May 2025 the company picked a Chinese state-owned yard for four hybrid-electric vessels after no local yard bid. On October 9 to 11 the Greens, the NDP and the Conservatives each announced ferry plans, and CentreBC's platform has two ferry items; none sets a new Swartz Bay schedule or cuts fares.

The province sets BC Ferries' mandate, service contract, funding and board rules. In May 2025 BC Ferries chose a Chinese state-owned shipyard for four large hybrid-electric vessels; the province says no local yard bid. The NDP announced a locals-first reservation pilot on October 10 (12% of advance booking space on two routes) and pledged in September that future vessels be built in BC. The Conservatives announced a BC Ferries Charter on October 11. The Greens released a ferry plan on October 9. CentreBC's platform has a shipyard fund and a fare credit. None of these sets a new Swartz Bay-Tsawwassen schedule or a fare cut.

The province sets BC Ferries' mandate, funding and board rules. In May 2025 BC Ferries selected a Chinese state-owned shipyard for four hybrid-electric vessels; the province says no Canadian yard bid. On September 18 Eby committed that future vessels be built in BC, with no timeline. On October 10 the NDP proposed a locals-first reservation pilot: 12% of advance booking space for residents of ferry-dependent communities, on Horseshoe Bay to Langdale and Westview to Little River only. On October 11 the Conservatives announced a BC Ferries Charter with service standards, board cuts and a federal 'fair share'. On October 9 the Greens proposed federal funding parity with Atlantic Canada, a governance review, electric ferries and locally built ships. CentreBC's platform offers Canadian-built vessels, a $25 million a year shipyard fund and a refundable 15% credit on multi-trip fares.
