Pilot a locals-first reservation on Horseshoe Bay to Langdale and Westview to Little River (10% of advance space until four days out plus 2% until 24 hours), and commit that future vessels be built in BC, with no timeline.
Set ferry service rules, hold the bosses to them, add no new costs.
Write service standards for on-time sailings and capacity, hold management to them, cut the board, and add no new costs.
Adopt a ferries charter with standards for reliability, on-time performance and capacity, hold management accountable, trim the board, and add no new costs.
Adopt a charter of reliability, capacity, affordability and service standards with leadership held to it, trim the board, seek fair federal funding, and add no new costs.

Adopt a BC Ferries Charter setting standards for reliability, on-time performance, capacity, affordability and service, with leadership held responsible; reduce board redundancy; negotiate a fair share of federal ferry funding; high-speed Wi-Fi through private procurement at no new public cost.
Give regular riders money back on multi-trip fares, and build ferries in Canada.
Give travellers a tax credit on multi-trip fares, require future ferries to be built in Canada, and fund shipyards.
Give a 15% tax credit on multi-trip ferry fares, require future vessels be built in Canada, and fund a $25 million yearly shipyard program.
Offer a refundable 15% credit on multi-trip fares and transit passes, require new ferries to be built in Canada, and put $25 million a year into shipyards and training.

Offer a refundable BC Commuter Credit returning 15% on transit passes and BC Ferries multi-trip fares, require future BC Ferries vessels to be built in Canada, and create a $25 million a year fund for BC shipyards and shipbuilder training.
Match east coast federal ferry money, rethink how ferries are run, build electric ships.
Seek federal funding equal to Atlantic Canada ferries, review how ferries are governed, plan electric ferries, and build ships locally.
Seek federal funding parity with Atlantic Canada ferries, review BC Ferries' governance and funding, plan electric ferries, and build ships locally with union labour.
Seek Atlantic-level federal ferry funding, review BC Ferries' governance and funding, upgrade terminals, plan electric ferries, and build ships locally with union labour.

Federal ferry funding parity with Atlantic Canada; review of BC Ferries' governance and long-term funding; terminal and dock upgrades and planning for electric ferries; ships built locally with union labour; next steps on Island rail with the Island Corridor Foundation.
questions/q_local_island_coast_ferries/p: This party would save part of each sailing's bookings for locals on two routes, and build future ferries here.

On October 10 the NDP proposed a locals-first reservation pilot: 12% of advance booking space for residents of ferry-dependent communities on Horseshoe Bay to Langdale and Westview to Little River, then work with other communities. In September Eby committed that future vessels be built in BC, with no timeline. No fare measure.

Release (October 10, 2026, Powell River): 12% of advance booking space for residents of ferry-dependent communities (10% until four days before sailing, 2% until 24 hours) on Horseshoe Bay to Langdale and Westview to Little River, then work with BC Ferries and other communities. September 18 (Union of BC Municipalities): future vessels built in BC, no timeline. Record: BC Ferries selected a Chinese state-owned yard for four hybrid-electric vessels in May 2025; the province says no local yard bid. No fare, schedule or governance commitment.
This party would set service rules for the ferries, hold the bosses to them, and add no new costs.

The Conservatives' October 11 BC Ferries Charter would set standards for reliability, on-time performance, capacity, affordability and customer service, hold leadership responsible, cut board duplication, negotiate a 'fair share' of federal ferry funding, and add Wi-Fi through private contracts 'with no new burden on fares or taxpayers'. No timeline, fare cut or shipbuilding position.

'Conservatives will fix BC Ferries' (October 11, 2026): a BC Ferries Charter with clear standards for reliability, on-time performance, capacity, affordability and customer service; leadership held responsible for meeting them; reduced redundancy at the board so resources go to service; negotiation with Ottawa for a fair share of federal ferry funding; high-speed Wi-Fi on major routes and terminals through competitive private procurement with performance standards and no new burden on fares or taxpayers. No dollar figures, timelines, fare reductions or position on where vessels are built.
This party wants the same federal money east coast ferries get, a rethink of how ferries are run, and electric ships built here.

The Greens' October 9 plan would work with Ottawa for ferry funding parity with Atlantic Canada, review BC Ferries' governance and long-term funding, expand terminal and dock infrastructure, plan for electric ferries, and build and maintain ships locally with union labour. They would also work with First Nations and the Island Corridor Foundation on Island rail.

Release (October 9, 2026): federal funding parity with Atlantic Canada; review of governance and long-term funding; expanded terminal and dock infrastructure and planning for electric ferries; ships built and maintained locally with union labour; next steps for Vancouver Island rail with First Nations and the Island Corridor Foundation (October 9). Within the same plan: free transit for riders under 25 and over 65 and province-wide passenger rail. No fare, reservation or charter item. The Greens are the only party with an Island rail position.
This party would give regular riders money back on multi-trip fares and build ferries in Canada with help for shipyards.

No service standard, reservation or governance item.

Platform (by October 11, 2026, Economy and Affordability, 'Buy Canadian' and 'Transportation that works'): future BC Ferries vessels and other provincial ships built in Canada; a $25 million a year fund to grow BC shipyards and train shipbuilders; a refundable BC Commuter Credit returning 15% on monthly and annual transit passes and BC Ferries multi-trip fares, within a $15 billion three-year transportation plan. No service standard, reservation, governance or schedule item. CentreBC is not running candidates in either Nanaimo riding.
This party has said nothing about ferries, so it is not scored here.
OneBC has no ferries or transportation position, so it is not scored on this question.

questions/q_local_island_coast_oldgrowth: Island mills are closing, and people disagree about cutting the oldest forests. What should happen?
The Crofton pulp mill closed and old-growth logging is still argued over on the Island. What should the province do about forests?
The Crofton pulp mill closed after the premier refused old-growth logs to supply it. What should be done with Island forests?
Crofton's mill closed when old-growth logs were ruled out; deferrals remain, with a 45 million cubic metre harvest goal. What now?
Domtar's Crofton pulp mill (350 jobs) closed after Eby said in December 2025 that pulping old growth to extend it was not an option; old-growth deferrals remain temporary. What now?

Logging has long been a big employer on the Island and the coast. A pulp mill near Duncan closed this year for lack of wood. Some of the oldest forests are off limits for now. Parties disagree on protecting versus cutting.

The Crofton pulp mill, with about 350 jobs, closed last December. The premier said limits on old-growth logging were necessary and refused to let old growth be pulped to keep the mill open. Some old forests are under temporary logging deferrals. Parties disagree on what to protect and how much to cut.

Domtar's Crofton pulp mill (about 350 jobs) closed after a December 2025 announcement. Eby said old-growth limits had raised Island fibre prices but were 'a necessary decision', and that pulping old growth to extend the mill was not an option. Old-growth deferrals from 2021 are temporary. The government's Working Forest plan would zone forests with a 45 million cubic metre goal. The Greens reject the plan; CentreBC would write it into law.

Domtar's Crofton pulp mill closed after a December 2025 announcement; Eby said old-growth restrictions had raised Island fibre prices but were 'a necessary decision', and that pulping old growth to extend the mill was not an option. Old-growth deferrals from 2021 remain temporary. The Forests minister's mandate letter sets a 45 million cubic metre harvest target while Budget 2026 projects about 30 million. Domtar's Crofton pulp mill in the Cowichan Valley (about 350 jobs) closed after a December 2025 announcement; Eby said restrictions on old-growth harvesting had raised Island fibre prices but were 'a necessary decision', and that pulping old growth to extend the mill was not an option. The 2021 old-growth deferrals remain temporary. Minister Parmar's mandate letter sets a 45 million cubic metre target; Budget 2026 projects about 30 million; the Working Forest model's first candidate area near Campbell River was announced September 15, 2026. On October 10 in Courtenay the NDP pledged $50 million to convert deferrals of 'the most irreplaceable and rarest forests' to permanent protection, with mill retrofit support for second growth. The Greens (October 4) would implement all 14 Old Growth Strategic Review recommendations and reject the 45 million target.
Protect big old trees for good, stop clearcutting, plan logging by region, help workers.
Protect big old trees for good, phase out clearcutting, set harvest levels by region, and pay workers for lost income.
Permanently protect big-treed old growth, implement all 14 old-growth review recommendations, phase out clearcutting, set harvest by region, and end raw-log exports.
Protect big-treed old growth for good, adopt all 14 old-growth panel recommendations, phase out clearcuts and raw-log exports, plan harvest by region, fund worker transition.

Permanently protect big-treed old growth; implement all 14 Old Growth Strategic Review recommendations with conservation financing for First Nations; shift to selective logging; set harvest by regional planning with no 45 million target; end raw-log exports; fund worker transition.
Protect the rarest old forests for good, keep logging zones, help mills retool.
Make rarest old-growth deferrals permanent, keep a working forest with a higher harvest goal, and help mills use second growth.
Spend $50 million to make rarest old-growth deferrals permanent, keep a working forest with a 45 million cubic metre goal, and help mills retrofit.
Spend $50 million to make the rarest old-growth deferrals permanent, keep the Working Forest model with zones and a 45 million cubic metre objective, and help mills retrofit.

Convert deferrals of 'the most irreplaceable and rarest forests' to permanent protection with $50 million; keep the Working Forest Landscape Model (zones, no net loss, 45 million cubic metre objective); support mill retrofits for value-added second growth.
Write logging zones into law, sell more public timber, and speed up permits.
Write a working forest into law with a high target, sell more public timber, speed up permits, and fund workers.
Set Working Forest zones in law with a 45 million cubic metre goal, raise timber sales, decide permits in 90 days, and fund workers.
Set Working Forest zones in law, aim for 45 million cubic metres, raise BC Timber Sales to 9 million, decide permits in 90 days, and put $100 million toward workers.

Legislate Working Forest zones; work toward 45 million cubic metres, 40 million by 2030; BC Timber Sales to 9 million cubic metres by 2029; a Forestry Fibre Task Force; One-Stop permits with 90-day decisions; $100 million for workers.
Allow more cutting, charge companies less for wood, and shorten permits and consultations.
Raise the allowed yearly cut, lower the fees companies pay for public timber, and shorten permit and consultation times.
Raise the allowable annual cut, cut stumpage fees to make mills more competitive, and shorten permit approvals and consultations, with no old-growth protection.
Raise the allowable annual cut for more fibre, cut stumpage fees for lumber companies, and speed up permits and consultations, with no zoning plan or old-growth protection.

Increase the allowable annual cut 'to ensure our forest sector has the available wood fibre to grow and thrive', reduce stumpage fees for lumber companies, speed up permit approval times and consultations, with no volume target or old-growth measure.
This party, in charge now, would protect the rarest old forests for good, keep a working forest, and help mills use younger trees.

The NDP government kept old-growth deferrals and refused old-growth pulping to save Crofton. On October 10 in Courtenay it pledged $50 million to make the rarest deferrals permanent while helping mills retrofit for second growth. Its Working Forest model zones forest with a 45 million cubic metre goal. Campaign releases do not restate that target.

Record: December 3, 2025, Eby said old-growth restrictions raised Island fibre prices but were necessary and ruled out pulping old growth for Crofton; mandate letter target of 45 million cubic metres; Budget 2026 projects about 30 million; Working Forest Landscape Model with its first candidate area near Campbell River (September 15, 2026). Pledges (October 10, 2026, Courtenay): $50 million to convert deferrals of the rarest forests to permanent protection, mill retrofit support for value-added second growth, $30 million a year for the Watershed Security Fund.
This party has not published a forestry plan this election, so it is not scored here.

The Conservatives' site shows a 'Forestry for the Future' heading with no text. Their October 7 release promises red tape cut to 2017 levels; the forestry critic blamed 'restrictive policies' and permitting delays for mill closures in 2025. With no published position on old growth, harvest levels or the zoning model, the party is not scored here.

conservativebc.ca (checked through October 11) lists 'Forestry for the Future' with no content. 'Supercharge' release (October 7): red tape to 2017 levels, a one-in two-out law, 120 Day Permitting Act for projects over $250 million, claim of 21 mills closed since 2023. Critic Ward Stamer (November 2025) called the 'Path to 45' 'a path to collapse' and blamed restrictive policy and permitting; The NDP claims the Conservatives oppose 30 by 30 (claim). No stated position on old-growth deferrals. No_position; recheck if a platform appears.
This party would protect big old trees for good, stop clearcutting, and plan logging region by region.

The Greens' October 4 forestry plan rejects the Working Forest model, sets harvest by regional area-based planning, ends raw-log exports, permanently protects big-treed old growth and large second growth, implements all 14 Old Growth Strategic Review recommendations with conservation financing for First Nations, and shifts to partial harvesting and longer rotations. Lowan criticized Domtar over Crofton.

Forestry plan (October 4, 2026): reject the Working Forest model and its 45 million cubic metre objective; regional area-based planning; end raw-log exports; permanently protect big-treed old growth and large second growth; implement all 14 Old Growth Strategic Review recommendations with conservation financing for First Nations; partial harvesting, selective logging, longer rotations; work toward 20% of the allowable cut for community forests; retraining, upskilling and employment supports for forestry workers. Economic vision (October 7): phase out industrial clear-cutting; criticism of Domtar for closing mills including Crofton. The platform has no old-growth section.

Platform (by October 11, 2026, Economy and Affordability): work toward 45 million cubic metres of economically viable timber, 40 million by 2030; Forestry Fibre Task Force; BC Timber Sales to 9 million cubic metres by 2029; long-term Working Forest zones in law alongside multiple-use and conservation areas; $100 million over three years for forestry workers and mass timber; Manufacturing Jobs Fund doubled to $60 million a year; Forestry One-Stop with 90-day decisions where consultation and environmental review do not apply. No old-growth text.
This party would allow more cutting, charge companies less for wood, and shorten permits and consultations.

OneBC would increase the allowable annual cut so the sector has more fibre, reduce stumpage fees for lumber companies, and speed up permit approvals and consultations. It gives no volume target and has no old-growth or zoning position; its only Island candidate has published none.

Priorities page: 'Increase the allowable yearly cut to ensure our forest sector has the available wood fibre to grow and thrive'; 'Reduce stumpage fees for lumber companies to make the market more competitive'; 'Speed up permit approval times and consultations'. October 5 plan graphic: 'Make the forestry and mining sectors competitive - reduce fees, faster approvals'. No volume target, no old-growth or Working Forest position; one Island candidate (Juan de Fuca-Malahat) with no published positions.
questions/q_local_island_coast_seniors/p: Island hospitals are short of space and seniors wait for care homes. What should come first?
Nanaimo's hospital still waits for its new tower, and care-home projects were paused. What should come first for seniors' care?
Nanaimo's hospital tower and cardiac lab are only in planning, and a Campbell River care home was paused. What should come first?
Budget 2026 funded only planning for Nanaimo's tower and paused a 153-bed Campbell River care home. What should come first?

Budget 2026 funded only concept planning for Nanaimo's tower and cath lab, paused a 153-bed Campbell River care home, and about 1,600 patients province-wide wait in hospital for care beds. Which approach?
questions/q_local_island_coast_seniors/c: The Island has the oldest population in the province. Nanaimo has waited years for a bigger hospital. A care home in Campbell River was put on hold, and seniors wait in hospital beds for a care home place. Parties disagree on what to build first.

The government promised Nanaimo a new hospital tower and heart lab in 2024, but the 2026 budget paid only for planning. The same budget paused seven care-home projects, including a 153-bed home in Campbell River. In October the government promised to restart them. Parties disagree on what comes first.

The NDP's 2024 pledge of a tower and cardiac lab at Nanaimo's hospital got only planning money in Budget 2026. The same budget paused seven long-term care builds, including a 153-bed facility in Campbell River. In October the NDP promised to restart the seven and put $90 million into a campus of care at the former Oak Bay Lodge. The Conservatives would let care funding follow seniors to qualified providers, including non-government ones; CentreBC would cut seniors stuck in hospital.

The NDP's 2024 pledge of a patient tower and cardiac catheterization lab at Nanaimo Regional General Hospital was absent from the 2025 budget; Budget 2026 funds only initial planning. Budget 2026 also paused seven long-term care builds including a 153-bed Campbell River facility. The NDP (October 5 to 6) would restart the seven and spend $90 million on an Oak Bay Lodge campus of care. The Conservatives (October 9) would give waiting seniors portable public funding with a choice of qualified providers, including non-government ones. CentreBC would cut patients stuck in hospital awaiting care from about 1,600 to 1,000 by 2030. No party has a 2026 commitment on the Nanaimo tower.

The NDP's 2024 pledge of a patient tower and cardiac catheterization lab at Nanaimo Regional General Hospital was not in the 2025 budget; Budget 2026 funds initial planning only, the ministry says concept planning takes up to 18 months, and the Nanaimo Regional Hospital District agreed to put $50 million up front for concept and business planning of the cath lab. Budget 2026 paused seven long-term care projects including a 153-bed Campbell River facility, while the province looks for ways to cut building costs. The NDP pledges to restart the seven, $90 million toward an Oak Bay Lodge campus of care, scanners and rural recruitment incentives. The Conservatives (October 9) would give waiting seniors portable public funding with a choice of qualified providers, including non-government ones, and cut design rules. CentreBC would cut patients awaiting long-term care in hospital from about 1,600 to 1,000 by 2030. The Greens want community health centres and public-only funding.
questions/q_local_island_coast_seniors/o: Restart the paused care homes, fund an Oak Bay seniors' campus, plan Nanaimo's tower.
Restart the paused care homes, put $90 million into an Oak Bay Lodge campus, and keep planning Nanaimo's tower.
Restart the seven paused care homes, fund a $90 million campus of care at Oak Bay Lodge, and continue planning Nanaimo's tower.
Restart the seven paused care homes including Campbell River's, put $90 million into an Oak Bay Lodge campus, keep planning Nanaimo's tower and cath lab, and add scanners.

Restart the seven paused long-term care projects including Campbell River's 153 beds via the July 2026 Canada-BC agreement; $90 million toward an Oak Bay Lodge campus of care; planning for Nanaimo's tower and cath lab; new scanners; public delivery only.
Let money follow seniors to an approved home, public or private; fund small-town clinics.
Let public funding follow seniors to qualified providers, including private ones, cut building rules, and create a rural practice fund.
Give seniors portable public funding with a choice of qualified providers, cut design rules, and create a $50 million rural practice fund.
Give seniors awaiting care portable public funding with a choice of qualified providers, including non-government ones, cut design rules, and add a $50 million rural practice fund.

Portable public funding for seniors waiting for long-term care, with a choice of qualified providers, including non-government options with strong performance safeguards; cut design rules; a $50 million emergency fund for rural practices; an expert commission; the 2026 health budget held.
Fewer seniors stuck in hospital, factory-built care homes, every emergency closure made public.
Cut seniors stuck in hospital, restart the paused homes with one factory-built design, and report every emergency closure.
Cut patients stuck in hospital awaiting long-term care, restart the seven paused homes with a prefabricated design, and legislate emergency room closure reporting.
Cut hospital patients awaiting care beds from 1,600 to 1,000 by 2030, restart the seven paused homes with a prefab design, and add a $25 million yearly rural fund.

Reduce patients in hospital awaiting long-term care from 1,600 to 1,000 by 2030; restart all seven paused homes with a pre-fabricated design, 2,500 beds under construction by 2031; Emergency Room Accountability Act and a $25 million yearly rural fund.
A public health centre in every area, safe nurse staffing, all care kept public.
Open a community health centre in every riding, fund safe nurse staffing, plan for rural seniors, and keep all care public.
Fund a community health centre in every riding, fund safe nurse-to-patient ratios, adopt a rural seniors strategy, and keep all care public.
Fund a community health centre per riding, fund safe nurse-to-patient ratios, adopt a rural seniors strategy, expand public care homes, and keep health dollars public.

Fund a Community Health Centre in every riding, fund nurses in the public system to support safe nurse-to-patient ratios, phase out private agency nurses, adopt a rural seniors strategy, expand publicly funded long-term care, and keep every public health dollar in public care.
Allow private paid care beside public care, rehire workers who left over vaccine rules.
Allow private-pay care alongside the publicly funded system, and reinstate nurses who lost jobs over vaccine mandates, with back pay.
Allow private health care alongside public care, reinstate nurses removed under vaccine mandates with back pay, and shift administration spending to the front line.
Allow private care beside fully funded public care, rehire nurses removed under vaccine mandates, and move admin money to staff.

Allow private health care alongside fully funded public care; reinstate nurses removed under vaccine mandates with back pay; shift administration and human resources spending to front-line staff; repeal the Health Professions and Occupations Act.
questions/q_local_island_coast_seniors/p: This party paused the care homes in its budget and now promises to restart them, fund an Oak Bay seniors' campus, and keep planning Nanaimo's tower.

The NDP government's 2024 Nanaimo tower pledge got only planning money in Budget 2026, and the same budget paused seven care homes including Campbell River's. On October 5 and 6 in Victoria Eby promised to restart the seven, put $90 million into an Oak Bay Lodge campus of care and offer free shingles vaccine over 50.

Record: 2024 Nanaimo tower and cath lab pledge absent from the 2025 budget; Budget 2026 funds initial planning only; seven long-term care projects paused, including 153 beds in Campbell River. Pledges: restart the seven with July 2026 Canada-BC money, $90 million for an Oak Bay Lodge campus of care, free shingles vaccine over 50 (October 5 to 6); eight MRI and ten CT scanners, regional surgical waitlists (October 6); rural tuition, loan forgiveness, moving costs, 1,000 seats, international graduate bridging (October 9). No 2026 Nanaimo tower commitment.
This party would let the money follow each senior to an approved home, public or private, and fund small-town clinics.

On October 9 the Conservatives promised portable public funding for seniors waiting for long-term care, giving 'a real choice among qualified providers, including non-government options with strong performance safeguards', and faster builds by cutting design rules. On October 5 they pledged a $50 million rural practice fund, an expert commission and no health cuts. No 2026 commitment on the Nanaimo tower.

October 9, 2026 release: portable public funding for seniors waiting for a bed, with 'a real choice among qualified providers, including non-government options with strong performance safeguards'; build beds faster by cutting unnecessary design rules; says 7,200 British Columbians are waiting for a long-term-care bed and that design rules pushed some proposed beds to $1.8 million each. October 5 (100 Mile House): $50 million rural practice fund, flexible staffing, automatic credential recognition, expert commission within 100 days, 2026 health budget kept. Nanaimo-Lantzville candidate Pringle wants cardiac care closer to home; no party commitment on the tower or cath lab was found for 2026.
This party would open a public health centre in every area, set safe nurse staffing, and keep all care public.

The Greens promise Community Health Centres in every riding, safe nurse-to-patient ratios, an end to private agency nurses, a rural seniors strategy, more publicly funded long-term care and 'every public health dollar in public care'. They have no Island hospital or Nanaimo tower item; option d is their care model applied to the Island.

Our Plan, Healthcare Policy Brief (October 6, 2026) and Supporting Seniors Policy Brief (October 4, 2026): Community Health Centres in every region, more funding for public-system nurses to support safe nurse-to-patient ratios, phase-out of private agency nurses and for-profit staffing agencies, a review of the health authority model focused on one consolidated provincial authority, public coverage of mental health care, a plan to increase publicly funded long-term care facilities and a rural seniors strategy (October 4), no growth of private care. No Nanaimo, Cowichan or Island Health item found. Option d is the model, not a project list.
This party would cut the number of seniors stuck in hospital, restart the care homes with one factory-built design, and report every emergency closure.

CentreBC's platform cuts patients stuck in hospital awaiting long-term care from about 1,600 to 1,000 by 2030, restarts the seven paused homes with a pre-fabricated design, passes an emergency room accountability law with public reporting and a $25 million a year rural fund, and keeps 'public health care, not private pay'. No Nanaimo, Cowichan or Island Health item.

Platform (by October 11, 2026, Health Care): reduce patients in hospital awaiting long-term care from about 1,600 to 1,000 by 2030; restart all seven paused homes with a pre-fabricated design, 2,500 beds under construction and 1,000 open by March 2031; Emergency Room Accountability Act with public reporting of every closure; halve unplanned closure hours by 2029/30; $25 million a year rural stabilization fund; permanent rural retention bonus; 30-day licensing; 'public health care, not private pay'. The PDF has no Nanaimo, Cowichan or Island Health item.
This party wants private, paid-for care allowed beside public care. It has no hospital or care-home plan.

OneBC would allow private health care alongside fully funded public care, move administration spending to the front line and reinstate nurses removed under vaccine mandates. Its leader said 'people are dying in waiting rooms' but offered no policy, so option e applies the general stance to seniors' care; inferred, low confidence.

Priorities page: 'Private Healthcare alongside fully-funded public healthcare'; shift administration and human resources spending to front-line staff; repeal the Health Professions and Occupations Act. October 11 post and video: reinstate, with back pay, nurses and front-line health workers still out of work over COVID-era mandates. CBC Q&A (October 3): 'people are dying in waiting rooms', no policy. No hospital, long-term care or Island item; one Island candidate (Juan de Fuca-Malahat) with no published positions. Option e is inferred; low confidence.
questions/q_local_interior_wildfire/prom: After this summer's big fire near Summerland, what should the province do first about wildfires?
After the Bald Range fire emptied Summerland and part of Peachland, where should the province put its wildfire effort first?
After the Bald Range fire near Summerland, where should the province put its main wildfire money and effort before next summer?
The Bald Range fire emptied Summerland and part of Peachland in August 2026 and damaged or destroyed about 150 structures. What comes first?

The Bald Range fire (August 7 to 27, 2026, about 25,000 hectares) emptied Summerland and part of Peachland, killed one person and damaged or destroyed about 150 structures. Which wildfire approach should the province take first?
questions/q_local_interior_wildfire/cont: A huge fire near Summerland this summer forced thousands of people from their homes and damaged or destroyed many buildings. The province fights fires, pays for prevention work around towns, and helps people rebuild. Parties disagree on what to spend the next money on.

The Bald Range fire started near Summerland on August 7. About 20,000 people were ordered out of Summerland and Peachland, one person died, and about 150 buildings were damaged or destroyed. Earlier this year the province's community fire-prevention grants ran out of money. Parties disagree on what to fund first.

The Bald Range fire began northwest of Summerland on August 7, 2026; all of Summerland and part of Peachland were evacuated, one woman died and about 150 structures were damaged or destroyed before it was held on August 27. In January the FireSmart community grant program closed its intake for lack of money; the 2026 budget later added $15 million. The NDP offers rebuilding help, the Conservatives aircraft, CentreBC guaranteed grants, the Greens long-term restoration funding. OneBC has no position.

The Bald Range fire (August 7 to 27, 2026) burned about 25,000 hectares northwest of Summerland; a provincial state of emergency on August 8 ordered about 20,000 residents of Summerland and Peachland out, one 80-year-old woman died, and about 150 structures were damaged or destroyed. The FireSmart Community Funding program closed its 2026 intake on January 30 for lack of funds; Budget 2026 then added $15 million and the 2027 intake opened October 1. Fire management was budgeted at $235.7 million for 2026/27 with spending forecast at $850 million by September. Prevention, aircraft, grants and recovery compete for the next dollar.

The Bald Range fire started August 7, 2026 about 15 km northwest of Summerland; a provincial state of emergency followed on August 8 with evacuation orders for about 20,000 people in Summerland and the Peachland area. One 80-year-old woman died while evacuating, about 150 structures were damaged or destroyed, and the fire was declared held on August 27 at about 25,000 hectares. The Union of BC Municipalities reported in January 2026 that the FireSmart Community Funding intake closed on January 30 for lack of funds; Budget 2026 added $15 million for core FireSmart. Fire management: $235.7 million voted for 2026/27, $850 million forecast as of September 14. On October 2 the Conservatives released a wildfire plan in the Okanagan and Eby announced recovery support in Summerland aimed especially at uninsured and underinsured owners.
questions/q_local_interior_wildfire/opti: Buy water bombers, fund fire-spotting technology, and log more forest near towns.
Buy firefighting planes, fund early-detection technology, make controlled burns easier, and log more risky forest near towns.
Buy firefighting aircraft including water bombers, fund early-detection technology, make prescribed burns easier, and log more high-risk forest near communities with timber sales paying.
Buy firefighting aircraft, fund early-detection technology, ease prescribed burns, deploy crews faster, and log more in high-risk areas near towns to fund prevention.

Implement a Protect Communities from Wildfire Action Plan immediately: buy water bombers and other aircraft, a dedicated early-detection technology fund, easier prescribed fire, faster deployment of qualified crews, more logging in high-risk areas near communities with sale revenue funding prevention.
Guarantee yearly fire-safety grants for every town and First Nation, and winter prevention crews.
Guarantee fire-prevention grants in law for every town and First Nation, keep crews through winter, and fund drones and cameras.
Restore FireSmart grants to $40 million a year guaranteed in law for every town and First Nation, keep crews through winter, and fund drones.
Restore prevention grants to $40 million a year, guaranteed in law for every community and First Nation, keep 300 crew through winter, and spend $10 million a year on drones.

FireSmart grants restored to $40 million a year and guaranteed in law for five years, fuel management eligible again; Forests Against Fire at $25 million a year; 300 seasonal crew kept through winter; a $10 million a year drone fund.
Put new money into helping this summer's fire victims rebuild, especially the uninsured.
Match donations for this summer's fire victims, help the uninsured rebuild, repair public works, and keep the current prevention budget.
Match Red Cross donations up to $20 million for this summer's victims, especially the uninsured, rebuild public infrastructure, and keep the current prevention budget.
Match Red Cross donations for fire victims up to $20 million, fund road repair and debris removal, lend to small businesses interest-free, and keep the prevention budget.

Match Red Cross donations up to $20 million for 2026 wildfire victims, prioritizing uninsured owners; fund road repairs, debris removal and soil remediation; interest-free loans up to $1 million from a $500 million fund shared with tariff-hit businesses; keep the current prevention budget.
Give towns and First Nations long-term money to prepare, and restore forests carefully.
Give First Nations and local governments long-term funding to prepare for fire, and restore forests with thinning and careful burning.
Give First Nations and local governments long-term funding to prepare for wildfire, and expand restoration, prescribed and cultural burning and thinning where ecologically appropriate.
Give First Nations and local governments stable hazard funding, expand restoration, prescribed and cultural burning, thinning and fuel work, and set no higher harvest target.

Stable long-term funding for First Nations and local governments to prepare for wildfire, flood, drought and heat; ecosystem restoration, prescribed and cultural burning, thinning and fuel management where ecologically appropriate; wildfire resilience treated as long-term skilled work; no harvest target.
questions/q_local_interior_wildfire/part: This party, in charge now, promises money to help fire victims rebuild, especially people without insurance.

In Summerland on October 2, Eby promised to match Red Cross donations up to $20 million for this summer's fire victims, especially the uninsured, and to fund rebuilding of public infrastructure. A $500 million fund for small businesses hit by the wildfires or US tariffs offers interest-free loans. The government let FireSmart grants run out in January, then added $15 million. No aircraft or new prevention pledge.

Pledges: match Canadian Red Cross donations up to $20 million for 2026 wildfire victims, prioritizing uninsured and underinsured owners, and fund road repairs, debris removal and soil remediation (October 2, announced in Summerland with candidate Tina Lee); a $500 million Small Business Tariff and Wildfire Relief Fund with interest-free loans up to $1 million for 72 months (October 7). Record: FireSmart intake closed January 30, 2026 for lack of funds; Budget 2026 added $15 million; the 2027 intake opened October 1. No aircraft, detection or guaranteed-grant pledge.
This party would buy water bombers, fund fire-spotting technology, and log more forest near towns.

The Conservatives' October 2 plan would buy firefighting aircraft including water bombers, reduce forest fuels around communities, make prescribed burns easier, let qualified crews deploy faster, and create a detection-technology fund. News reports put the aircraft at $400 million and the fund at $100 million; the release gives no figures. News reports say the plan would largely pay for itself, through sales of timber logged near communities and by renting the planes to other jurisdictions.

'Fighting Wildfires, Protecting Communities' (October 2, 2026): implement a Protect Communities from Wildfire Action Plan immediately, buy aircraft including water bombers, reduce fuels around communities, easier prescribed fire without lowering safety standards, faster deployment of qualified resources, a dedicated early-detection fund, a wildfire cabinet committee chaired by the leader. AM 1150 reports $400 million for aircraft and a $100 million fund; Today in BC reports more logging in high-risk areas with sale revenue funding prevention and 'more predictable FireSmart funding'. Today in BC reported the plan would largely pay for itself; the Canadian Press reported the province could help pay for the planes by renting them to other jurisdictions.
This party would give towns and First Nations steady money to prepare, and restore forests with careful burning.

The Greens promise stable long-term funding for First Nations and local governments to prepare for wildfire, flood, drought and heat, and would expand restoration, prescribed and cultural burning, thinning and fuel management 'where ecologically appropriate', treating it as long-term skilled work. They oppose using higher harvest targets to pay for it and make no aircraft pledge.

Climate, LNG and Royalties Policy Brief (October 10, 2026): stable long-term funding for First Nations and local governments to assess climate risks and prepare for wildfire and other hazards. A New Economic Direction (October 7): treat forest restoration, wildfire resilience and climate adaptation as long-term skilled work; expand ecosystem restoration, prescribed and cultural burning, thinning and fuel management where ecologically appropriate; develop markets for low-grade fibre where they improve risk reduction. Forestry plan (October 4) rejects a 45 million cubic metre harvest target. No aircraft or dollar figures.
This party would guarantee yearly fire-safety grants for every town and First Nation and keep crews on all winter.

CentreBC's platform restores FireSmart grants to $40 million a year, guaranteed in law for five years and shared by formula with every local government and First Nation; raises Forests Against Fire to $25 million a year; keeps about 300 seasonal crew through winter; and funds $10 million a year for detection cameras and drones. No aircraft purchase.

Platform (October 10, Public Safety section): FireSmart to $40 million a year guaranteed in law for five years, formula-shared with every local government and First Nation, fuel management eligible with 30-day decisions; Forests Against Fire to $25 million a year starting near the highest-risk communities (thinning, prescribed fire, salvage, replanting, a set share for First Nations crews and cultural burning); about 300 seasonal crew kept through winter; a $10 million a year technology fund for detection cameras, mapping drones and a water-drop drone pilot.
This party has said nothing about wildfires, so it is not scored here.
OneBC has no wildfire position, so it is not scored on this question.
OneBC's priorities page and its October 5 platform summary have no wildfire or fire item (checked October 12), so this question is left out of its score.
questions/q_local_interior_downtown/prom: Kelowna wants forced care for the sickest drug users. What should the province do?
Kelowna's council wants a regional forced-treatment facility and its downtown drug-use site closed. What should the province do?
Kelowna's council wants a regional involuntary care facility and its downtown consumption site closed. What should be done?
Kelowna asked for a regional involuntary care facility and for Health Canada not to renew its consumption site. What now?

Kelowna council asked Health Canada not to renew the Outreach Urban Health consumption site (3,466 RCMP calls since 2021) and asked the province for a regional mandatory care facility. Which provincial approach?
questions/q_local_interior_downtown/cont: Kelowna's downtown has people living on the street with addiction and mental illness. The city wants a regional centre where the sickest can be made to get care, and wants a downtown supervised drug-use site closed. Parties disagree on what the province should pay for.

In a letter made public September 1, Kelowna's council asked Ottawa not to renew a downtown site where people use drugs under supervision, citing thousands of police calls. It also asked the province for a regional facility where the sickest people could be treated against their will. The province decides where such facilities go and how police and hospitals are funded. Parties differ widely.

In a letter made public September 1, Kelowna council asked Health Canada not to renew the downtown supervised consumption site in 2027, citing 3,466 police calls since 2021, and repeated its request to the province for a regional mandatory care facility. Eby said on October 2 the province is looking for a site that could be used right away; the Conservatives would expand police powers; CentreBC would fund downtown safety teams; the Greens would expand supervised sites; OneBC would close them.

Kelowna council's letter (dated August 26, made public September 1) asked Health Canada to deny the 2027 renewal of the Pandosy Street supervised consumption site, citing 3,466 RCMP calls since 2021, and repeated its request to the province for 'a regional mandatory care facility within the Okanagan'. The province's involuntary care beds are in Surrey and Maple Ridge, none in the Okanagan. Site licences are federal; the provincial decisions are where a regional facility goes, Mental Health Act changes, and health and policing funding. questions/q_local_north_resources/contex: The north has big projects waiting: gas export plants, new mines, and a long power line to run them. The province decides whether and how fast to approve them, and what pollution and First Nations rules apply. Parties disagree on speed and conditions.

In September the companies behind the Kitimat gas export plant agreed to build a second phase. Another gas plant near Prince Rupert has its permits but no final go-ahead, new mines are waiting on permits, and construction has started on a north coast power line. The province sets approval timelines, pollution rules, the carbon price for industry, and First Nations partnership rules. Parties disagree on speed and conditions.

The Kitimat gas export plant's owners are doubling it after a September decision. The Ksi Lisims plant near Prince Rupert is permitted but awaits its investment decision, mine proposals are in the permit queue, and the first phase of the North Coast power line is under construction. The NDP requires new plants to be net-zero ready by 2030. The Conservatives would legislate 120-day approvals and drop emissions limits. CentreBC would set a one-year legal deadline. The Greens would approve no new gas plants.

LNG Canada announced its Phase 2 final investment decision on September 29, doubling Kitimat capacity to 28 million tonnes. The NDP requires new projects to be net-zero ready by 2030, would run assessments and permits at the same time, double mineral exports and fast-track the North Coast line with Canadian steel. The Conservatives' plan doubles gas production by 2032, ends emissions limits, legislates 120-day permits and sets a fixed deadline for the line. CentreBC backs LNG with First Nations partners and net-zero plans, a 12-month decision deadline and ten mine decisions by 2030. The Greens would end approvals for new LNG and pipelines.

LNG Canada's Phase 2 final investment decision (September 29, 2026) doubles Kitimat capacity to 28 million tonnes. On the NDP's own numbers, capacity reaches nearly 48 million tonnes by 2035, above the Conservatives' 'triple by 2035' target, so the real dispute is conditions and process. The NDP pledges to double critical mineral exports in five years, run permits concurrently, build the North Coast Transmission Line with Canadian steel, and keep the net-zero-ready requirement. The Conservatives would double gas by 2032 and triple by 2035, end emissions limits, pass a 120 Day Permitting Act and fix a line deadline. CentreBC requires First Nations partners and credible net-zero plans, keeps industrial carbon pricing, sets a 12-month provincial deadline and promises decisions on 10 mines by 2030. The Greens would approve no new LNG or pipelines.

Approve projects that can reach zero emissions, speed up permits, build the power line.

Decide in 12 months, back LNG only with First Nations partners and a net-zero-ready plan, keep industrial carbon pricing, rule on ten mines by 2030, and fund port access.

Approve big projects within four months by law, double gas output, drop emissions limits.
Pass a law requiring decisions on big projects within 120 days, double gas production by 2032, and drop emissions limits.

Permit big projects in 120 days, double gas output by 2032 and triple it by 2035, drop emissions limits, replace the LNG carbon-tax rules, and set a power line deadline.

Approve projects and a coast pipeline without long consultations, and cut fees.

questions/q_local_north_resources/party_: This party, in charge now, backs more gas plants and mines if they can reach zero emissions, with faster permits and a new power line.

The NDP government permitted LNG Canada Phase 2 and Ksi Lisims and requires new plants to be net-zero ready by 2030. It pledges to double critical mineral exports in five years, run assessments and permits at the same time, fast-track the North Coast Transmission Line with Canadian steel, and start a fund from new oil and gas revenue.

Record and pledges: LNG Canada Phase 1 operating, Cedar and Woodfibre under construction, Phase 2, Tilbury Phase 2 and Ksi Lisims permitted, nearly 48 million tonnes of capacity by 2035, net-zero-ready by 2030 required (September 28 release); double critical mineral exports within five years with concurrent assessment and permitting and fixed exploration timelines, North Coast Transmission Line fast-tracked and Prince Rupert port expanded (September 28); 70% then 100% Canadian steel for the line (September 24); $50 million Clean Futures Fund from new oil and gas revenue (October 10).
This party would approve big projects within four months by law, double gas output, and drop emissions limits.

The Conservatives' Energy Superpower plan (September 28) would double gas production by 2032 and triple it by 2035, legislate 120-day permitting for projects over $250 million, end the emissions limits it says block investment beyond LNG Canada, replace the LNG carbon-tax framework, expedite Ksi Lisims, and put the North Coast Transmission Line on a fixed deadline.

BC Energy Superpower Plan (September 28, 2026): double LNG production by 2032 and triple by 2035; 120 Day Permitting Act for projects over $250 million; end emissions limits and replace the LNG carbon-tax framework with 'stable guidance'; competitive royalty framework; expedite Ksi Lisims; back Coastal GasLink phase 2 and Prince Rupert Gas Transmission; North Coast Transmission Line on a fixed deadline; gas plans with Treaty 8 nations; the Montney as a strategic asset. Skeena candidate Rattée welcomed Phase 2 (September 29).
This party would approve no new gas plants or pipelines, and allow mines only within ecological limits and strict rules.

The Greens would end approvals for new fracking expansion, LNG terminals and pipelines, manage a decline of existing production, end subsidies and collect 50% of net profits in royalties. Lowan said she was 'deeply disappointed' to see Phase 2 go ahead. The Greens would set ecological limits on where mining can happen and world-leading mining standards; public support for mineral processing would require First Nations participation, a long-term economic case and strong pollution standards.

Climate, LNG and Royalties Policy Brief (October 10, 2026): end approvals for new fracking expansion, LNG terminals and expansions and new fossil fuel pipelines; managed decline; end provincial subsidies; royalties reformed to 50% of net profits. Healthcare Policy Brief: an independent health impact assessment of LNG and fracking. Statement on Phase 2 (September 29): 'deeply disappointed to see LNG Canada Phase 2 move ahead', at most 150 permanent jobs. Economic Vision (October 7): ecological limits set before deciding where mining can occur, world-leading mining standards, critical minerals recycling, a value chain plan, and public support for processing and refining only with First Nations participation, a long-term economic case and strong pollution standards; no new large dams.
This party would set a one-year legal deadline for decisions, require First Nations partners and a zero-emissions plan, and decide on ten new mines.

CentreBC would back LNG projects 'that have First Nations partners and a credible plan to be net-zero ready, as BC requires', keep carbon pricing on large emitters, run one coordinated review with a 12-month provincial decision deadline, make permitting decisions on ten new mines by 2030, add 2,000 megawatts of BC Hydro supply and fund port roads and rail.

Platform (October 10, Economy and Affordability): back LNG with First Nations partners and a credible net-zero-ready plan; industrial carbon pricing kept, no consumer carbon tax; BC Hydro expanded by at least 2,000 megawatts by 2033; one coordinated review with a 12-month provincial decision deadline; permitting decisions on 10 new mines by 2030 and 3 processing facilities by 2032; $1.5 billion federal ask for Prince Rupert and Roberts Bank matched by $750 million provincial road and rail over five years; Canadian steel pressed for Phase 2.
This party would approve the projects and an oil pipeline to the coast without long consultations, and cut fees.

OneBC would approve a pipeline to the Port of Prince Rupert or Kitimat 'to get Canadian energy to foreign markets', push major projects through without consultations it says act as vetoes, cut fees and approval times for mining and forestry, and work with Alberta and Saskatchewan. It has no LNG-specific, emissions or transmission position.

Priorities page: 'Approve a pipeline to the Port of Prince Rupert or Kitimat to get Canadian energy to foreign markets'; speed up permit approvals and consultations for forestry. X (September 26): major projects approved without 'consultations' that act as vetoes. October 5 post: make forestry and mining competitive with lower fees and faster approvals. No position on LNG Canada Phase 2, Ksi Lisims, emissions rules, carbon pricing or the North Coast Transmission Line; option e combines the published items.
questions/q_local_north_er/prompt/1: Emergency rooms in northern towns keep closing for lack of staff. What would help most?
questions/q_local_north_er/prompt/2: Emergency rooms in Fort St. James, Chetwynd and Hudson's Hope keep closing for lack of staff. What would help most?
questions/q_local_north_er/prompt/3: Emergency rooms in Fort St. James, Chetwynd, Hudson's Hope and 100 Mile House keep closing for lack of staff. What comes first?
questions/q_local_north_er/prompt/4: Northeast BC had 115 hours of emergency and maternity closures in March 2026; 100 Mile House's emergency room closed 38 times by August. What comes first?
questions/q_local_north_er/prompt/5: Northern Health recorded 115 hours of emergency or maternity closures in the northeast in March 2026; Fort St. James closed again in May; Interior Health's 100 Mile House emergency room had closed 38 times by August 24. Which approach?
questions/q_local_north_er/context/1: In many northern towns the hospital emergency room shuts for hours or days because no doctor or nurse can staff it. People drive long distances for help. The province pays for hospitals and decides how to attract staff. Parties disagree on what would work fastest.
questions/q_local_north_er/context/2: Small northern hospitals closed their emergency rooms repeatedly in 2026 because of staff shortages, including Fort St. James, Hudson's Hope, Chetwynd and 100 Mile House. In March the northeast lost 115 hours of emergency and maternity care. The province has opened hospitals in Terrace and Fort St. James, but staffing them is the problem. Parties disagree on the fix.
questions/q_local_north_er/context/3: Northern Health reported 115 hours of emergency or maternity closures in northeast BC in March 2026, including 60 hours at Hudson's Hope, citing staffing. Fort St. James closed again on May 26, and 100 Mile House, in Interior Health, had closed 38 times by late August. The Conservatives launched a $50 million rural fund in 100 Mile House on October 5. CentreBC promises a closure-reporting law and a yearly fund. The NDP offers tuition and moving help for rural work and would phase out private agency nurses.
questions/q_local_north_er/context/4: Northern Health logged 115 hours of emergency or related closures in northeast BC in March 2026 (Hudson's Hope 60), citing staffing. Fort St. James closed again on May 26; Interior Health's 100 Mile House emergency room had closed 38 times by August 24. New hospitals opened in Terrace (2024), Fort St. James (2025) and Prince Rupert (2025), but staffing drives the closures. The Conservatives launched a $50 million rural practice fund with flexible staffing in 100 Mile House on October 5. CentreBC promises an accountability law and a $25 million a year fund. The NDP offers rural tuition, loan forgiveness and moving support, and would phase out private agency nurses (October 12). The Greens want community health centres; OneBC private care alongside public.
questions/q_local_north_er/context/5: Northern Health reported 115 hours of emergency or related closures in northeast BC in March 2026, including 60 at Hudson's Hope, with staffing the stated cause. Fort St. James closed again on May 26, and Interior Health's 100 Mile House emergency room had closed 38 times by August 24. The Conservatives pledge a $50 million rural practice fund, flexible staffing, automatic credential recognition and an expert commission (October 5, 100 Mile House); CentreBC an Emergency Room Accountability Act, halved unplanned closure hours by 2029/30, a $25 million a year fund and a permanent retention bonus; the NDP rural tuition discounts, loan forgiveness, moving costs and 1,000 nursing and care training seats (October 9) and a three-year phase-out of private agency nurses with savings to rural travel nurses (October 12); the Greens a community health centre per riding and a review toward a single authority; OneBC private care alongside public.
questions/q_local_north_er/options/a/tex: Make every closure public, set a target to cut them, and fund fill-in doctors.
Pass a law reporting every closure, aim to halve closure hours, and fund a pot for fill-in doctors and backup.
Legislate reporting of every closure, aim to halve closure hours by 2030, fund a rural pot for locums and backup, with permanent retention bonuses.
Publicly report every closure, halve unplanned closure hours by 2029/30, spend $25 million a year on rural locums and backup, and make the retention bonus permanent.

Enact an Emergency Room Accountability Act requiring public reporting of every closure, halve unplanned closure hours by 2029/30, fund a $25 million a year rural stabilization fund for locums, travel and virtual backup, and make the rural retention bonus permanent.
questions/q_local_north_er/options/b/tex: Set up an emergency fund for small-town clinics and emergency rooms about to close.
Create a $50 million emergency fund for rural practices at risk of closing, loosen staffing rules, and fast-track foreign-trained doctors.
Create a $50 million emergency fund for rural practices at risk of closing, allow flexible staffing, fast-track credentials, and appoint an expert commission.
Put $50 million into rural practices at risk of closing, allow flexible staffing, accept other provinces' credentials, hold health spending, and form an expert panel.

Create a $50 million emergency fund for rural medical practices at risk of closing, flexible staffing to prevent closures, automatic recognition of other provinces' credentials and faster recognition for Canadian doctors trained abroad, an expert commission within 100 days, and no cuts to the 2026 health budget.
questions/q_local_north_er/options/c/tex: Recruit more doctors with cheaper tuition, loan help and moving money for rural jobs.
Recruit: tuition discounts, loan forgiveness and moving costs for rural posts, more training seats, and a bridge for foreign-trained doctors.
Recruit staff through tuition discounts, loan forgiveness and moving costs for rural areas, 1,000 more nursing and care training seats, and a bridging program for international graduates.
Give rural health workers tuition discounts, loan forgiveness and moving costs, add 1,000 nursing and care seats, help foreign-trained doctors qualify, and open 20 team clinics.

Recruit through discounted tuition, loan forgiveness and moving expenses for health workers taking rural and emergency posts, 1,000 added training seats for nurses, nurse practitioners, allied health workers and care aides, a bridging-to-practice program for internationally trained doctors, 20 team-based primary care clinics, and eight MRI and ten CT scanners.
questions/q_local_north_er/options/d/tex: Open a public health centre in every area so fewer people need emergency rooms.
Open a community health centre in every riding, fund safe nurse-to-patient ratios, phase out private agency nurses, and keep care public.
Change the model: a community health centre in every riding, funding for safe nurse-to-patient ratios, an end to private agency nurses, a review toward one provincial health authority.
Fund a community health centre in every riding, fund nurse-to-patient ratios, phase out agency nurses, review a move to one health authority, and keep health dollars public.

Fund a Community Health Centre in every riding, increase funding for nurses to support safe nurse-to-patient ratios, phase out private agency nurses and for-profit staffing agencies, review the health authority model with a focus on one consolidated provincial authority, and keep every public health dollar in public care.
questions/q_local_north_er/options/e/tex: Allow private clinics beside public care, and rehire workers who left over vaccine rules.
Allow private health care alongside public care, and reinstate nurses who lost jobs over vaccine mandates, with back pay.
Allow private health care alongside public care, reinstate nurses removed under vaccine mandates with back pay, and shift administration spending to the front line.
Allow private care beside fully funded public care, reinstate nurses removed under vaccine mandates with back pay, and move admin spending to front-line staff.

Allow private health care alongside fully funded public care, reinstate nurses removed under vaccine mandates with back pay, shift administration and human resources spending to front-line staff, attract medical professionals, and repeal the Health Professions and Occupations Act.
questions/q_local_north_er/party_positio: This party is in charge now. It offers cheaper tuition and moving money to bring doctors to rural areas.

The NDP government opened new hospitals in Terrace, Fort St. James and Prince Rupert, but the closures happened under it. Its October 9 plan offers discounted tuition, loan forgiveness and moving costs for health workers in underserved rural areas, a bridging program for international graduates, 1,000 nursing and care training seats and 20 team-based clinics. On October 12 it pledged to phase out hospitals' reliance on private agency nurses over three years and put the savings into Go Health BC travel nurses for rural emergency rooms. No rural emergency fund or reporting law.

Record: Ksyen Regional Hospital (Terrace, November 2024), Stuart Lake Hospital (Fort St. James, January 2025), Prince Rupert emergency redevelopment (September 2025), the Prince George tower and Peace Villa under way; the 2026 closures occurred under its government. Pledges (October 9, 2026): discounted tuition, loan forgiveness and moving expenses for health workers in underserved rural areas, bridging to practice for international medical graduates, 1,000 added training seats for nurses, nurse practitioners, allied health workers and care aides, 20 team-based primary care clinics, more evening and weekend care. October 6: eight MRI and ten CT scanners. October 12: phase out hospitals' reliance on private agency nurses over three years by capping fees and hours, with the savings going to Go Health BC travel nurses for rural emergency rooms. No dedicated rural emergency fund and no closure-reporting law.
This party would set up an emergency fund to stop small-town emergency rooms from closing.

In 100 Mile House on October 5 the Conservatives pledged a $50 million emergency fund for rural medical practices at risk of closing, flexible staffing to avoid emergency and maternity closures, automatic recognition of other provinces' credentials, faster recognition for Canadian doctors trained abroad, priority for BC students in medical training, an expert commission within 100 days and no health cuts. They did not say whether the fund is one-time or yearly.

'Keep Emergency Rooms Open' (October 5, 2026, launched in 100 Mile House; release plus Doerkson's speech as reported by the 100 Mile Free Press): $50 million emergency fund for rural practices at risk of closing (one-time or recurring not stated), flexible staffing to prevent emergency and maternity closures, automatic recognition of other provinces' credentials and faster recognition for Canadian doctors trained abroad, priority for BC students in medical training, an expert commission within 100 days, the system kept universal and publicly funded, no cuts to the 2026 health budget. Former caucus member Kealy's call to replace Northern Health with local boards is his own, not party policy.
This party would open a public health centre in every area so fewer people need emergency rooms.

The Greens promise a Community Health Centre in every riding, safe nurse-to-patient ratios, an end to private agency nurses, a review toward one provincial health authority and 'every public health dollar in public care', plus a rural seniors strategy. They have no emergency room specific commitment; option d is their care model applied to the closures.

Community health centre pledge (October 6, 2026) and Healthcare Policy Brief: Community Health Centre in every riding, more funding for nurses to support safe nurse-to-patient ratios, phase-out of private agency nurses and for-profit staffing agencies, review of the health authority model 'with a focus on creating a consolidated health authority for the whole province', push back on 'the creeping privatization of healthcare', 'keep every public health dollar in public care', rural seniors strategy (October 4). Skeena candidate Gottlieb raised emergency closures at the Kitimat forum. No rural emergency fund or reporting commitment.
This party would make every closure public, set a target to cut them, and pay for fill-in doctors.

CentreBC's platform would cut unplanned emergency room closure hours in half by 2029/30, pass an accountability law with public reporting of every closure, fund a $25 million a year rural stabilization fund for locums, travel and virtual backup, make the rural retention bonus permanent for every community with repeated closures, and license doctors from other provinces within 30 days.

Platform (October 10, Health Care): Emergency Room Accountability Act with public reporting of every closure and a live open-or-closed dashboard; halve unplanned closure hours by 2029/30; $25 million a year rural stabilization fund for locums, nurses, travel and virtual backup; permanent rural retention bonus extended to every community with repeated closures; licensing of doctors and nurses from other provinces, the US, UK and Australia within 30 days; 100 more residency positions by 2030; 600 nurse practitioner positions; no private pay for essential care.
This party would allow private clinics beside public care and rehire workers who left over vaccine rules.

OneBC would allow private health care alongside fully funded public care, reinstate nurses it says were removed under COVID-era mandates with back pay, move administration spending to the front line and 'attract medical professionals'. It has no rural emergency room commitment.

Priorities page: private health care alongside fully funded public care, shift administration and human resources spending to front-line staff, repeal the Health Professions and Occupations Act. October 11 post and video: reinstate, with back pay, nurses and front-line health workers still out of work over COVID-era mandates. October 5 platform summary: reduce wait times, grow services and attract medical professionals. No rural or northern emergency room item; option e is the party's health model applied to the closures.

local/context/results_history/2024/note: Brar 9,923, Gill (Conservative) 9,170, Binnema (Green) 1,321; 20,414 valid votes; margin 753, per the Elections BC Statement of Votes. BC United ran no candidate.

how_to_vote/voting_day: Saturday, October 24, 2026, 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. Pacific time.
how_to_vote/advance_voting: Friday October 16 to Wednesday October 21, 2026, 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. local time. Not every location is open every day; check yours.
how_to_vote/mail_in: Request a vote-by-mail package online or by phone (1-800-661-8683) by October 18. Elections BC must receive it by 8 p.m. Pacific time on October 24 for it to be counted. If you are not registered or your voter information is out of date, prove your identity and address by uploading ID to Elections BC's ID upload system or by including photocopies of your ID with the returned package.
how_to_vote/eligibility: Canadian citizen, 18 or older on October 24, 2026, and a BC resident since April 23, 2026.
how_to_vote/id_rules: Prove identity and address one of three ways: (1) one government photo ID with your name and address (BC driver's licence, BCID, BC Services Card with photo, Certificate of Indian Status, or another government card with name, photo and address); (2) two documents with your name, at least one with your current address (electronic accepted, handwritten generally not); (3) someone vouches for you: a registered voter in your electoral district, a spouse, parent, grandparent, adult child, adult grandchild or adult sibling, or a person with authority to make personal care decisions for you. A voucher who is not a relative or personal care authority can vouch for only one voter, and you and the voucher each make a solemn declaration.
how_to_vote/where: Find advance and election-day locations with the voting-place lookup on elections.bc.ca. District electoral offices also take voters until 4 p.m. on October 24. The October 17 municipal election is a separate vote with its own locations.
how_to_vote/other_dates: Municipal elections October 17, 2026. Televised leaders' debate October 14 (Eby, Doerkson, Lowan). Final count November 6 to 10 (planned).

how_to_vote/kid_note/1: You must be 18 to vote. Younger people can still help their family think it through and go along to the voting place. Voting is private, so each person chooses whether to share how they voted.
